mdcat-b3-bio-33.explainHtml: PEP carboxylase has no oxygenase activity. It fixes CO₂ into 4-carbon oxaloacetate/malate, which is pumped into bundle sheath cells where CO₂ is concentrated around RuBisCO, eliminating photorespiration.

mdcat-b3-bio-34.qHtml: In the Krebs citric acid cycle, which single reaction generates high-energy nucleotide triphosphate by substrate-level phosphorylation?
optionsHtml: Conversion of succinyl-CoA to succinate by succinyl-CoA synthetase (generating GTP or ATP)
Condensation of acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate to form citrate
mdcat-b3-bio-34.explainHtml: Succinyl-CoA synthetase cleaves the high-energy thioester bond of succinyl-CoA to produce succinate, coupling the exergonic energy to phosphorylate GDP to GTP (or ADP to ATP).

mdcat-b3-bio-35.qHtml: During which phase of the eukaryotic cell cycle does semi-conservative replication of genomic DNA occur?
mdcat-b3-bio-35.explainHtml: The S phase (Synthesis phase) of interphase is dedicated to duplicating cellular DNA and synthesizing histones, ensuring sister chromatids are ready for mitosis.

mdcat-b3-bio-36.qHtml: In which stage of meiosis do homologous chromosome pairs align along the equatorial metaphase plate as bivalents (tetrads)?
mdcat-b3-bio-36.explainHtml: During Metaphase I of meiosis, paired homologous chromosomes (bivalents/tetrads) align at the spindle equator, with kinetochores of sister chromatids attached to the same pole.

mdcat-b3-bio-37.qHtml: What is the term for the failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate properly during meiotic cell division?
mdcat-b3-bio-37.explainHtml: Nondisjunction is the failure of homologous pairs (in anaphase I) or sister chromatids (in anaphase II) to segregate, producing aneuploid gametes (monosomy or trisomy).

mdcat-b3-bio-38.qHtml: During which sub-stage of Prophase I does genetic crossing over (reciprocal exchange of non-sister chromatid segments) take place?
mdcat-b3-bio-38.explainHtml: Prophase I stages: Leptotene (condensation), Zygotene (synapsis begins), Pachytene (crossing over occurs at recombination nodules), Diplotene (chiasmata visible), Diakinesis (terminalization).

mdcat-b3-bio-39.qHtml: What is the biological function of the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) during eukaryotic mitotic cell division?
optionsHtml: To prevent the onset of anaphase until all kinetochores are properly attached to microtubules and tension is established
To initiate nuclear envelope breakdown during early prophase
To trigger DNA replication during G1 phase
To phosphorylate histone H1 for chromosome condensation
mdcat-b3-bio-39.explainHtml: The SAC inhibits the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) via the mitotic checkpoint complex (Mad2/BubR1) until every kinetochore achieves bi-orientation on the spindle.

mdcat-b3-bio-40.qHtml: How does cytokinesis in dividing plant cells fundamentally differ from cytokinesis in animal cells?
optionsHtml: Plant cells construct a centrifugal cell plate via Golgi-derived vesicles fusing from the center outwards, whereas animal cells form a centripetal cleavage furrow via an actomyosin contractile ring
Plant cells pinch from the outside in using microfilaments
Plant cells do not divide their cytoplasm following mitosis
Plant cells dissolve the outer wall entirely prior to furrowing
mdcat-b3-bio-40.explainHtml: Rigid plant walls prevent furrowing; instead, phragmoplast microtubules guide Golgi vesicles carrying pectins to the center to form a centrifugal cell plate. Animals use a contractile actin-myosin ring.

mdcat-b3-bio-41.qHtml: Which molecular complex is ubiquitinated and degraded by the anaphase-promoting complex (APC/C) to trigger sister chromatid separation at anaphase onset?
optionsHtml: Securin (releasing active separase to cleave cohesin)
mdcat-b3-bio-41.explainHtml: APC/C targets securin for proteasomal degradation. Destruction of securin liberates active separase, an endopeptidase that cleaves the Scc1 subunit of cohesin complexes holding sister chromatids together.

mdcat-b3-bio-42.qHtml: In human female oogenesis, at which developmental meiotic stage are primary oocytes arrested from late fetal gestation until puberty?
optionsHtml: Diplotene stage of Prophase I (Dictyate stage)
mdcat-b3-bio-42.explainHtml: Primary oocytes begin meiosis during fetal life and arrest at the diplotene stage of Prophase I (the prolonged dictyate stage). Meiosis I resumes under the LH surge immediately prior to ovulation.

mdcat-b3-bio-43.qHtml: Which cellular organelle is responsible for synthesizing ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and assembling ribosomal subunit complexes in eukaryotes?
mdcat-b3-bio-43.explainHtml: The nucleolus is the dense non-membrane-bound nuclear structure where rRNA genes are transcribed by RNA polymerase I and processed, assembling with ribosomal proteins into 40S and 60S subunits.

mdcat-b3-bio-44.qHtml: Which membrane-bound organelle contains acid hydrolase enzymes operating at pH ~4.5–5.0 to degrade endocytosed macromolecules and cellular debris?
mdcat-b3-bio-44.explainHtml: Lysosomes contain over 50 acidic hydrolytic enzymes (proteases, nucleases, lipases, phosphatases) maintained at acidic pH by vacuolar H⁺-ATPases in their limiting membrane.

mdcat-b3-bio-45.qHtml: According to the fluid mosaic model proposed by Singer and Nicolson, what is the fundamental organization of the plasma membrane?
optionsHtml: A fluid lipid bilayer of amphipathic phospholipids with integral proteins embedded within and peripheral proteins loosely attached to the surface
A rigid solid sandwich of phospholipids enclosed on both sides by continuous protein sheets
A monolayer of neutral triacylglycerols covered by carbohydrate polymers
A static meshwork of cholesterol molecules lacking mobile proteins
mdcat-b3-bio-45.explainHtml: The fluid mosaic model describes membranes as a 2D fluid lipid bilayer with polar head groups facing aqueous environments and hydrophobic tails sequestered inside, with proteins floating dynamically like a mosaic.

mdcat-b3-bio-46.qHtml: Which cytoskeletal filament system composed of tubulin heterodimers forms the internal 9+2 axonemal architecture of eukaryotic cilia and flagella?
mdcat-b3-bio-46.explainHtml: Microtubules (composed of α- and β-tubulin heterodimers) form the 9+2 doublet axoneme of motile cilia and flagella, powered by ciliary dynein motor arms.

mdcat-b3-bio-47.qHtml: What is the primary function of the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) in eukaryotic cells?
optionsHtml: Synthesis, co-translational translocation, and folding of secretory, lysosomal, and integral membrane proteins
Detoxification of lipid-soluble drugs and synthesis of steroid hormones
Generation of ATP via oxidative phosphorylation
Synthesis of cellulose for the cell wall
mdcat-b3-bio-47.explainHtml: The RER is studded with ribosomes on its cytosolic face, directing nascent polypeptides containing N-terminal signal peptides into its lumen for folding, glycosylation, and transport to the Golgi.

mdcat-b3-bio-48.qHtml: Which organelle houses catalase to decompose potentially cytotoxic hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) generated during the β-oxidation of very long chain fatty acids?
mdcat-b3-bio-48.explainHtml: Peroxisomes contain flavin oxidases that produce H₂O₂ as a byproduct of oxidative catabolism, and abundant catalase which converts 2 H₂O₂ into 2 H₂O and O₂.

mdcat-b3-bio-49.qHtml: Which intercellular junction provides direct electrical and metabolic coupling between neighboring animal cells via hexameric connexon channels?
mdcat-b3-bio-49.explainHtml: Gap junctions consist of transmembrane protein complexes called connexons (composed of 6 connexin subunits) that align across extracellular space to form aqueous pores permitting ions and small metabolites (<1 kDa) to pass.

mdcat-b3-bio-50.qHtml: In eukaryotic vesicular trafficking, which coat protein complex mediates retrograde transport of vesicles from the cis-Golgi back to the rough endoplasmic reticulum?
mdcat-b3-bio-50.explainHtml: COPI-coated vesicles transport escaped ER resident proteins (bearing KDEL signals) and recycling membrane components backwards from the Golgi to the ER (retrograde pathway). COPII mediates anterograde ER-to-Golgi transport.

mdcat-b3-bio-51.qHtml: What is the standard resting membrane potential of a typical mammalian giant axon?
mdcat-b3-bio-51.explainHtml: The typical neuronal resting membrane potential is around -70 mV, maintained predominantly by high resting permeability to K⁺ via leak channels and the electrogenic Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump.

mdcat-b3-bio-52.qHtml: Which endocrine hormone produced by the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) stimulates uterine contractions during labor and milk ejection during lactation?
mdcat-b3-bio-52.explainHtml: Oxytocin is synthesized in the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei of the hypothalamus, stored and released by the posterior pituitary, stimulating myometrial contractions and myoepithelial milk letdown.

mdcat-b3-bio-53.qHtml: Which division of the autonomic nervous system mediates the catabolic "f-or-fl" physiological response during acute emergencies?
mdcat-b3-bio-53.explainHtml: The sympathetic nervous system triggers tachycardia, bronchodilation, pupillary mydriasis, glycogenolysis, and redistribution of blood flow to skeletal musculature during acute stress.

mdcat-b3-bio-54.qHtml: During the rapid depolarization phase of a neuronal action potential, which ion channels open?
optionsHtml: Voltage-gated sodium (Na⁺) channels open, causing rapid influx of Na⁺ down its electrochemical gradient
Voltage-gated potassium (K⁺) channels open, causing K⁺ influx
Calcium (Ca2⁺) pumps pump Ca2⁺ into the extracellular fluid
mdcat-b3-bio-54.explainHtml: Depolarization above threshold triggers rapid activation of m-gates in voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, driving an explosive influx of Na⁺ that drives membrane potential toward the sodium equilibrium potential (+60 mV).

mdcat-b3-bio-55.qHtml: How does saltatory conduction in myelinated nerve axons accelerate action potential propagation speed?
optionsHtml: The insulating myelin sheath forces action potentials to electrotonically jump between unmyelinated nodes of Ranvier
Myelin generates extra ATP along the axonal membrane
Myelin increases the total number of open potassium channels under the sheath
Action potentials travel through the interior core of the myelin sheath itself
mdcat-b3-bio-55.explainHtml: Myelin acts as an electrical insulator with low capacitance and high resistance. Local currents spread rapidly beneath the internode, regenerating action potentials only at the clustered Na⁺ channels of nodes of Ranvier.

mdcat-b3-bio-56.qHtml: What is the endocrine role of calcitonin secreted by the parafollicular (C-cells) of the thyroid gland?
optionsHtml: It lowers elevated blood calcium levels by inhibiting osteoclastic bone resorption and promoting renal calcium excretion
It elevates blood calcium levels by activating osteoclasts
It stimulates dietary calcium absorption in the duodenum
It stimulates the synthesis of active 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol
mdcat-b3-bio-56.explainHtml: Calcitonin is released in response to hypercalcemia. It acts as an antagonist to parathyroid hormone (PTH), inhibiting osteoclast activity and reducing bone calcium mobilization.

mdcat-b3-bio-57.qHtml: What is the precise molecular trigger that induces exocytic fusion of synaptic vesicles with the presynaptic active zone membrane?
optionsHtml: Influx of extracellular Ca2⁺ through voltage-gated calcium channels upon action potential arrival, binding to synaptotagmin-1
Efflux of intracellular K⁺ through delayed rectifier channels
Direct electrical spark across the synaptic cleft
Depletion of presynaptic neurotransmitter reuptake transporters
mdcat-b3-bio-57.explainHtml: Depolarization opens presynaptic voltage-gated N- or P/Q-type Ca2⁺ channels. Calcium binds to the calcium-sensor synaptotagmin, triggering complete zippering of the SNARE complex (syntaxin, SNAP-25, synaptobrevin) and neurotransmitter exocytosis.

mdcat-b3-bio-58.qHtml: In the molecular mechanism of steroid hormone signaling, where do steroid receptors predominantly reside and how do they alter cellular physiology?
optionsHtml: Inside the cytoplasm or nucleus; the hormone-receptor complex acts as a ligand-activated transcription factor binding hormone response elements (HREs) on genomic DNA
On the outer surface of plasma membranes as G-protein coupled receptors activating cAMP
Inside lysosomes where they digest ingested proteins
Inside the mitochondrial matrix activating electron transport enzymes directly
mdcat-b3-bio-58.explainHtml: Lipophilic steroids diffuse across the plasma membrane, bind intracellular nuclear receptors, dimerize, translocate to the nucleus, and bind specific HREs on DNA to regulate mRNA transcription.

mdcat-b3-bio-59.qHtml: Which hypothalamic nuclei synthesize antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) and monitor plasma osmolality via central osmoreceptors?
mdcat-b3-bio-59.explainHtml: Magnocellular neurosecretory cells in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus synthesize ADH and oxytocin. ADH is transported via axonal tracts down the infundibulum to the posterior pituitary.

mdcat-b3-bio-60.qHtml: Which animal phylum is characterized by a water vascular (ambulacral) system, pentaradial symmetry in adults, and tube feet?
mdcat-b3-bio-60.explainHtml: Echinoderms (e.g., starfish, sea urchins) feature a water vascular system operating hydraulic tube feet, a mesodermal calcified endoskeleton, and secondary pentaradial symmetry.

mdcat-b3-bio-61.qHtml: Which phylum possesses a metamerically segmented chitinous exoskeleton that must be periodically shed by ecdysis (molting)?
mdcat-b3-bio-61.explainHtml: Arthropoda is the largest phylum, characterized by a rigid chitinous exoskeleton, jointed appendages, and ecdysis controlled by hormones such as ecdysone.

mdcat-b3-bio-62.qHtml: Which class of chordates is characterized by possessing mammary glands, hair (fur), and three middle ear ossicles (malleus, incus, and stapes)?
mdcat-b3-bio-62.explainHtml: Mammals are unique in possessing milk-producing mammary glands, keratinaceous body hair, three middle ear ossicles derived from ancestral jaw bones, and a muscular diaphragm.

mdcat-b3-bio-63.qHtml: How does an acoelomate animal (such as a flatworm of Phylum Platyhelminthes) differ anatomically from a coelomate animal?
optionsHtml: It completely lacks a secondary fluid-filled body cavity between the gut and body wall, with the intervening space filled with mesodermal parenchyma tissue
It has a body cavity completely lined by mesodermal peritoneum
It possesses a pseudocoel derived from the persistent embryonic blastocoel
It has an open circulatory system with a hemocoel
mdcat-b3-bio-63.explainHtml: Acoelomates (Platyhelminthes) have no true body cavity (coelom); solid mesodermal parenchyma tissue fills the space between the ectoderm and endoderm.

mdcat-b3-bio-64.qHtml: What is the diagnostic anatomical characteristic of Phylum Cnidaria used for prey capture and defense?
optionsHtml: Cnidocytes containing specialized stinging organelles called nematocysts
mdcat-b3-bio-64.explainHtml: Cnidarians (hydra, jellyfish, corals) possess cnidocytes containing barbed, venom-filled stinging capsules called nematocysts that discharge upon tactile stimulation.

mdcat-b3-bio-65.qHtml: Which of the following is a key developmental feature distinguishing deuterostomes (e.g., Chordates, Echinoderms) from protostomes (e.g., Arthropods, Mollusks)?
optionsHtml: In deuterostomes, the embryonic blastopore develops into the anus, and cleavage is radial and indeterminate
In deuterostomes, the blastopore develops directly into the mouth
Deuterostomes exhibit spiral, determinate embryonic cleavage
Deuterostomes form their coelom exclusively by schizocoely
mdcat-b3-bio-65.explainHtml: In deuterostomes ("second mouth"), the blastopore becomes the anus while the mouth forms secondarily, accompanied by radial indeterminate cleavage and enterocoelous coelom development.

mdcat-b3-bio-66.qHtml: What anatomical adaptation in birds (Class Aves) allows continuous, unidirectional airflow through the parabronchial lungs during both inhalation and exhalation?
optionsHtml: An interconnected system of anterior and posterior air sacs functioning as bellows
A muscular diaphragm that pulls the lung bases downwards
Blind-ended alveoli that expand during inspiration
Spiracles connecting directly to systemic blood vessels
mdcat-b3-bio-66.explainHtml: Avian respiratory anatomy includes non-vascular air sacs acting as bellows, moving air unidirectionally through rigid, tubular parabronchi in a two-cycle flow that enables continuous countercurrent gas exchange.

mdcat-b3-bio-67.qHtml: Which larval form with bilateral symmetry provides crucial phylogenetic evidence linking non-chordate Echinoderms to primitive Hemichordates and Chordates?
mdcat-b3-bio-67.explainHtml: The tornaria larva of hemichordates closely resembles the bipinnaria/dipleurula larva of echinoderms, exhibiting ciliated bands and enterocoely that affirm their common deuterostome ancestry.

mdcat-b3-bio-68.qHtml: Which primitive egg-laying (oviparous) mammalian order includes the platypus and echidna, retaining reptilian-like cloacal anatomy?
mdcat-b3-bio-68.explainHtml: Monotremes are primitive prototherian mammals that lay leathery eggs, possess a cloaca, lack teats (milk secretes onto abdominal fur), but possess hair and produce milk.

mdcat-b3-bio-69.qHtml: How do enzymes accelerate the rate of chemical reactions in biological systems?
optionsHtml: By lowering the activation energy barrier required to reach the transition state
By shifting the equilibrium constant (Keq) towards products
By increasing the total internal free energy of the substrate molecules
By raising the physiological temperature of the intracellular medium
mdcat-b3-bio-69.explainHtml: Enzymes stabilize transition states via catalytic interactions at the active site, thereby decreasing the free energy of activation (ΔG‡) without altering the net free energy change (ΔG) or equilibrium constant.

mdcat-b3-bio-70.qHtml: What is the non-protein, tightly and permanently bound organic prosthetic group essential for the catalytic activity of certain conjugated enzymes (holoenzymes)?
mdcat-b3-bio-70.explainHtml: A prosthetic group is a non-amino acid component (such as heme, FAD, or biotin) that is firmly and covalently or coordination-bound to the apoenzyme protein.

mdcat-b3-bio-71.qHtml: In competitive enzyme inhibition, how are the kinetic parameters Km (Michaelis constant) and Vmax (maximum reaction velocity) altered in the presence of the inhibitor?
optionsHtml: Apparent Km increases, while Vmax remains unchanged
Both Km and Vmax decrease proportionally
Km remains unchanged, while Vmax decreases
mdcat-b3-bio-71.explainHtml: Competitive inhibitors bind reversibly to the active site, competing with substrate. High substrate concentrations displace the inhibitor, reaching original Vmax, but requiring higher [S] (increased apparent Km).

mdcat-b3-bio-72.qHtml: According to Daniel Koshland's induced fit model of enzymatic action, how does an enzyme interact with its substrate?
optionsHtml: Substrate binding induces precise conformational remodeling of the active site to optimize catalytic alignment
The active site is a rigid, pre-formed geometric template matching the substrate like a lock and key
The enzyme unfolds entirely before contacting the substrate
The substrate alters its covalent bonds before approaching the active site
mdcat-b3-bio-72.explainHtml: The induced fit hypothesis states that initial substrate binding induces dynamic conformational changes in the enzyme protein, molding the active site residues into optimal catalytic orientation around the transition state.

mdcat-b3-bio-73.qHtml: What type of enzyme inhibition occurs when an inhibitor binds exclusively to an allosteric regulatory site away from the active site, whether or not substrate is bound?
mdcat-b3-bio-73.explainHtml: In pure non-competitive inhibition, the inhibitor binds an allosteric site on both free enzyme (E) and enzyme-substrate complex (ES) with equal affinity, lowering catalytic efficiency (decreasing Vmax) without altering substrate affinity (Km unchanged).

mdcat-b3-bio-74.qHtml: In the catalytic triad of serine proteases (such as chymotrypsin and trypsin), which three amino acid residues collaborate to generate the nucleophilic alkoxide ion on serine?
mdcat-b3-bio-74.explainHtml: The catalytic triad consists of Asp102, His57, and Ser195. Aspartate polarizes histidine, which acts as a general base to deprotonate the hydroxyl of serine, creating a potent nucleophile to attack the peptide carbonyl carbon.

mdcat-b3-bio-75.qHtml: On a Lineweaver-Burk double reciprocal plot (1/V versus 1/[S]), what does the intercept on the horizontal axis (-1/Km) represent?
optionsHtml: Negative reciprocal of the Michaelis constant (-1/Km)
mdcat-b3-bio-75.explainHtml: The Lineweaver-Burk equation is 1/V = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax. When 1/V = 0, 1/[S] = -1/Km (the x-intercept), whereas the y-intercept is 1/Vmax.

mdcat-b3-bio-76.qHtml: Which diagnostic enzyme biomarker exhibits a steep elevation in serum within 4–8 hours following acute myocardial infarction and remains elevated for up to 10–14 days?
mdcat-b3-bio-76.explainHtml: Cardiac troponins (cTnI and cTnT) are highly sensitive and specific regulatory proteins/enzymatic markers released upon myocardial necrosis, peaking at 24 hours and persisting for up to 10-14 days.

mdcat-b3-bio-77.qHtml: What is the primary mechanism of gaseous exchange (O₂ and CO₂) across the respiratory alveolar-capillary membrane?
optionsHtml: Simple passive diffusion down partial pressure gradients
Active transport driven by ATP hydrolysis
mdcat-b3-bio-77.explainHtml: Respiratory gases dissolve in lipid bilayers and cross alveolar epithelial and endothelial cell membranes by simple passive diffusion governed by Fick's law.

mdcat-b3-bio-78.qHtml: In what chemical form is the majority (approximately 70%) of carbon dioxide transported in human systemic venous blood?
optionsHtml: Bicarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻) dissolved in blood plasma
Carbaminohemoglobin bound to globin amino groups
Physically dissolved CO₂ gas in plasma
mdcat-b3-bio-78.explainHtml: About 70% of CO₂ is converted by erythrocyte carbonic anhydrase into carbonic acid, which dissociates into H⁺ and bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻), which is transported in plasma via the chloride shift.

mdcat-b3-bio-79.qHtml: Which specialized pulmonary cells synthesize and secrete dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) surfactant to reduce alveolar surface tension and prevent atelectasis?
mdcat-b3-bio-79.explainHtml: Type II pneumocytes are cuboidal alveolar cells that produce pulmonary surfactant (DPPC and surfactant apoproteins SP-A, B, C, D) to prevent end-expiratory alveolar collapse.

mdcat-b3-bio-80.qHtml: What is the physiological phenomenon known as the Bohr effect in respiratory physiology?
optionsHtml: Decreased pH (acidosis) and increased pCO₂ reduce hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, shifting the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the r
Increased pO₂ promotes CO₂ unloading from hemoglobin
Hypothermia enhances oxygen unloading in peripheral muscles
Carbon monoxide binds irreversibly to hemoglobin
mdcat-b3-bio-80.explainHtml: The Bohr effect describes the rightward shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve in metabolically active tissues due to high pCO₂, low pH, and elevated temperature, facilitating O₂ delivery.

mdcat-b3-bio-81.qHtml: What occurs during the chloride shift (Hamburger phenomenon) when venous blood traverses systemic capillary beds?
optionsHtml: Bicarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻) diffuse out of erythrocytes into plasma, while chloride ions (Cl⁻) diffuse into erythrocytes via band 3 anion exchangers
Chloride ions diffuse out of erythrocytes while bicarbonate enters
Sodium ions leave erythrocytes to balance extracellular potassium
Hydrogen ions are pumped out of erythrocytes into the interstitium
mdcat-b3-bio-81.explainHtml: As carbonic anhydrase generates HCO₃⁻ inside RBCs, the accumulating bicarbonate exits into plasma down its gradient in exchange for extracellular Cl⁻ entering the RBC via the Band 3 antiporter, maintaining electrical neutrality.

mdcat-b3-bio-82.qHtml: Where are the central chemoreceptors located and what is their primary physiological chemical stimulus for driving ventilation?
optionsHtml: Ventral surface of the medulla oblongata; responding to hydrogen ion (H⁺) concentration in brain cerebrospinal fluid derived from arterial CO₂
Aortic arch; responding directly to arterial partial pressure of oxygen (pO₂)
Carotid sinus; responding to blood pressure oscillations
Pulmonary parenchyma; responding to lung inflation stretch
mdcat-b3-bio-82.explainHtml: Central chemoreceptors in the ventrolateral medulla respond to H⁺ in cerebrospinal fluid. CO₂ diffuses across the blood-brain barrier and forms carbonic acid, liberating H⁺ that directly stimulates respiratory motor drive.

mdcat-b3-bio-83.qHtml: What is the Haldane effect and how does it facilitate pulmonary carbon dioxide excretion?
optionsHtml: Deoxygenation of hemoglobin increases its affinity for CO₂ and H⁺, whereas oxygenation in pulmonary capillaries promotes CO₂ unloading
Elevated oxygen levels stimulate red blood cell carbonic anhydrase synthesis
Bicarbonate ions are actively pumped into the alveolar lumen
Hemoglobin undergoes conformational denaturation at high alveolar pO₂
mdcat-b3-bio-83.explainHtml: The Haldane effect describes how binding of O₂ to hemoglobin in lung capillaries alters its conformation, weakening carbamino bonds and proton affinity, causing rapid unloading of CO₂ and release of H⁺ to drive bicarbonate back into CO₂.

mdcat-b3-bio-84.qHtml: In chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with severe emphysema, what pathophysiological alteration primarily compromises alveolar gas transfer capacity?
optionsHtml: Destruction of alveolar septal walls reducing effective surface area, combined with loss of elastance causing air trapping
Hypertrophy of type II pneumocytes secreting excess surfactant
Severe proliferation of pulmonary capillary beds
Excessive ciliary motility in terminal bronchioles
mdcat-b3-bio-84.explainHtml: Emphysema involves protease-mediated (elastase) destruction of interalveolar septa, drastically diminishing surface area for gas diffusion and destroying elastic recoil, leading to expiratory airflow obstruction and gas trapping.

mdcat-b3-bio-85.qHtml: What is Mendel's law of segregation?
optionsHtml: The two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation so that each gamete carries only one allele
Alleles of different genes assort completely independently into gametes
Dominant alleles always suppress recessive traits in all subsequent generations
Linked genes on the same chromosome never separate during meiosis
mdcat-b3-bio-85.explainHtml: Mendel's first law (law of segregation) states that during meiosis, the two homologous alleles for a locus segregate into separate gametes, restoring diploid status upon fertilization.

mdcat-b3-bio-86.qHtml: In human ABO blood group genetics, which pair of alleles demonstrates codominance when co-inherited?
optionsHtml: Allele IA and Allele I^{B}
Allele IA and Allele i
Allele IB and Allele i
mdcat-b3-bio-86.explainHtml: Alleles IA and IB both encode active glycosyltransferases, resulting in simultaneous expression of both A and B erythrocyte surface antigens in individuals with genotype IAIB (type AB blood).

mdcat-b3-bio-87.qHtml: A man with hemophilia A (an X-linked recessive coagulopathy) marries a phenotypically normal woman whose father had hemophilia A. What is the probability that their first child will have hemophilia A?
mdcat-b3-bio-87.explainHtml: Father is Xh Y. Mother is an obligate carrier XHXh (received Xh from her father). Possible children: XHXh (carrier daughter), XhXh (affected daughter), XH Y (normal son), Xh Y (affected son). Exactly 2 of 4 (50%) will have hemophilia A.

mdcat-b3-bio-88.qHtml: In a dihybrid cross between two heterozygous pea plants (RrYy × RrYy), what phenotypic ratio is expected in the F2 generation under independent assortment?
mdcat-b3-bio-88.explainHtml: For two independently assorting unlinked autosomal genes with complete dominance, the classic Mendelian F2 dihybrid phenotypic ratio is 9 (dominant/dominant) : 3 (dominant/recessive) : 3 (recessive/dominant) : 1 (recessive/recessive).

mdcat-b3-bio-89.qHtml: What genetic phenomenon occurs when a single gene mutation produces multiple seemingly unrelated phenotypic effects across diverse organ systems (e.g., Marfan syndrome)?
mdcat-b3-bio-89.explainHtml: Pleiotropy describes a situation where one gene affects multiple organ systems. A mutation in the fibrillin-1 (FBN1) gene causes ocular ectopia lentis, aortic dissection, and skeletal tall stature in Marfan syndrome.

mdcat-b3-bio-90.qHtml: In Drosophila, two genes are 18 map units (centimorgans, cM) apart on the same autosome. In a testcross between a heterozygous female (in coupling phase, AB/ab) and a homozygous recessive male (ab/ab), what percentage of recombinant offspring (Ab or aB) is expected?
mdcat-b3-bio-90.explainHtml: By definition, 1 map unit (1 cM) equals 1% recombination frequency. Therefore, 18 cM distance yields a total recombinant progeny frequency of 18% (9% Ab and 9% aB).

mdcat-b3-bio-91.qHtml: What is the precise molecular consequence of the single nucleotide point mutation in the β-globin gene that causes sickle cell anemia?
optionsHtml: A transversion of GAG to GTG in codon 6, substituting non-polar valine for charged hydrophilic glutamate
A transition substituting lysine for arginine at codon 12
A frameshift insertion creating a premature termination stop codon
A deletion of codon 508 resulting in defective folding
mdcat-b3-bio-91.explainHtml: Sickle cell mutation is a single base transversion (A→T in the GAG codon) at position 6 of the β-globin chain, substituting hydrophobic valine for acidic glutamate, leading to deoxygenated polymer formation.

mdcat-b3-bio-92.qHtml: What is the chromosomal karyotype associated with Klinefelter syndrome in humans, and what is its primary clinical feature?
optionsHtml: 47,XXY; phenotypic male with hypogonadism, azoospermia, gynecomastia, and elevated gonadotropins
45,X; phenotypic female with webbed neck and streak ovaries
mdcat-b3-bio-92.explainHtml: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) results from meiotic nondisjunction of sex chromosomes. Patients are phenotypic males characterized by testicular dysgenesis, eunuchoid body habitus, gynecomastia, and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.

mdcat-b3-bio-93.qHtml: What is the functional microscopic filtration unit of the human kidney?
mdcat-b3-bio-93.explainHtml: The nephron is the structural and functional filtration unit of the kidney, consisting of a renal corpuscle (glomerulus and Bowman's capsule) and a tubular system.

mdcat-b3-bio-94.qHtml: Which endocrine hormone secreted by the adrenal cortex increases renal tubular sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct?
mdcat-b3-bio-94.explainHtml: Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid released from the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex that upregulates basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPases and apical ENaC channels in principal cells to retain Na⁺ and excrete K⁺.

mdcat-b3-bio-95.qHtml: Which physiological homeostatic mechanism acts to restore an internal parameter back towards its set point when an initial perturbation is detected?
mdcat-b3-bio-95.explainHtml: Negative feedback operates by detecting a deviation from an internal set point (via sensors) and triggering effector responses that counteract and reverse the direction of change (e.g., thermoregulation, blood glucose).

mdcat-b3-bio-96.qHtml: In the mammalian nephron, where does the majority (approximately 65–70%) of filtered water, sodium, and 100% of filtered glucose and amino acids undergo reabsorption?
optionsHtml: Descending limb of loop of Henle
Ascending thick limb of loop of Henle
mdcat-b3-bio-96.explainHtml: The proximal convoluted tubule possesses dense microvillar brush borders and high metabolic capacity, reabsorbing ~67% of filtered NaCl and water, and virtually 100% of filtered glucose and amino acids via secondary active Na⁺-cotransport.

mdcat-b3-bio-97.qHtml: What is the countercurrent multiplier mechanism in the juxtamedullary nephrons and what is its primary function?
optionsHtml: A hyperosmotic medullary concentration gradient established by differential permeability and active NaCl transport in Henle's loop, enabling urinary concentration
Passive filtration of proteins across glomerular capillaries
Isotonic reabsorption of potassium in the distal tubule
Excretion of excessive urea into the renal cortex
mdcat-b3-bio-97.explainHtml: The countercurrent multiplier uses water-permeable descending limbs and water-impermeable active NaCl-pumping ascending thick limbs to generate an osmotic gradient in the medullary interstitium (up to 1200 mOsm/L).

mdcat-b3-bio-98.qHtml: How does antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) increase water reabsorption in renal medullary collecting ducts at the cellular level?
optionsHtml: It binds V2 basolateral receptors, activating cAMP to trigger exocytic insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane
It directly stimulates primary active pumping of water molecules across cell membranes
It opens large paracrine gap junctions between adjacent collecting duct cells
It degrades sodium-potassium ATPases in the tubule lining
mdcat-b3-bio-98.explainHtml: Vasopressin binds Gs-coupled V2 receptors on principal cells, stimulating adenylyl cyclase/cAMP/PKA signaling to induce fusion of aquaporin-2-bearing vesicles into the luminal apical membrane, rendering it water-permeable.

mdcat-b3-bio-99.qHtml: What are the macula densa cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus and what is their sensory role in renal autoregulation?
optionsHtml: Specialized epithelial cells in the early distal tubule that sense luminal NaCl delivery and signal juxtaglomerular cells to modulate renin secretion and afferent arteriolar resistance
Modified smooth muscle cells in afferent arterioles that secrete erythropoietin
Podocytes lining the parietal layer of Bowman's capsule
Endocrine cells of the adrenal medulla releasing catecholamines
mdcat-b3-bio-99.explainHtml: Macula densa cells monitor luminal Na⁺ and Cl⁻ flow rate. Decreased NaCl delivery signals juxtaglomerular granular cells to secrete renin and dilates afferent arterioles to maintain glomerular filtration rate.

mdcat-b3-bio-100.qHtml: In the hepatic urea cycle, which initial mitochondrial enzyme condenses ammonia and bicarbonate to form carbamoyl phosphate, consuming 2 molecules of ATP?
mdcat-b3-bio-100.explainHtml: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS-I) catalyzes the rate-limiting committed step of the hepatic urea cycle in the mitochondrial matrix: NH₄⁺ + HCO₃⁻ + 2 ATP → carbamoyl phosphate + 2 ADP + Pi (allosterically activated by N-acetylglutamate).

mdcat-b3-bio-101.qHtml: Which digestive endopeptidase is secreted in an inactive zymogen form by the chief cells of the gastric mucosa?
mdcat-b3-bio-101.explainHtml: Gastric chief cells secrete inactive pepsinogen, which is cleaved into active pepsin in the presence of acidic gastric juice (pH 1.5–2.0 produced by parietal cell HCl).

mdcat-b3-bio-102.qHtml: Which plant hormone is primarily responsible for promoting apical dominance by inhibiting the outgrowth of lateral axillary buds?
mdcat-b3-bio-102.explainHtml: Auxin synthesized in the apical shoot tip moves basipetally in the stem and suppresses the growth of lateral axillary buds, maintaining vertical shoot dominance.

mdcat-b3-bio-103.qHtml: Which plant vascular tissue is specialized for the bidirectional translocation of photosynthesized organic assimilates (sucrose)?
mdcat-b3-bio-103.explainHtml: Phloem consists of living sieve tube elements and companion cells responsible for translocating organic photoassimilates (mainly sucrose) from sources to sinks.

mdcat-b3-bio-104.qHtml: What is the functional role of bile salts (such as sodium glycocholate and sodium taurocholate) in dietary lipid digestion?
optionsHtml: Emulsifying dietary fat globules into tiny micro-droplets, dramatically expanding surface area for pancreatic lipase action
Hydrolyzing triglycerides directly into fatty acids and glycerol
Neutralizing gastric pepsin without interacting with lipids
mdcat-b3-bio-104.explainHtml: Bile salts are amphipathic detergents that disperse large dietary triglyceride droplets into microscopic emulsion droplets, dramatically accelerating enzymatic hydrolysis by pancreatic lipase and colipase.

mdcat-b3-bio-105.qHtml: Which phytohormone is commonly termed the "plant stress hormone" because it induces rapid stomatal closure during drought stress?
mdcat-b3-bio-105.explainHtml: Under water deficit, roots synthesize abscisic acid (ABA), which translocates via xylem to leaves, binding guard cell receptors to trigger potassium and anion efflux, causing guard cell turgor loss and stomatal closure.

mdcat-b3-bio-106.qHtml: In the small intestine, how are dietary monosaccharides D-glucose and D-galactose absorbed across the apical brush-border membrane of enterocytes?
optionsHtml: Secondary active transport coupled to the sodium gradient via SGLT1 (sodium-glucose cotransporter 1)
Simple passive diffusion across the phospholipid bilayer
Primary active transport driven by a dedicated glucose-cleaving ATPase
mdcat-b3-bio-106.explainHtml: SGLT1 transports 2 Na⁺ ions down their steep electrochemical gradient into the enterocyte, symporting 1 glucose or galactose against its concentration gradient into the cytoplasm.

mdcat-b3-bio-107.qHtml: According to Ernst Münch's pressure flow hypothesis, what thermodynamic process generates high hydrostatic turgor pressure at the photosynthesizing source tissue?
optionsHtml: Active phloem loading of sucrose into sieve tubes lowers water potential, causing osmotic influx of water from adjacent xylem vessels
Active pumping of water directly into phloem tubes by ATP-driven water pumps
Transpirational pull suctioning sap backwards from the roots
Enzymatic evaporation of phloem sap inside leaves
mdcat-b3-bio-107.explainHtml: Proton-coupled sucrose symport concentrates sucrose into sieve tube elements at the source. This osmotic loading draws water in from the xylem, generating elevated hydrostatic turgor pressure that drives bulk flow towards sinks.

mdcat-b3-bio-108.qHtml: What is the role of enteropeptidase (enterokinase) anchored to the brush-border membrane of duodenal enterocytes?
optionsHtml: It converts pancreatic trypsinogen into active trypsin, initiating a proteolytic activation cascade
It digests dietary cellulose into glucose monomers
It hydrolyzes maltose into two glucose units
mdcat-b3-bio-108.explainHtml: Enteropeptidase cleaves the N-terminal hexapeptide from trypsinogen to liberate active trypsin. Trypsin then autocatalytically activates more trypsinogen as well as chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, and procarboxypeptidases.

mdcat-b3-bio-109.qHtml: Where does fertilization (fusion of spermatozoon and secondary oocyte) typically take place in the human female reproductive tract?
mdcat-b3-bio-109.explainHtml: Fertilization normally occurs in the ampulla, which is the widest and longest section of the fallopian (uterine) tube.

mdcat-b3-bio-110.qHtml: Which endocrine hormone secreted by the developing syncytiotrophoblast maintains the corpus luteum and prevents menstruation during early pregnancy?
mdcat-b3-bio-110.explainHtml: Syncytiotrophoblast cells of the blastocyst secrete hCG, which shares structural homology with LH, sustaining corpus luteum progesterone secretion during the first trimester.

mdcat-b3-bio-111.qHtml: In the male testis, which cells are stimulated by luteinizing hormone (LH) to synthesize and secrete testosterone?
mdcat-b3-bio-111.explainHtml: Leydig cells reside in the interstitial connective tissue between seminiferous tubules and express LH receptors, synthesizing testosterone from cholesterol.

mdcat-b3-bio-112.qHtml: What is the physiological hormonal trigger that precipitates ovulation (rupture of the mature Graafian follicle) on approximately day 14 of the human menstrual cycle?
optionsHtml: A sharp pre-ovulatory luteinizing hormone (LH) surge triggered by high sustained estrogen positive feedback
A precipitous plunge in circulating progesterone levels
A sudden surge in human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)
Complete suppression of pituitary gonadotropin synthesis
mdcat-b3-bio-112.explainHtml: When late follicular estradiol levels exceed 200 pg/mL for over 48 hours, negative feedback switches to positive feedback on the anterior pituitary, triggering the massive LH surge that induces ovulation within 24–36 hours.

mdcat-b3-bio-113.qHtml: What are Sertoli cells and which crucial physiological barrier do they establish within the seminiferous epithelium?
optionsHtml: Somatic nurse cells connected by t junctions forming the blood-testis barrier to protect haploid germ cells from autoimmune attack
Endocrine cells secreting testosterone into testicular capillaries
Motile cells transporting mature sperm through the rete testis
Contractile myofibroblasts squeezing sperm out of the epididymis
mdcat-b3-bio-113.explainHtml: Sertoli cells nourish developing spermatogenic cells. Intercellular t junctions near their bases establish the blood-testis barrier, sequestering post-meiotic antigens from systemic circulating antibodies.

mdcat-b3-bio-114.qHtml: What is the acrosome reaction in mammalian fertilization?
optionsHtml: Exocytosis of hydrolytic enzymes (hyaluronidase and acrosin) from the sperm head upon binding to zona pellucida glycoprotein ZP3
The initial swimming movement of sperm in seminal fluid
Fusion of male and female pronuclei
Depolarization of the sperm tail flagellar axoneme
mdcat-b3-bio-114.explainHtml: Binding to ZP3 on the zona pellucida triggers Ca2⁺ influx and exocytosis of the acrosomal cap, releasing acrosin and hyaluronidase to digest a path through the zona pellucida.

mdcat-b3-bio-115.qHtml: How does the cortical reaction establish the permanent "slow block" to polyspermy upon single sperm penetration?
optionsHtml: Intracellular Ca2⁺ wave triggers exocytosis of cortical granules, releasing proteases that cleave ZP3 and crosslink the zona pellucida (zona reaction)
Immediate reversal of oocyte resting potential from -70 mV to +20 mV via sodium influx
Immediate expulsion of the sperm pronucleus by active transport
mdcat-b3-bio-115.explainHtml: Sperm-egg fusion triggers a cytosolic Ca2⁺ wave, driving cortical granule exocytosis. Cortical enzymes cleave ZP receptors and harden the zona pellucida, forming an impenetrable barrier to further sperm (slow block).

mdcat-b3-bio-116.qHtml: In angiosperm plant reproduction, what is the process of "double fertilization"?
optionsHtml: One sperm nucleus fertilizes the egg cell to form a diploid (2n) zygote, while the second sperm nucleus fuses with two polar nuclei to form a triploid (3n) endosperm
Two sperm cells fertilize two separate egg cells in the same ovule
A pollen tube delivers sperm to two different flowers simultaneously
Fertilization occurs twice in successive generations
mdcat-b3-bio-116.explainHtml: Double fertilization is unique to angiosperms: one haploid sperm nucleus fuses with the haploid egg to form the diploid zygote (2n), while the second sperm fuses with the diploid central cell (two polar nuclei) to form the triploid endosperm (3n).

mdcat-b3-bio-117.qHtml: During embryonic development, which extraembryonic membrane directly encloses the fluid-filled amniotic cavity that cushions the embryo from mechanical concussions?
mdcat-b3-bio-117.explainHtml: The amnion is the innermost extraembryonic membrane enclosing the fetus in amniotic fluid, which provides mechanical shock absorption, maintains uniform temperature, and allows symmetric embryonic musculoskeletal expansion.

mdcat-b3-bio-118.qHtml: What is the structural and functional contractile unit of a skeletal muscle myofibril bounded between two adjacent Z-discs?
mdcat-b3-bio-118.explainHtml: A sarcomere is the basic repeating contractile unit of striated muscle, extending from one Z-disc to the adjacent Z-disc, containing overlapping actin and myosin filaments.

mdcat-b3-bio-119.qHtml: Which fibrous connective tissue bands anchor skeletal muscles securely to bones?
mdcat-b3-bio-119.explainHtml: Tendons are dense regular connective tissue structures composed of parallel collagen fibers that transmit mechanical contractile force from muscles to bones. Ligaments connect bone to bone.

mdcat-b3-bio-120.qHtml: According to the sliding filament theory of muscle contraction, which band of the sarcomere shortens and may completely disappear during maximal contraction?
optionsHtml: H-zone and I-band shorten, while the A-band maintains constant length
A-band shortens while I-band remains constant
mdcat-b3-bio-120.explainHtml: As thin actin filaments slide past thick myosin filaments toward the M-line, the I-band and central H-zone narrow and disappear, while the dark A-band (representing total myosin length) remains constant.

mdcat-b3-bio-121.qHtml: In the molecular mechanism of skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling, what is the role of calcium ions released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum?
optionsHtml: Calcium binds to troponin C, inducing a conformational shift in tropomyosin that uncovers the myosin-binding sites on actin filaments
Calcium directly phosphorylates the myosin l chain
Calcium hydrolyzes ATP at the cross-bridge head
Calcium repolarizes the T-tubule transverse invaginations
mdcat-b3-bio-121.explainHtml: Resting muscle has tropomyosin physically blocking myosin-binding sites on actin. Released Ca2⁺ binds troponin C, shifting the troponin-tropomyosin complex away from binding sites, permitting cross-bridge formation.

mdcat-b3-bio-122.qHtml: What type of synovial joint allows multiaxial movement in all three anatomical planes, exemplified by the glenohumeral (shoulder) and acetabulofemoral (hip) joints?
mdcat-b3-bio-122.explainHtml: Ball-and-socket synovial joints (spheroidal joints) provide maximum range of motion including flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, circumduction, and rotation in three planes.

mdcat-b3-bio-123.qHtml: What is the biochemical cause of rigor mortis (muscular stiffening) that develops several hours after death?
optionsHtml: Postmortem cessation of aerobic respiration depletes cellular ATP, preventing ATP from binding to myosin heads to dissociate actin-myosin cross-bridges
Excessive accumulation of calcium inside mitochondria
Rapid enzymatic hydrolysis of actin microfilaments
Massive hyperpolarization of motor nerve terminals
mdcat-b3-bio-123.explainHtml: Cross-bridge detachment requires new ATP to bind the myosin ATPase head. When death halts ATP synthesis, myosin remains locked in stable cross-linked rigor complexes with actin until autolysis begins.

mdcat-b3-bio-124.qHtml: How does excitation-contraction coupling in smooth muscle fundamentally differ from that in skeletal muscle?
optionsHtml: Smooth muscle lacks troponin; calcium binds calmodulin, activating myosin l-chain kinase (MLCK) which phosphorylates the regulatory l chains of myosin
Smooth muscle relies entirely on intracellular sodium rather than calcium
Smooth muscle filaments slide without requiring ATP hydrolysis
Smooth muscle contractions are mediated exclusively by voluntary somatic motor neurons
mdcat-b3-bio-124.explainHtml: Smooth muscle has no troponin. Influx of Ca2⁺ binds calmodulin; the Ca2⁺-calmodulin complex activates MLCK, which phosphorylates myosin regulatory l chains, enabling myosin ATPase activity and actin cross-bridge cycling.

mdcat-b3-bio-125.qHtml: In compact cortical bone histology, what is an osteon (Haversian system)?
optionsHtml: A cylindrical structural unit consisting of concentric lamellae of calcified matrix surrounding a central neurovascular canal, interconnected by canaliculi
A trabecular sponge-like network filled with red bone marrow
A fibrous sheath enveloping the outer bone surface
An unmineralized cartilaginous growth plate at the epiphysis
mdcat-b3-bio-125.explainHtml: An osteon is the cylindrical structural unit of compact bone, consisting of concentric bone lamellae surrounding a Haversian canal containing blood vessels and nerves, with osteocytes residing in lacunae.

mdcat-b3-bio-126.qHtml: Which muscle fiber type is rich in myoglobin and mitochondria, relies on oxidative phosphorylation, and is highly resistant to muscle fatigue during endurance activities?
mdcat-b3-bio-126.explainHtml: Type I (slow-twitch) fibers contain high concentrations of myoglobin, extensive capillary beds, and numerous mitochondria. They generate ATP primarily through aerobic oxidative phosphorylation, resisting fatigue.

mdcat-b3-bio-127.qHtml: What is the normal cardiac electrical pacemaker of the human heart that generates spontaneous rhythmic action potentials at 60–100 bpm?
mdcat-b3-bio-127.explainHtml: The sinoatrial (SA) node, situated at the junction of the superior vena cava and r atrium, possesses the fastest intrinsic spontaneous diastolic depolarization rate, dictating the cardiac rhythm.

mdcat-b3-bio-128.qHtml: Which blood vessels possess thin endothelial walls, lack smooth muscle and elastic tunics, and serve as the primary site of microvascular nutrient and gas exchange?
mdcat-b3-bio-128.explainHtml: Capillaries consist of a single endothelial cell layer supported by a basal lamina, maximizing surface area and minimizing diffusion distance for metabolic exchange with tissue interstitial fluid.

mdcat-b3-bio-129.qHtml: According to the cohesion-tension theory (Dixon and Joly), what is the primary driving physical force pulling continuous water columns up through xylem vessels to the tops of tall trees?
optionsHtml: Transpirational pull generated by negative hydrostatic pressure (suction) at leaf mesophyll surfaces, supported by water-water cohesion and water-wall adhesion
Active positive root pressure pumping water upwards from below
Atmospheric barometric pressure pushing water up like a mercury barometer
mdcat-b3-bio-129.explainHtml: Transpiration evaporates water from leaf stomata, generating a negative hydrostatic tension. Hydrogen-bonded water molecules cohere together, pulling an unbroken water column up through lignified xylem conduits.

mdcat-b3-bio-130.qHtml: What does the P wave on a standard clinical electrocardiogram (ECG) represent?
mdcat-b3-bio-130.explainHtml: The ECG P wave corresponds to the spread of electrical depolarization across r and left atria originating from the SA node, preceding atrial mechanical systole.

mdcat-b3-bio-131.qHtml: How does the lymphatic system maintain circulatory fluid homeostasis in the human body?
optionsHtml: It collects excess interstitial fluid and filtered plasma proteins not reabsorbed by venous capillaries and returns them to the systemic venous circulation via the thoracic and r lymphatic ducts
It pumps oxygenated arterial blood to visceral organs
It synthesizes erythrocytes and granulocytes in peripheral nodes
It reabsorbs dietary glucose directly from interstitial spaces
mdcat-b3-bio-131.explainHtml: Starling forces favor net capillary ultrafiltration of ~2-4 L of fluid and proteins into the interstitium daily. Blind-ended lymphatic capillaries absorb this fluid, returning lymph to subclavian veins.

mdcat-b3-bio-132.qHtml: In plant root anatomy, which hydrophobic suberized structural barrier in the endodermal radial cell walls forces incoming water and dissolved mineral ions to leave the apoplastic pathway and cross the selectively permeable plasma membrane into the symplast?
mdcat-b3-bio-132.explainHtml: The Casparian strip is an impermeable band of suberin in the radial and transverse walls of root endodermal cells. It blocks non-selective apoplastic flow, forcing water and solutes through selectively permeable symplastic membranes.

mdcat-b3-bio-133.qHtml: During the cardiac cycle, what mechanical event produces the first heart sound ("lub", S1)?
optionsHtml: Turbulent closure of the atrioventricular (mitral and tricuspid) valves at the onset of ventricular isovolumetric contraction
Closure of the semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves at the onset of ventricular diastole
Rapid passive filling of ventricles during early diastole
Atrial systole forcing blood into non-compliant ventricles
mdcat-b3-bio-133.explainHtml: As intraventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure at the onset of ventricular systole, the AV valves (mitral and tricuspid) snap shut, vibrating surrounding myocardium and blood, producing S1.

mdcat-b3-bio-134.qHtml: In the cardiac ventricular action potential, what ionic conductance maintains the prolonged plateau phase (Phase 2)?
optionsHtml: Inward current through L-type voltage-gated calcium channels (I_Ca,L) balancing outward delayed rectifier potassium current (I_K)
Fast influx of sodium through voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
Rapid hyperpolarization driven by chloride influx
Inactivation of all membrane ion channels
mdcat-b3-bio-134.explainHtml: Phase 2 (plateau) of ventricular action potentials lasts ~200-300 ms, mediated by sustained inward Ca2⁺ influx via L-type channels balanced by outward K⁺ efflux, preventing premature tetanic contraction.

mdcat-b3-bio-135.qHtml: In capillary fluid dynamics described by Starling's principle, what pressure gradient primarily opposes hydrostatic capillary filtration, favoring fluid reabsorption back into the capillary lumen?
optionsHtml: Capillary oncotic (colloid osmotic) pressure generated by plasma albumin (~25–28 mmHg)
mdcat-b3-bio-135.explainHtml: Plasma albumin cannot freely cross healthy capillary endothelium, creating an oncotic (colloid osmotic) pressure of ~25-28 mmHg that draws interstitial water back into the vascular lumen.

mdcat-b4-bio-1.qHtml: Which monosaccharide is the universal metabolic fuel and primary building block of glycogen, starch, and cellulose?
mdcat-b4-bio-1.explainHtml: D-Glucose is an aldohexose that serves as the central energy currency of cellular respiration and the monomeric subunit of storage (glycogen, starch) and structural (cellulose) polysaccharides.

mdcat-b4-bio-2.qHtml: What type of chemical linkage is formed between glycerol and three fatty acid molecules in the synthesis of a triacylglycerol (triglyceride)?
mdcat-b4-bio-2.explainHtml: Triglycerides are formed when the three hydroxyl (-OH) groups of glycerol condense with the carboxyl (-COOH) groups of three fatty acids via ester bonds, with elimination of 3 water molecules.

mdcat-b4-bio-3.qHtml: Which non-reducing disaccharide common in table sugar yields equimolar D-glucose and D-fructose upon enzymatic hydrolysis by sucrase (invertase)?
mdcat-b4-bio-3.explainHtml: Sucrose is a non-reducing disaccharide composed of an α-D-glucopyranosyl and β-D-fructofuranoside unit linked by an α-1,β-2-glycosidic bond, yielding glucose and fructose upon hydrolysis.

mdcat-b4-bio-4.qHtml: What is the characteristic repeating glycosidic bond in the unbranched linear helical chain of amylose starch?
mdcat-b4-bio-4.explainHtml: Amylose consists of unbranched D-glucose residues joined exclusively by α-1,4-glycosidic linkages. In contrast, cellulose consists of β-1,4-glycosidic linkages, and amylopectin has α-1,6 branches.

mdcat-b4-bio-5.qHtml: Which amphipathic lipid forms the essential lipid bilayer matrix of all biological plasma membranes?
mdcat-b4-bio-5.explainHtml: Phospholipids are amphipathic, consisting of a hydrophilic polar phosphate head group and two hydrophobic nonpolar hydrocarbon fatty acid tails, spontaneously assembling into fluid bilayers in water.

mdcat-b4-bio-6.qHtml: Which steroid alcohol is an essential structural component regulating eukaryotic membrane fluidity and the biochemical precursor of steroid hormones and bile acids?
mdcat-b4-bio-6.explainHtml: Cholesterol intercalates between membrane phospholipids, dampening fluidity at high temperatures and hindering crystallization at low temperatures. It also serves as the precursor for cortisol, testosterone, estrogen, and bile salts.

mdcat-b4-bio-7.qHtml: In nucleic acids, what is the chemical linkage connecting the 3′-hydroxyl of one pentose sugar to the 5′-phosphate group of the adjacent nucleotide?
mdcat-b4-bio-7.explainHtml: The repeating sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA and RNA is formed by covalent 3′,5′-phosphodiester bonds linking adjacent nucleotide units.

mdcat-b4-bio-8.qHtml: Why can humans and other mammals not utilize cellulose as an energetic dietary source, despite it consisting entirely of D-glucose?
optionsHtml: Mammalian digestive enzymes lack cellulase capable of hydrolyzing β-1,4-glycosidic linkages
Cellulose contains toxic branching nitrogenous residues
Cellulose is absorbed intact and immediately excreted by the kidneys
Cellulose inhibits salivary amylase through allosteric antagonism
mdcat-b4-bio-8.explainHtml: Human digestive enzymes like α-amylase specifically cleave α-1,4-glycosidic bonds. Humans do not produce cellulase, leaving the rigid β-1,4-glycosidic chains of cellulose indigestible dietary fiber.

mdcat-b4-bio-9.qHtml: In eukaryotic plant cells, where do the l-dependent reactions of photosynthesis take place?
optionsHtml: Thylakoid membranes and granum discs of chloroplasts
mdcat-b4-bio-9.explainHtml: The l-dependent reactions occur within the thylakoid membranes where photosystems I and II, electron transport chains, and ATP synthase are embedded. Dark reactions (Calvin cycle) occur in the stroma.

mdcat-b4-bio-10.qHtml: What is the immediate source of electrons to replace those photo-excited and ejected from the P680 reaction center of Photosystem II?
mdcat-b4-bio-10.explainHtml: The oxygen-evolving complex of PS II extracts electrons through the photolysis of water molecules, replenishing the electron hole in oxidized P680 and releasing molecular oxygen as a byproduct.

mdcat-b4-bio-11.qHtml: What is the net yield of ATP molecules produced directly by substrate-level phosphorylation from one molecule of glucose during glycolysis?
mdcat-b4-bio-11.explainHtml: Glycolysis consumes 2 ATP in the preparatory phase (hexokinase and phosphofructokinase-1) and produces 4 ATP in the payoff phase, resulting in a net yield of 2 ATP per glucose.

mdcat-b4-bio-12.qHtml: What 5-carbon compound acts as the primary carbon dioxide acceptor in the carboxylation stage of the Calvin cycle (dark reactions)?
mdcat-b4-bio-12.explainHtml: RuBP (Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate) is carboxylated by the enzyme RuBisCO, combining with CO₂ to form an unstable 6-carbon intermediate that immediately splits into two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA).

mdcat-b4-bio-13.qHtml: In the mitochondrial electron transport chain, what molecule functions as the ultimate terminal electron acceptor?
optionsHtml: Molecular oxygen (O₂), which is reduced to water
mdcat-b4-bio-13.explainHtml: Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) transfers electrons to molecular oxygen (O₂), which combines with matrix protons to form H₂O.

mdcat-b4-bio-14.qHtml: According to Peter Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis, how is ATP synthesized by mitochondrial ATP synthase (F₀F₁ complex)?
optionsHtml: Protons (H⁺) flow down their electrochemical gradient from the intermembrane space back into the matrix through the F₀ channel
Direct transfer of phosphate from NADH to ADP
Active pumping of sodium ions across the inner membrane
Diffusion of pyruvate into the matrix
mdcat-b4-bio-14.explainHtml: Proton pumping by electron transport complexes establishes a proton-motive force across the inner membrane. Protons return through the F₀ channel of ATP synthase, driving mechanical rotation of the F₁ headpiece to phosphorylate ADP to ATP.

mdcat-b4-bio-15.qHtml: How many molecules of CO₂, NADH, FADH₂, and ATP/GTP are produced by one complete turn of the Krebs citric acid cycle from one acetyl-CoA?
mdcat-b4-bio-15.explainHtml: For each acetyl-CoA (2 carbons) entering the citric acid cycle: 2 carbons are released as CO₂, 3 NAD⁺ are reduced to NADH, 1 FAD is reduced to FADH₂, and 1 ATP/GTP is generated by substrate-level phosphorylation.

mdcat-b4-bio-16.qHtml: In cyclic photophosphorylation occurring in chloroplasts, which photosystem operates independently and what is the energetic product?
optionsHtml: Photosystem I (P700) alone; generates ATP without producing NADPH or O₂
Photosystem II (P680) alone; generates NADPH only
Both PS I and PS II; generates ATP and NADPH
mdcat-b4-bio-16.explainHtml: Cyclic electron flow involves only Photosystem I. Excited electrons from P700 cycle through ferredoxin, cytochrome b6f, and plastocyanin back to P700. This pumps protons across the thylakoid membrane to drive ATP synthesis without generating NADPH or evolving oxygen.

mdcat-b4-bio-17.qHtml: What are restriction endonucleases commonly referred to as in genetic engineering?
optionsHtml: Molecular scissors that cleave DNA at specific palindromic sequences
Molecular glue that joins DNA fragments
mdcat-b4-bio-17.explainHtml: Restriction endonucleases act as molecular scissors, recognizing specific 4- to 8-base-pair palindromic nucleotide sequences and cleaving phosphodiester backbones, often generating cohesive "sticky ends".

mdcat-b4-bio-18.qHtml: Which enzyme is used as "molecular glue" to covalently join fragments of foreign DNA into cloning vectors?
mdcat-b4-bio-18.explainHtml: DNA ligase catalyzes the formation of covalent phosphodiester bonds between adjacent 3′-OH and 5′-phosphate ends of DNA fragments.

mdcat-b4-bio-19.qHtml: In the Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) thermal cycling protocol, at what approximate temperature range does the initial thermal denaturation of double-stranded template DNA into single strands occur?
mdcat-b4-bio-19.explainHtml: Denaturation occurs at 94°C–96°C to disrupt the hydrogen bonds between complementary strands of template DNA, producing single strands required for primer annealing.

mdcat-b4-bio-20.qHtml: Why is Taq polymerase isolated from Thermus aquaticus uniquely suited for the Polymerase Chain Reaction?
optionsHtml: It remains enzymatic and thermally stable at denaturation temperatures up to 95°C
It can synthesize DNA without a complementary primer
It proofreads with 100% fidelity without error
mdcat-b4-bio-20.explainHtml: Taq polymerase is isolated from thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus. Its thermostability allows it to withstand repeated heat denaturation steps (94–95°C) without losing activity.

mdcat-b4-bio-21.qHtml: In agarose gel electrophoresis, in which direction do nucleic acid fragments migrate and why?
optionsHtml: Toward the positive anode because DNA has a negatively charged sugar-phosphate backbone
Toward the negative cathode because DNA has basic purines
Toward the positive anode because DNA is hydrophobic
Toward the negative cathode due to osmotic forces
mdcat-b4-bio-21.explainHtml: Phosphate groups give DNA an overall negative charge at neutral pH. In an electric field, DNA fragments migrate through the agarose mesh toward the positive electrode (anode), with smaller fragments moving faster.

mdcat-b4-bio-22.qHtml: What retroviral enzyme is utilized in biotechnology to synthesize complementary DNA (cDNA) from an isolated eukaryotic mRNA template?
mdcat-b4-bio-22.explainHtml: Reverse transcriptase uses an mRNA template to synthesize a single-stranded cDNA without introns, allowing eukaryotic genes to be cloned and expressed in bacterial hosts.

mdcat-b4-bio-23.qHtml: What is the characteristic feature of a genetic palindromic sequence recognized by Type II restriction endonucleases like EcoRI (5′-GAATTC-3′)?
optionsHtml: The base sequence on the complementary strand reads identically when both strands are read in the 5′ to 3′ direction
The sequence contains only alternating guanine and cytosine bases
The sequence forms a closed circular loop structure
The sequence is present only in retroviral genomes
mdcat-b4-bio-23.explainHtml: A palindromic DNA sequence exhibits twofold rotational symmetry: the 5′→3′ sequence of one strand is identical to the 5′→3′ sequence of the complementary antiparallel strand (5′-GAATTC-3′ and 3′-CTTAAG-5′).

mdcat-b4-bio-24.qHtml: In recombinant plasmid vectors like pBR322 or pUC19, what is the role of an antibiotic resistance gene (such as ampR or tetR)?
optionsHtml: Selectable marker to identify and isolate transformed host bacteria that have successfully taken up the plasmid
Origin of replication for plasmid copy control
Promoter site for transcribing the cloned insert
mdcat-b4-bio-24.explainHtml: Selectable marker genes (like β-lactamase conferring ampicillin resistance) allow researchers to grow cells on antibiotic-containing media, selecting only transformed cells that took up the plasmid.

mdcat-b4-bio-25.qHtml: In transgenic animal technology, what is the significance of "gene pharming"?
optionsHtml: Using transgenic livestock to produce therapeutic human proteins secreted in milk or body fluids
Synthesizing synthetic insecticides inside bacterial plasmids
Eradicating agricultural viral infections via phage therapy
mdcat-b4-bio-25.explainHtml: Gene pharming refers to the use of genetically modified farm animals (e.g., goats, sheep, cows) harboring human genes to synthesize complex therapeutic pharmaceuticals (such as antithrombin or factor IX) secreted into their milk.

mdcat-b4-bio-26.qHtml: In which phase of the eukaryotic cell cycle does semi-conservative replication of genomic DNA take place?
mdcat-b4-bio-26.explainHtml: During the S phase of interphase, nuclear DNA replicates completely, doubling the genetic content from 2C to 4C while maintaining the chromosome number (2n).

mdcat-b4-bio-27.qHtml: What is the characteristic biological event occurring during Anaphase of mitotic cell division?
optionsHtml: Sister chromatids split at the centromere and migrate toward opposite spindle poles
Chromosomes align along the equatorial metaphase plate
Nuclear envelope disintegrates and chromatin condenses
Cytoplasm divides into two distinct daughter cells
mdcat-b4-bio-27.explainHtml: Anaphase begins when the protein cohesin is cleaved, splitting sister chromatids at the centromere. Kinetochore microtubules shorten, pulling individual daughter chromosomes toward opposite poles.

mdcat-b4-bio-28.qHtml: During which specific substage of Prophase I of meiosis does crossing over (genetic recombination) occur between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes?
mdcat-b4-bio-28.explainHtml: Synapsis is established during zygotene. Genetic crossing over occurs at the pachytene stage, mediated by recombination nodules that exchange reciprocal non-sister chromatid segments.

mdcat-b4-bio-29.qHtml: What morphological structures become visible under l microscopy during Diplotene of Meiotic Prophase I, representing physical sites of prior crossing over?
mdcat-b4-bio-29.explainHtml: During diplotene, the synaptonemal complex disassembles and homologous chromosomes begin to separate, remaining held together at cross-shaped junctions called chiasmata.

mdcat-b4-bio-30.qHtml: What is the primary cellular difference between cytokinesis in plant cells and animal cells?
optionsHtml: Plant cells form a cell plate (phragmoplast) from the center outward, whereas animal cells divide by an actin-myosin contractile cleavage furrow from the outside inward
Plant cells divide by binary fission while animal cells form phragmoplasts
Plant cells lack spindle fibers completely
mdcat-b4-bio-30.explainHtml: Because rigid plant cell walls prevent pinching, Golgi vesicles align along the equator to form a phragmoplast and cell plate growing centrifugally outward. Animal cells pinch inward centripetally via a contractile ring of actin microfilaments.

mdcat-b4-bio-31.qHtml: What genetic condition results from non-disjunction of chromosome pair 21 during meiotic anaphase in human gametogenesis?
mdcat-b4-bio-31.explainHtml: Meiotic non-disjunction of chromosome 21 produces an egg or sperm with an extra copy. Fertilization results in trisomy 21 (47, +21), known as Down syndrome.

mdcat-b4-bio-32.qHtml: Which molecular complex controls progression through cell cycle checkpoints by phosphorylating target regulatory proteins when bound to regulatory cyclins?
mdcat-b4-bio-32.explainHtml: Cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) are serine/threonine protein kinases activated upon binding specific cyclins, phosphorylating downstream targets like Rb to drive cell cycle transition.

mdcat-b4-bio-33.qHtml: What is the biological significance of apoptosis (programmed cell death) during embryonic morphogenesis and cellular homeostasis?
optionsHtml: Orderly elimination of superfluous, damaged, or autoreactive cells without releasing intracellular contents or causing inflammation
Uncontrolled cell swelling and membrane rupture leading to tissue inflammation
Direct stimulation of neoplastic mitotic growth
Permanent arrest in the G0 quiescent state
mdcat-b4-bio-33.explainHtml: Apoptosis is genetically programmed cell suicide characterized by chromatin condensation, cell shrinkage, and formation of apoptotic bodies that are phagocytosed without triggering an inflammatory response (unlike necrosis).

mdcat-b4-bio-34.qHtml: Which organelle is universally present in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, functioning as the site of protein translation?
mdcat-b4-bio-34.explainHtml: Ribosomes are non-membrane-bound ribonucleoprotein complexes present in all living cells (70S in prokaryotes, 80S in eukaryotic cytosol) that translate mRNA into polypeptides.

mdcat-b4-bio-35.qHtml: Which eukaryotic organelle contains hydrolytic acid hydrolases specialized for intracellular digestion of macromolecules, old organelles, and engulfed pathogens?
mdcat-b4-bio-35.explainHtml: Lysosomes are membrane-bound vesicles containing acid hydrolases (optimum pH ~4.5–5.0) that degrade endocytosed material, cellular debris (autophagy), and phagocytosed microorganisms.

mdcat-b4-bio-36.qHtml: What is the primary lipid component forming the foundational bilayer matrix in Singer and Nicolson's Fluid Mosaic Model?
mdcat-b4-bio-36.explainHtml: The fluid mosaic model depicts the biological membrane as a two-dimensional viscous fluid bilayer of amphipathic phospholipids with embedded (integral) and attached (peripheral) proteins.

mdcat-b4-bio-37.qHtml: What is the structural composition of eukaryotic microtubules found in the spindle apparatus, cilia, and flagella?
optionsHtml: Hollow cylinders formed by heterodimers of α-tubulin and β-tubulin
Fibrous tetramers of keratin and lamin
mdcat-b4-bio-37.explainHtml: Microtubules are hollow cylindrical polymers (~25 nm outer diameter) assembled from alternating α- and β-tubulin heterodimers that arrange into 13 protofilaments.

mdcat-b4-bio-38.qHtml: What enzymatic activity distinguishes peroxisomes from lysosomes in animal and plant cells?
optionsHtml: Catalase converting harmful hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) into water and oxygen
mdcat-b4-bio-38.explainHtml: Peroxisomes contain oxidases that produce hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) during fatty acid β-oxidation, and high levels of catalase, which breaks down toxic H₂O₂ into H₂O and O₂.

mdcat-b4-bio-39.qHtml: What is the internal membrane architecture of the eukaryotic Golgi apparatus?
optionsHtml: A series of flattened, membrane-bound disc-like cisternae organized into cis-, medial-, and trans-faces
An interconnected network of tubular cisternae studded with ribosomes
mdcat-b4-bio-39.explainHtml: The Golgi complex consists of stacks of flattened membrane sacs called cisternae with distinct polarity: a cis face receiving vesicles from the rough ER and a trans face shipping sorted proteins.

mdcat-b4-bio-40.qHtml: How does the prokaryotic bacterial cell wall differ biochemically from the plant cell wall?
optionsHtml: Bacterial walls contain peptidoglycan (murein), whereas plant walls consist of cellulose, hemicellulose, and pectin
Bacterial walls contain chitin, whereas plant walls have peptidoglycan
Bacterial walls are made of pure silica
mdcat-b4-bio-40.explainHtml: Bacterial cell walls consist of peptidoglycan (chains of alternating N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid cross-linked by short peptide chains), whereas plant cell walls are made of cellulose microfibrils in a hemicellulose/pectin matrix.

mdcat-b4-bio-41.qHtml: Which cellular junction forms an impermeable barrier sealing adjacent epithelial cells together to prevent intercellular fluid leakage across mucosal linings?
mdcat-b4-bio-41.explainHtml: T junctions (zonula occludens) are formed by transmembrane proteins (claudins and occludins) that stitch adjacent cell membranes together, creating a watert barrier across epithelial sheets (e.g., intestinal mucosa and blood-brain barrier).

mdcat-b4-bio-42.qHtml: What is the principal intracellular cation responsible for maintaining resting membrane potential across neuronal axolemmas?
optionsHtml: Calcium ion (Ca2⁺)
mdcat-b4-bio-42.explainHtml: Potassium (K⁺) is the predominant intracellular cation (~140 mM inside vs 4 mM outside). High resting membrane permeability to K⁺ via leak channels establishes the negative resting potential (-70 mV).

mdcat-b4-bio-43.qHtml: Which endocrine hormone released by beta cells of the islets of Langerhans lowers elevated blood glucose concentrations?
mdcat-b4-bio-43.explainHtml: Insulin stimulates glucose uptake in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue via GLUT4 translocation and promotes glycogen synthesis in the liver, lowering blood glucose.

mdcat-b4-bio-44.qHtml: What is the functional gap between an axon terminal of a presynaptic neuron and the dendrite of a postsynaptic neuron called?
mdcat-b4-bio-44.explainHtml: The synaptic cleft is the narrow extracellular space (~20–40 nm) across which neurotransmitters diffuse from the presynaptic active zone to postsynaptic membrane receptors.

mdcat-b4-bio-45.qHtml: During the depolarizing phase of a neuronal action potential, which ion channels open rapidly to drive membrane potential from -70 mV to +30 mV?
mdcat-b4-bio-45.explainHtml: When the membrane depolarizes to threshold (~ -55 mV), voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open rapidly. Influx of Na⁺ down its electrochemical gradient drives the membrane potential up toward +30 mV.

mdcat-b4-bio-46.qHtml: Which brain structure acts as the primary autonomic coordinator, regulating body temperature, hunger, thirst, circadian rhythms, and pituitary hormone secretion?
mdcat-b4-bio-46.explainHtml: The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems, controlling homeostatic set-points (thermoregulation, osmoregulation, appetite) and directing pituitary gland secretions.

mdcat-b4-bio-47.qHtml: What is saltatory conduction in the human nervous system?
optionsHtml: Rapid propagation of action potentials jumping between unmyelinated nodes of Ranvier along a myelinated axon
Diffusion of sodium ions across gap junctions in cardiac muscle
Continuous slow conduction across unmyelinated sensory fibers
Retrograde transport of vesicles along microtubules
mdcat-b4-bio-47.explainHtml: Myelin sheaths prevent ionic leakage along internodes. Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are clustered at the nodes of Ranvier, allowing action potentials to jump from node to node, speeding conduction up to 120 m/s.

mdcat-b4-bio-48.qHtml: What endocrine disorder is characterized by hypercortisolemia, facial roundness ("moon face"), truncal obesity, abdominal striae, and hypertension?
mdcat-b4-bio-48.explainHtml: Cushing's syndrome results from prolonged exposure to excessive glucocorticoids (cortisol), causing characteristic buffalo hump, moon facies, skin striae, osteoporosis, and hyperglycemia.

mdcat-b4-bio-49.qHtml: Which plant hormone promotes stem elongation, induces seed germination by activating α-amylase in cereal aleurone layers, and overcomes genetic dwarfism?
mdcat-b4-bio-49.explainHtml: Gibberellins trigger the synthesis of hydrolytic enzymes like α-amylase in the aleurone layer of germinating seeds to mobilize endosperm starch, and stimulate stem and internode elongation.

mdcat-b4-bio-50.qHtml: What ion influx into the presynaptic terminal triggers the exocytosis of neurotransmitter-filled synaptic vesicles into the synaptic cleft?
optionsHtml: Calcium ions (Ca2⁺) via voltage-gated calcium channels
Potassium ions (K⁺) via inward rectifier channels
mdcat-b4-bio-50.explainHtml: Action potential depolarization reaching the presynaptic bouton opens voltage-gated Ca2⁺ channels. Calcium influx binds synaptotagmin, triggering SNARE-mediated fusion of synaptic vesicles with the presynaptic membrane.

mdcat-b4-bio-51.qHtml: Which animal phylum lacks true tissues and organs, possessing an asymmetric cellular level of organization and choanocyte collar cells?
mdcat-b4-bio-51.explainHtml: Porifera (sponges) exhibit cellular-level organization without true germ layers or tissues. Flagellated collar cells (choanocytes) line internal chambers to drive water currents for filter feeding.

mdcat-b4-bio-52.qHtml: Which phylum is characterized by stinging cells called cnidocytes containing specialized toxin-injecting organelles termed nematocysts?
mdcat-b4-bio-52.explainHtml: Cnidarians (hydra, jellyfish, corals) possess specialized cnidocytes with nematocysts that discharge venomous harpoon-like threads for prey capture and defense.

mdcat-b4-bio-53.qHtml: What type of body cavity is found in roundworms belonging to Phylum Nematoda (Aschelminthes)?
optionsHtml: Pseudocoelom (cavity not completely lined by mesoderm)
mdcat-b4-bio-53.explainHtml: Nematodes possess a pseudocoelom: a fluid-filled body cavity derived from embryonic blastocoel that is lined by mesoderm only on the outer body wall, not around the gut.

mdcat-b4-bio-54.qHtml: Which invertebrate phylum has a jointed chitinous exoskeleton, segmented body tagmata, and open circulatory system, representing the largest animal phylum?
mdcat-b4-bio-54.explainHtml: Arthropoda is the largest phylum, characterized by a hardened chitinous exoskeleton, metameric segmentation grouped into tagmata, jointed appendages, and an open hemocoel.

mdcat-b4-bio-55.qHtml: What respiratory structure and rasping feeding organ are unique defining characteristics of many members of Phylum Mollusca?
optionsHtml: Ctenidia (gills) and a chitinous toothed Radula
mdcat-b4-bio-55.explainHtml: Molluscs have a mantle cavity enclosing ctenidia (gills) for respiration and a chitinous ribbon of teeth known as a radula used to scrape food particles.

mdcat-b4-bio-56.qHtml: What water-vascular system structure enables locomotion, food handling, and respiration in Phylum Echinodermata?
optionsHtml: Tube feet (podia) connected to ampullae and radial canals
mdcat-b4-bio-56.explainHtml: Echinoderms possess a hydraulic water vascular system. Fluid pumped into flexible tube feet (podia) provides hydrostatic suction and stepping movements for locomotion.

mdcat-b4-bio-57.qHtml: Which group of chordates are amniotes characterized by pneumatic porous bones, high metabolic endothermy, and a four-chambered heart with a r systemic aortic arch?
mdcat-b4-bio-57.explainHtml: Birds (Aves) have hollow pneumatic bones, high endothermy, feathers, and a 4-chambered heart with a r systemic arch (mammals have a left aortic arch).

mdcat-b4-bio-58.qHtml: What anatomical features definitively diagnose all chordate embryos at some stage of ontogeny?
optionsHtml: Notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal gill slits, and post-anal tail
Ventral solid nerve cord, exoskeleton, and open hemocoel
