The free substrate in solution, preventing it from diffusing toward the active site
mdcat-b9-bio-21.explainHtml: Uncompetitive inhibitors cannot bind the free enzyme; they bind exclusively to the ES complex, trapping substrate in the active site. This decreases Vmax (depleting productive ES complexes) and also decreases apparent Km by shifting the E + S ⇌ ES equilibrium toward ES formation.

mdcat-b9-bio-22.qHtml: What is the biochemical significance of an enzyme displaying a very low Michaelis constant (low Km) for a particular metabolic substrate?
optionsHtml: The enzyme possesses high substrate affinity and operates at near-maximal velocity even at very low physiological substrate concentrations
The enzyme requires extremely high substrate concentrations to reach half-maximal velocity
The enzyme is catalytically inefficient and easily denatures at body temperature
The enzyme undergoes irreversible suicidal denaturation after completing a single turnover
mdcat-b9-bio-22.explainHtml: Km is the substrate concentration at which the reaction velocity is half-maximal (Vmax/2). An inverse relationship exists between Km and affinity: a lower Km reflects higher binding affinity of enzyme for substrate.

mdcat-b9-bio-23.qHtml: Which of the following classes of enzymes catalyzes the hydrolytic cleavage of chemical bonds without utilizing water, often generating double bonds or rings?
mdcat-b9-bio-23.explainHtml: Lyases catalyze the non-hydrolytic cleavage of C-C, C-O, C-N, or other bonds by elimination, leaving double bonds, or catalyze the addition of groups to double bonds without ATP consumption. Hydrolases cleave bonds with the introduction of water.

mdcat-b9-bio-24.qHtml: Why does excessive elevation of temperature beyond the optimum (e.g., heating human salivary amylase above 65°C) abolish catalytic activity?
optionsHtml: Thermal kinetic energy disrupts weak non-covalent hydrogen bonds and ionic interactions stabilizing the native tertiary conformation
Heat cleaves primary covalent peptide bonds directly into single amino acids
Elevated thermal energy forces the competitive binding of water to all prosthetic groups
Thermal excitation increases enzyme activation energy to infinity
mdcat-b9-bio-24.explainHtml: Above the thermal optimum, excessive vibrational energy breaks hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, and hydrophobic interactions responsible for tertiary and quaternary protein conformation, causing unfolding (denaturation) and collapse of the active site.

mdcat-b9-bio-25.qHtml: During the cell cycle, the Spindle Assembly Checkpoint (SAC) arrests mitotic progression at metaphase until:
optionsHtml: All kinetochores are amphitelically attached to spindle microtubules and experience balanced bipolar mechanical tension
Centrosomes complete semiconservative replication during early prophase
Nuclear lamina phosphorylation by Cdk1 triggers complete envelope breakdown
DNA topoisomerase II decatenates all sister chromatids during G2 phase
mdcat-b9-bio-25.explainHtml: The SAC monitors kinetochore-microtubule attachments. Unattached or tension-free kinetochores generate the Mad2-Cdc20 mitotic checkpoint complex (MCC), inhibiting the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) until every sister kinetochore is stably attached to opposite spindle poles.

mdcat-b9-bio-26.qHtml: Which multiprotein complex is responsible for holding replicated sister chromatids together from S phase until anaphase onset?
mdcat-b9-bio-26.explainHtml: Cohesin forms a ring-shaped protein complex (containing Smc1, Smc3, and Scc1) that entraps sister chromatids along their length from S-phase until separase cleaves Scc1 at the metaphase-to-anaphase transition.

mdcat-b9-bio-27.qHtml: In meiotic prophase I, crossing over and reciprocal genetic recombination occur between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during which specific sub-stage?
mdcat-b9-bio-27.explainHtml: In meiotic prophase I: Leptotene involves chromatin condensation; Zygotene involves synapsis and synaptonemal complex assembly; Pachytene is the stage where crossing over and reciprocal recombination occur; Diplotene features dissolution of synaptonemal complex revealing chiasmata; Diakinesis is terminalization.

mdcat-b9-bio-28.qHtml: The tumor suppressor protein p53 induces G1/S cell cycle arrest in response to double-stranded DNA breaks primarily by activating the transcription of which cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor?
mdcat-b9-bio-28.explainHtml: In response to DNA damage, ATM/ATR kinases phosphorylate and stabilize p53. p53 acts as a transcription factor for p21 (CIP1/WAF1), a Cdk inhibitor that binds and inhibits Cyclin D-Cdk4/6 and Cyclin E-Cdk2 complexes, preventing Rb phosphorylation and arresting cells in G1.

mdcat-b9-bio-29.qHtml: A human primary oocyte completing meiosis I produces:
optionsHtml: One secondary oocyte (23 chromosomes, each with 2 chromatids) and a smaller non-functional first polar body
Two identical functional secondary oocytes each with 46 sister chromatids
Four haploid mature ootids each containing 23 single chromatids
One diploid zygote and three haploid polar bodies
mdcat-b9-bio-29.explainHtml: Cytokinesis in female meiosis I is markedly asymmetric: almost all cytoplasm is retained by the secondary oocyte (23 duplicated chromosomes, 1n, 2c), while the small first polar body receives minimal cytoplasm and degenerates.

mdcat-b9-bio-30.qHtml: Failure of homologous chromosomes to segregate properly during Meiosis I or sister chromatids during Meiosis II is designated as:
optionsHtml: Nondisjunction, resulting in aneuploid gametes (e.g., trisomy 21)
mdcat-b9-bio-30.explainHtml: Nondisjunction is the failure of homologous chromosome pairs to separate in meiosis I, or sister chromatids in meiosis II, resulting in daughter cells with an abnormal chromosome number (n+1 or n-1), which produces aneuploid conditions such as Down syndrome (trisomy 21).

mdcat-b9-bio-31.qHtml: During plant cell cytokinesis, cytoplasmic division occurs from the inside out through the formation of a phragmoplast, which assembles:
optionsHtml: Golgi-derived pectin-rich vesicles that fuse along the equatorial plane to form the cell plate
A contractile ring of actin microfilaments and myosin II that pinches the plasma membrane inward
Collagen fibers secreted by the cortical microtubule array
Chitinous transverse septa synthesized by chloroplast ribosomes
mdcat-b9-bio-31.explainHtml: Unlike animal cells that utilize an actomyosin contractile cleavage furrow, plant cells divide via a phragmoplast: Golgi-derived vesicles containing cell wall precursors (pectins and hemicelluloses) fuse along the equator to form the cell plate, developing into the middle lamella.

mdcat-b9-bio-32.qHtml: Apoptosis (programmed cell death) is distinguished biochemically and morphologically from necrosis by which of the following hallmarks?
optionsHtml: Caspase cascade activation, internucleosomal DNA laddering, and formation of intact apoptotic bodies without inflammation
Passive cellular swelling, early plasma membrane lysis, and massive leakage of cytoplasmic contents inducing acute inflammation
Massive intracellular ATP overproduction and spontaneous mitotic chromosome replication
Disruption of lysosomal membranes accompanied by unregulated cytoplasmic calcification
mdcat-b9-bio-32.explainHtml: Apoptosis is an ATP-dependent, regulated physiological cell death executed by cysteine proteases (caspases). Hallmarks include cell shrinkage, pyknosis, caspase-activated DNase (CAD) internucleosomal DNA fragmentation (180-200 bp ladders), and apoptotic bodies that are phagocytosed without inflammatory response.

mdcat-b9-bio-33.qHtml: Which of the following phyla comprises triploblastic, bilateral, pseudocoelomate organisms possessing a tough non-cellular collagenous cuticle that is periodically shed through ecdysis?
mdcat-b9-bio-33.explainHtml: Nematodes are pseudocoelomates (body cavity derived from blastocoel, not lined entirely by mesoderm), triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical, and possess a resistant, multi-layered cuticle shed periodically via ecdysis.

mdcat-b9-bio-34.qHtml: Cnidocytes with coiled eversible nematocysts are unique diagnostic evolutionary characteristics of which animal phylum?
mdcat-b9-bio-34.explainHtml: Cnidarians (hydras, jellyfish, corals, sea anemones) possess specialized stinging cells called cnidocytes containing organelle-like nematocysts, which discharge barbed threads containing paralyzing neurotoxins upon tactile stimulation.

mdcat-b9-bio-35.qHtml: In deuterostome development (exhibited by Echinodermata and Chordata), what is the embryonic developmental fate of the blastopore?
optionsHtml: It develops into the anus, while the mouth develops secondarily from a separate anterior invagination
It directly forms the mouth, while the anus forms secondarily
It differentiates into the primitive neural tube and notochord
It closes completely, and both mouth and anus arise from lateral mesoderm splits
mdcat-b9-bio-35.explainHtml: In deuterostomes (echinoderms, chordates), the blastopore becomes the anus (deuterostome = "second mouth"), and cleavage is radial and indeterminate. In protostomes (annelids, mollusks, arthropods), the blastopore forms the mouth, with spiral and determinate cleavage.

mdcat-b9-bio-36.qHtml: Which of the following excretory structures is characteristic of Platyhelminthes (flatworms such as Planaria), functioning primarily in osmoregulation?
optionsHtml: Malpighian tubules operating with uric acid precipitation
Antennal green glands at the base of the rostrum
mdcat-b9-bio-36.explainHtml: Platyhelminthes possess a network of closed protonephridial tubules terminating in specialized bulb-like flame cells. The beating of a tuft of cilia resembles a flickering flame, propelling interstitial fluid through filtering slits for osmoregulatory ultrafiltration.

mdcat-b9-bio-37.qHtml: The water vascular system (ambulacral system) utilizing hydraulic pressure to operate rows of locomotive tube feet (podia) is an exclusive anatomical specialization of:
mdcat-b9-bio-37.explainHtml: Echinoderms uniquely possess a coelomic water vascular system consisting of a madreporite, stone canal, ring canal, radial canals, ampullae, and tube feet (podia) that generate hydraulic suction for locomotion, prey capture, and gas exchange.

mdcat-b9-bio-38.qHtml: Which diagnostic morphological feature definitively distinguishes the class Chondrichthyes (cartilaginous fishes) from Osteichthyes (bony fishes)?
optionsHtml: Lack of a bony operculum over separate gill slits and absence of a gas-filled swim bladder
Possession of a terminal mouth and homocercal caudal fin
Presence of cycloid and ctenoid dermal scales
External fertilization in all species with lack of intromittent claspers
mdcat-b9-bio-38.explainHtml: Chondrichthyes (sharks, rays, skates) possess a cartilaginous skeleton, placoid scales, lack a swim bladder (relying on oil-rich squalene livers for buoyancy), and lack a bony operculum (possessing 5-7 exposed gill slits). Male chondrichthyans also possess pelvic claspers for internal fertilization.

mdcat-b9-bio-39.qHtml: Which extraembryonic membrane forms a fluid-filled protective sac immediately surrounding the embryo in reptiles, birds, and mammals, preventing mechanical shock and desiccation?
mdcat-b9-bio-39.explainHtml: The amnion encloses the amniotic cavity filled with amniotic fluid, creating an aquatic microenvironment that buffers the terrestrial embryo from desiccation and mechanical impact. Hence reptiles, birds, and mammals are amniotes.

mdcat-b9-bio-40.qHtml: Mammals belonging to the subclass Prototheria (monotremes, such as the duck-billed platypus and echidna) are biologically unique among living mammals because they:
optionsHtml: Lay shelled cleidoic eggs (oviparous) and secrete milk from modified mammary glands onto abdominal fur without teats
Possess an external abdominal marsupial pouch to house altricial embryos
Develop an advanced invasive hemochorial chorioallantoic placenta
Lack homeothermic thermoregulation and breathe through cutaneous vascular beds
mdcat-b9-bio-40.explainHtml: Monotremes (Prototheria: platypus and spiny anteater) are egg-laying (oviparous) mammals. They possess a cloaca, lack nipples/teats (milk oozes from modified skin glands licked off mother's belly fur), yet possess hair and feed young on milk.

mdcat-b9-bio-41.qHtml: In human gastric juice, the proenzyme pepsinogen is secreted by which cell type and converted into active pepsin by which mechanism?
optionsHtml: Secreted by chief (zymogenic) cells; activated by hydrochloric acid (HCl) cleavage and autocatalytic active pepsin cleavage
Secreted by parietal (oxyntic) cells; activated by intrinsic factor binding
Secreted by enteroendocrine G cells; activated by alkaline pancreatic secretions
Secreted by surface mucous neck cells; activated by enterokinase in the duodenum
mdcat-b9-bio-41.explainHtml: Gastric chief (peptic/zymogenic) cells synthesize and secrete inactive pepsinogen. Exposure to HCl (secreted by parietal cells at pH 1.5-2.0) causes removal of a 44-amino-acid masking peptide, activating pepsin. Active pepsin then autocatalyzes further pepsinogen activation.

mdcat-b9-bio-42.qHtml: Which peptide hormone, synthesized and released by mucosal I cells of the upper small intestine in response to chyme containing fatty acids and peptides, stimulates gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion?
mdcat-b9-bio-42.explainHtml: CCK is released from enteroendocrine I cells in the duodenum and jejunum in response to dietary peptides and fat digestion products. It stimulates gallbladder muscular contraction (ejecting bile), relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, and triggers pancreatic acinar enzyme secretion.

mdcat-b9-bio-43.qHtml: The digestion of dietary triacylglycerols in the small intestine requires the detergent action of bile salts to form mixed micelles because:
optionsHtml: Bile salts emulsify large lipid droplets into micro-droplets, vastly increasing the surface area accessible to water-soluble pancreatic lipase
Bile salts covalently cleave ester linkages at the sn-2 position of triglycerides
Bile salts convert toxic free fatty acids into water-soluble glycogen granules
Bile salts directly synthesize chylomicrons inside the intestinal lumen
mdcat-b9-bio-43.explainHtml: Pancreatic lipase is a water-soluble enzyme that functions at oil-water interfaces. Bile salts (amphipathic steroids like cholate and chenodeoxycholate) emulsify macroscopic fat globules into tiny droplets (0.2-2.0 μm), multiplying available surface area for lipase and colipase.

mdcat-b9-bio-44.qHtml: Dietary glucose and galactose are absorbed across the apical brush-border membrane of intestinal enterocytes against their concentration gradient via which transporter?
optionsHtml: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 1 (SGLT1) via secondary active transport driven by the Na⁺ electrochemical gradient
Glucose transporter 2 (GLUT2) via ATP-independent facilitative diffusion only
Glucose transporter 4 (GLUT4) via insulin-dependent vesicular translocation
Proton-coupled oligopeptide transporter (PepT1) utilizing stomach acid
mdcat-b9-bio-44.explainHtml: Glucose and galactose absorption across enterocyte apical microvilli is mediated by SGLT1, a symporter that transports 2 Na⁺ ions down their electrochemical gradient alongside 1 monosaccharide molecule. GLUT2 then mediates facilitated exit across the basolateral membrane into capillaries.

mdcat-b9-bio-45.qHtml: Which pancreatic zymogen is initially cleaved and activated by brush-border enteropeptidase (enterokinase), initiating a cascade that activates all other pancreatic proteases?
mdcat-b9-bio-45.explainHtml: Enteropeptidase (enterokinase), an integral brush-border enzyme in the duodenum, selectively hydrolyzes an N-terminal hexapeptide from trypsinogen to yield active trypsin. Trypsin then autocatalytically cleaves and activates chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidase, and proelastase.

mdcat-b9-bio-46.qHtml: In plant nutrition, the Casparian strip in the endodermal root cell layer is impregnated with suberin and lignin to:
optionsHtml: Block the apoplastic flow of water and dissolved solutes, forcing them to traverse the selectively permeable plasma membrane symplastically
Facilitate the rapid uncontrolled lateral bulk flow of soil water directly into tracheids
Synthesize root nodules for endosymbiotic nitrogen fixation
Prevent root cell division by inhibiting the apical meristem
mdcat-b9-bio-46.explainHtml: The Casparian strip is a waterproof band of suberin and lignin embedded in the radial and transverse walls of root endodermal cells. It blocks the non-selective apoplastic pathway (cell walls and intercellular spaces), forcing water and mineral ions across living endodermal cell membranes for selective regulatory filtration.

mdcat-b9-bio-47.qHtml: Carnivorous plants (such as the Venus flytrap and Nepenthes pitcher plant) trap and digest insects primarily to supplement their nutritional requirement for which element in nitrogen-deficient bogs?
mdcat-b9-bio-47.explainHtml: Carnivorous plants photosynthesize normally to synthesize their own carbon compounds, but inhabit waterlogged, acidic bogs where nitrate availability is extremely poor. Digesting insect proteins provides assimilable organic nitrogen, amino acids, and phosphates.

mdcat-b9-bio-48.qHtml: Intrinsic factor, an essential glycoprotein required for the physiological receptor-mediated absorption of cobalamin (Vitamin B12) in the terminal ileum, is synthesized by which cells?
mdcat-b9-bio-48.explainHtml: Intrinsic factor is produced and secreted by parietal (oxyntic) cells of the gastric mucosa. In the terminal ileum, the intrinsic factor-B12 complex binds to cubam receptors on enterocyte membranes, enabling endocytic absorption. Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells leads to pernicious anemia.

mdcat-b9-bio-49.qHtml: In the small intestine, long-chain fatty acids and 2-monoacylglycerols absorbed by enterocytes are re-esterified into triacylglycerols within the smooth ER, packaged with apolipoproteins and cholesterol, and released as:
optionsHtml: Chylomicrons, which enter lacteals (lymphatic capillaries) rather than blood capillaries
Low-density lipoproteins (LDL), which enter portal vein venules directly
Very low-density lipoproteins (VLDL), which exit through fenestrated splenic sinusoids
Micelles, which diffuse directly through mesenteric venules into the inferior vena cava
mdcat-b9-bio-49.explainHtml: Within the smooth ER of enterocytes, digested lipids are re-synthesized into triglycerides and assembled into chylomicrons (surrounded by Apo B-48 and phospholipids). Because chylomicrons (~100-500 nm) are too large to cross continuous blood capillary basements, they exocytose into central lacteals (lymphatics).

mdcat-b9-bio-50.qHtml: In the l-dependent reactions of oxygenic photosynthesis, the primary electron donor that replenishes the photo-oxidized reaction center P680 of Photosystem II is:
optionsHtml: Water (H2O), through catalytic photolysis at the oxygen-evolving manganese cluster (Mn4CaO5)
Plastoquinone (PQH2) returning from the cytochrome b6f complex
mdcat-b9-bio-50.explainHtml: P680⁺ is one of the strongest biological oxidizing agents known (E°' ≈ +1.25 V). It extracts electrons from water via the oxygen-evolving complex (Mn4CaO5 cluster) of PSII: 2H2O → O2 + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻. This reaction generates atmospheric O2 and lumenal protons.

mdcat-b9-bio-51.qHtml: During cyclic photophosphorylation in chloroplasts, electrons excited from Photosystem I (P700) are routed through ferredoxin back to which complex to generate ATP without producing NADPH or O2?
optionsHtml: RuBisCO large subunit in the stroma
mdcat-b9-bio-51.explainHtml: In cyclic electron flow, electrons from P700 pass to ferredoxin, but instead of reducing NADP⁺ via FNR, they return to the cytochrome b6f complex through plastoquinone. This pumps protons across the thylakoid membrane, generating an electrochemical gradient for ATP synthesis without generating NADPH or evolving O2.

mdcat-b9-bio-52.qHtml: In the Calvin cycle (C3 pathway), how many molecules of ATP and NADPH are stoichiometrically consumed to fix 3 molecules of CO2 into one net triose phosphate (G3P)?
mdcat-b9-bio-52.explainHtml: Fixing 3 CO2 yields 6 molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA). Phosphorylation consumes 6 ATP to form 6 1,3-bisphosphoglycerates; reduction consumes 6 NADPH to yield 6 glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (G3P). Regeneration of 3 ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP) from 5 G3P consumes 3 additional ATP. Total: 9 ATP and 6 NADPH.

mdcat-b9-bio-53.qHtml: Photorespiration occurs when RuBisCO binds oxygen (O2) instead of carbon dioxide (CO2), generating one molecule of 3-phosphoglycerate and one molecule of:
mdcat-b9-bio-53.explainHtml: RuBisCO exhibits bifunctional carboxylase/oxygenase activity. When it binds O2, RuBP is cleaved into one molecule of 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA, 3C) and one molecule of 2-phosphoglycolate (2C), initiating the costly photorespiratory glycolate pathway involving chloroplasts, peroxisomes, and mitochondria.

mdcat-b9-bio-54.qHtml: In aerobic cellular respiration, which specific glycolytic reaction involves substrate-level phosphorylation to generate ATP?
optionsHtml: Conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) to pyruvate by pyruvate kinase
Phosphorylation of glucose to glucose 6-phosphate by hexokinase
Phosphorylation of fructose 6-phosphate to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate by PFK-1
Cleavage of fructose 1,6-bisphosphate into DHAP and G3P by aldolase
mdcat-b9-bio-54.explainHtml: Substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis occurs at two steps: (1) 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to 3-phosphoglycerate by phosphoglycerate kinase, and (2) phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) to pyruvate by pyruvate kinase, transferring a high-energy phosphate directly onto ADP.

mdcat-b9-bio-55.qHtml: In the mitochondrial electron transport chain, which enzyme complex is directly shared with the citric acid (Krebs) cycle and does NOT pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane?
mdcat-b9-bio-55.explainHtml: Succinate dehydrogenase is an integral inner mitochondrial membrane protein that oxidizes succinate to fumarate in the Krebs cycle, transferring electrons via FAD and Fe-S centers to ubiquinone (forming Complex II of the ETC). It spans the membrane without translocating protons into the intermembrane space.

mdcat-b9-bio-56.qHtml: According to Peter Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis, ATP synthesis by F0F1-ATP synthase is directly powered by:
optionsHtml: The proton motive force (electrochemical gradient Δp) driving protons through the F0 channel from the intermembrane space into the matrix
Direct covalent electron donation from ubiquinone to the catalytic beta subunits
Osmotic water pressure compressing ADP and inorganic phosphate together
Active pumping of sodium ions out of the mitochondrial matrix into the cytosol
mdcat-b9-bio-56.explainHtml: Proton pumping by Complexes I, III, and IV creates an electrochemical proton gradient (proton motive force: membrane potential ΔΨ + pH gradient ΔpH) across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Dissipation of this gradient as protons flow back down into the matrix through F0 drives rotation of the gamma stalk and catalytic phosphorylation in F1.

mdcat-b9-bio-57.qHtml: Under anaerobic conditions in vigorously contracting human skeletal muscle, the conversion of pyruvate to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is biologically necessary to:
optionsHtml: Regenerate oxidized NAD⁺ so that the GAPDH step of glycolysis can continue producing ATP
Generate excess carbon dioxide to buffer intracellular acidity
Transport lactic acid into mitochondria for direct β-oxidation
mdcat-b9-bio-57.explainHtml: In the absence of oxygen, the mitochondrial ETC cannot oxidize NADH. Glycolysis would arrest due to lack of NAD⁺ required by glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH). Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate, concurrently oxidizing NADH back to NAD⁺ to maintain glycolytic flux.

mdcat-b9-bio-58.qHtml: How many turns of the citric acid (Krebs) cycle occur per molecule of glucose fully degraded via aerobic glycolysis, and what is the net yield of reduced cofactors produced strictly during these cycles?
mdcat-b9-bio-58.explainHtml: One glucose yields 2 pyruvates, which form 2 acetyl-CoA. Entering the Krebs cycle, each acetyl-CoA produces 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, and 1 GTP/ATP. Thus, per original glucose molecule, 2 complete turns yield 6 NADH, 2 FADH2, 2 GTP/ATP, and 4 CO2.

mdcat-b9-bio-59.qHtml: According to Dixon and Joly's Cohesion-Tension theory, the primary physical force driving the upward ascent of sap through xylem tracheary elements against gravity is:
optionsHtml: Negative hydrostatic tension generated by transpirational pull at mesophyll cell surfaces transmitted down continuous water columns via hydrogen-bonded cohesion
Positive root pressure generated by active mineral pumping across the pericycle
Capillary action acting independently inside vessel lumina without surface evaporation
Rhythmic peristaltic contractions of living xylem parenchyma cells
mdcat-b9-bio-59.explainHtml: Transpiration evaporates water from substomatal cavities, creating a strong negative water potential that exerts tension (pull) on the continuous xylem water column. High tensile strength of water due to inter-molecular hydrogen bonds (cohesion) and water-cell wall adhesion allows sap to ascend over 100 meters without cavitating.

mdcat-b9-bio-60.qHtml: In the human cardiac conduction system, the physiological delay in action potential propagation (approximately 0.1 second) occurs at which node, and what is its physiological significance?
optionsHtml: Atrioventricular (AV) node; allows complete atrial mechanical contraction and ventricular end-diastolic filling before ventricular systole
Sinoatrial (SA) node; allows the left ventricle to relax before aortic valve opening
Bundle of His; prevents retrograde depolarization of Purkinje fibers
mdcat-b9-bio-60.explainHtml: Conduction velocity drops to ~0.05 m/s in the AV node (due to smaller fiber diameter and fewer gap junctions). This ~0.1 s delay ensures atria complete their mechanical systole, emptying blood into the ventricles before ventricular excitation and systole begin.

mdcat-b9-bio-61.qHtml: On a standard 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG), ventricular repolarization is represented by which waveform?
mdcat-b9-bio-61.explainHtml: On an ECG: P wave = atrial depolarization; QRS complex = ventricular depolarization (atrial repolarization is masked); T wave = ventricular repolarization; PR interval = time from onset of atrial activation to ventricular activation.

mdcat-b9-bio-62.qHtml: According to the Pressure-Flow Hypothesis (Münch hypothesis), phloem translocation from source to sink is driven by:
optionsHtml: A turgor pressure gradient (hydrostatic pressure differential) created by active sucrose loading at the source and osmotic water influx, contrasted with unloading at the sink
Active peristalsis of sieve tube companion cells driven by microfilament streaming
Electro-osmotic potential gradients across sieve plates mediated by potassium currents
Atmospheric evaporation pulling phloem sap through companion cell plasmodesmata
mdcat-b9-bio-62.explainHtml: Active loading of sucrose into sieve elements at source leaves decreases water potential, causing osmotic water influx from adjacent xylem and elevating hydrostatic (turgor) pressure. At sinks, sucrose is unloaded, water exits, and turgor pressure drops. Phloem sap moves by mass flow down this hydrostatic gradient.

mdcat-b9-bio-63.qHtml: In the cardiac cycle, the first heart sound ("lub" / S1) is produced by the acoustic vibrations associated with the closure of which valves at the onset of ventricular systole?
optionsHtml: The venous valves of the coronary sinus
mdcat-b9-bio-63.explainHtml: The first heart sound (S1, "lub") is caused by turbulent blood flow and vibrations of the ventricular walls and leaflets following closure of the atrioventricular (AV) valves (mitral and tricuspid) at the beginning of ventricular systole. S2 ("dub") is caused by semilunar valve closure at the onset of diastole.

mdcat-b9-bio-64.qHtml: Erythroblastosis fetalis (hemolytic disease of the newborn) typically occurs during a subsequent pregnancy when which parental and fetal Rh antigen combinations exist?
optionsHtml: Rh-negative mother pregnant with an Rh-positive fetus, after prior maternal sensitization to Rh(D) antigen
Rh-positive mother pregnant with an Rh-negative fetus
Rh-positive father and Rh-positive mother with identical ABO blood types
mdcat-b9-bio-64.explainHtml: If an Rh⁻ mother carries an Rh⁺ fetus, fetal red cells leaking into maternal circulation during delivery stimulate maternal anti-D IgG production. In a subsequent Rh⁺ pregnancy, maternal anti-D IgG crosses the placenta, causing immune hemolysis of fetal RBCs (erythroblastosis fetalis).

mdcat-b9-bio-65.qHtml: Which plasma protein accounts for approximately 60% of total blood plasma proteins and is the principal determinant of plasma colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure, preventing peripheral edema?
optionsHtml: α-1 antitrypsin
mdcat-b9-bio-65.explainHtml: Albumin, synthesized by hepatocytes, generates ~80% of the normal plasma oncotic pressure (~25 mmHg). This inward osmotic force balances outward capillary hydrostatic pressure according to Starling's forces; hypoalbuminemia leads to fluid extravasation and peripheral edema.

mdcat-b9-bio-66.qHtml: The opening of stomata in plant leaves during dayl is initiated biochemically by:
optionsHtml: Active proton pumping (H⁺-ATPase) out of guard cells, which hyperpolarizes the membrane and drives massive K⁺ and Cl⁻ influx, leading to osmotic water entry and swelling
Efflux of malate and potassium ions into subsidiary cells, causing guard cell flaccidity
Synthesis of high concentrations of abscisic acid (ABA) within guard cell chloroplasts
Rapid degradation of guard cell starch into insoluble cellulose microfibrils
mdcat-b9-bio-66.explainHtml: Blue l activates plasma membrane H⁺-ATPases in guard cells, pumping protons out. The resulting hyperpolarization activates inward-rectifying voltage-gated K⁺ channels. Influx of K⁺ and Cl⁻/malate drops guard cell water potential, causing osmotic water uptake. Turgor increases, bowing radially micellated cellulose microfibrils and opening the pore.

mdcat-b9-bio-67.qHtml: In the human circulatory system, which anatomical vessel possesses the greatest total cross-sectional area and the lowest velocity of blood flow, optimizing capillary exchange?
mdcat-b9-bio-67.explainHtml: By the law of continuity (Flow = Velocity × Total Cross-Sectional Area), velocity is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area. Although individual capillaries are microscopic (5-10 μm), their vast parallel branching gives a total cross-sectional area of ~4500 cm2 (vs ~4.5 cm2 for the aorta), dropping velocity to <0.1 cm/s to allow adequate diffusion time.

mdcat-b9-bio-68.qHtml: In the mammalian nephron, the single-effect countercurrent multiplier mechanism that establishes the hyperosmotic corticomedullary interstitial gradient depends crucially on which property of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle?
optionsHtml: Active transport of Na⁺, K⁺, and 2Cl⁻ (NKCC2 cotransporter) into the interstitium while being completely impermeable to water
High passive permeability to water via aquaporin-1 channels with no active salt transport
Active secretion of urea into the tubular fluid under aldosterone regulation
Passive paracellular diffusion of bicarbonate coupled to glucose reabsorption
mdcat-b9-bio-68.explainHtml: The thick ascending limb actively reabsorbs Na⁺, K⁺, and 2Cl⁻ via the apical NKCC2 cotransporter into the medullary interstitium. Because it is strictly impermeable to water, solutes enter the interstitium without water, building a progressive osmotic gradient up to 1200 mOsm/L at the hairpin turn.

mdcat-b9-bio-69.qHtml: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH / arginine vasopressin) increases the reabsorption of water in the collecting duct by binding to basolateral V2 receptors and stimulating:
optionsHtml: cAMP-PKA pathway signaling, triggering exocytic trafficking of Aquaporin-2 (AQP2) water channels to the apical membrane
Direct opening of voltage-gated potassium channels in intercalated cells
Inhibition of basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps in principal cells
Cleavage of luminal angiotensinogen to active angiotensin II
mdcat-b9-bio-69.explainHtml: ADH binds Gs-coupled V2 receptors on the basolateral surface of principal cells, elevating intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) and activating Protein Kinase A (PKA). This phosphorylates Aquaporin-2 (AQP2) storage vesicles, inducing their fusion with the apical plasma membrane, permitting osmotic water reabsorption.

mdcat-b9-bio-70.qHtml: In the ornithine-urea cycle occurring in the human liver, which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting, ATP-dependent committed step inside the mitochondrial matrix?
mdcat-b9-bio-70.explainHtml: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS-I) catalyzes the condensation of ammonia (NH4⁺), bicarbonate (HCO3⁻), and 2 ATP to form carbamoyl phosphate inside hepatic mitochondria. CPS-I requires N-acetylglutamate (NAG) as an obligatory allosteric activator and represents the committed pacemaker of ureagenesis.

mdcat-b9-bio-71.qHtml: Juxtaglomerular granular cells located in the afferent arteriole of the renal corpuscle synthesize, store, and secrete the proteolytic enzyme renin in response to:
optionsHtml: Decreased renal perfusion pressure, reduced NaCl delivery to the macula densa, and sympathetic β-1 adrenergic stimulation
Severe systemic hypertension and elevated atrial stretch (ANP release)
High hydrostatic filtration pressure across glomerular podocyte pedicels
mdcat-b9-bio-71.explainHtml: Renin release is triggered by: (1) decreased stretch in afferent arteriolar baroreceptors (renal hypoperfusion), (2) decreased NaCl delivery sensed by macula densa cells in the early distal tubule, and (3) increased renal sympathetic nerve activity acting via β1-adrenergic receptors.

mdcat-b9-bio-72.qHtml: Freshwater bony fishes (such as carp and trout) face the constant osmotic danger of water influx and solute loss. How do they maintain homeostatic osmoregulatory balance?
optionsHtml: Excreting large volumes of dilute hypotonic urine and actively absorbing salts (Na⁺, Cl⁻) across specialized gill chloride cells
Drinking copiously from surrounding river water and actively excreting concentrated hypertonic urine
Accumulating high concentrations of urea and trimethylamine oxide (TMAO) in their muscle tissues
Ceasing glomerular filtration entirely through aglomerular nephrons
mdcat-b9-bio-72.explainHtml: Freshwater teleosts are hyperosmotic to their surrounding hypotonic medium. They actively pump Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions inward across gill ionocytes against concentration gradients, produce copious volumes of very dilute urine, and minimize drinking to prevent internal fluid dilution.

mdcat-b9-bio-73.qHtml: Which anatomical zone of the adrenal cortex synthesizes and secretes aldosterone in response to elevated extracellular potassium (K⁺) or circulating angiotensin II?
mdcat-b9-bio-73.explainHtml: The adrenal cortex has three zones: (1) Zona glomerulosa (outermost) secretes mineralocorticoids (aldosterone); (2) Zona fasciculata secretes glucocorticoids (cortisol); (3) Zona reticularis (innermost) secretes androgens (DHEA).

mdcat-b9-bio-74.qHtml: In the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT), approximately what percentage of filtered water, sodium, and chloride is isotonically reabsorbed under normal physiological conditions?
mdcat-b9-bio-74.explainHtml: The proximal convoluted tubule is the primary site of obligatory reabsorption, recovering ~65-70% of filtered water and NaCl, 100% of filtered glucose and amino acids, and ~85% of filtered bicarbonate.

mdcat-b9-bio-75.qHtml: In physiological thermoregulation, non-shivering thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue (BAT) generates heat without producing ATP via which mitochondrial uncoupling protein?
mdcat-b9-bio-75.explainHtml: Thermogenin (uncoupling protein 1, UCP1) provides an alternative inner mitochondrial membrane conductance pathway that allows protons to flow back down into the matrix, bypassing ATP synthase. The free energy of the proton electrochemical gradient is dissipated directly as heat.

mdcat-b9-bio-76.qHtml: Which nitrogenous waste product requires the least volume of water for safe excretion due to its extremely low water solubility and is excreted as a semisolid paste by reptiles and birds?
mdcat-b9-bio-76.explainHtml: Uric acid is virtually insoluble in water (precipitates as a crystalline paste). Uricotelic organisms (birds, terrestrial reptiles, insects) expend more ATP to synthesize uric acid from purines, saving massive amounts of body water compared to ammonotelic or ureotelic organisms.

mdcat-b9-bio-77.qHtml: According to the Bohr effect, which set of physiological changes in metabolically active systemic tissues shifts the hemoglobin oxygen-dissociation curve to the r, promoting oxygen unloading?
optionsHtml: Decreased pH (increased H⁺), increased PCO2, increased temperature, and elevated 2,3-BPG
Increased pH, decreased PCO2, decreased temperature, and decreased 2,3-BPG
Decreased PCO2 and elevated carbon monoxide concentration
Complete saturation of all four heme iron centers with fetal hemoglobin
mdcat-b9-bio-77.explainHtml: A rightward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve (Bohr effect) means hemoglobin has a lower affinity for O2 at any given PO2, facilitating O2 unloading to active tissues. This shift is triggered by high metabolic activity: increased [H⁺] (low pH), increased PCO2, elevated temperature, and increased 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG).

mdcat-b9-bio-78.qHtml: What is the primary chemical form in which carbon dioxide (CO2) is transported in systemic venous blood from peripheral tissues to the pulmonary capillaries?
optionsHtml: As bicarbonate ions (HCO3⁻) dissolved in blood plasma (accounting for ~70% of total CO2)
As carbaminohemoglobin bound to the globin amino termini (~70%)
As physically dissolved CO2 gas bubbles inside erythrocyte cytoplasm (~85%)
As carbonic acid bound directly to plasma albumin (~60%)
mdcat-b9-bio-78.explainHtml: CO2 is transported in three forms: (1) Bicarbonate ions (HCO3⁻) in plasma (~70%), generated within RBCs by carbonic anhydrase and exported via the chloride shift; (2) Carbamino compounds bound to globin amino groups (~23%); (3) Physically dissolved gas in plasma (~7%).

mdcat-b9-bio-79.qHtml: The chloride shift (Hamburger phenomenon) across the erythrocyte plasma membrane during carbon dioxide uptake in systemic capillaries involves:
optionsHtml: Electroneutral exchange of intracellular bicarbonate (HCO3⁻) for extracellular chloride (Cl⁻) via the Band 3 (AE1) anion exchanger
Active transport of Cl⁻ out of erythrocytes by an ATP-driven chloride pump
Direct coupling of sodium influx with potassium efflux through open CFTR pores
Precipitation of calcium chloride within the erythrocyte cytoskeleton
mdcat-b9-bio-79.explainHtml: Inside erythrocytes, carbonic anhydrase converts CO2 + H2O into H⁺ + HCO3⁻. To maintain cellular electroneutrality as accumulating HCO3⁻ diffuses down its gradient into plasma, the Band 3 anion exchanger (AE1) imports one Cl⁻ ion into the erythrocyte for every HCO3⁻ exported.

mdcat-b9-bio-80.qHtml: Pulmonary surfactant, which reduces alveolar surface tension and prevents end-expiratory atelectasis (alveolar collapse), is synthesized and secreted by:
optionsHtml: Type II alveolar epithelial pneumocytes (rich in dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine)
Type I flat squamous alveolar pneumocytes
mdcat-b9-bio-80.explainHtml: Type II pneumocytes (great alveolar cells) secrete pulmonary surfactant, a complex of dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) and surfactant apoproteins (SP-A, B, C, D). By disrupting hydrogen bonds between water molecules at the air-liquid interface, surfactant dramatically decreases surface tension, especially at small alveolar radii (LaPlace's law), preventing collapse.

mdcat-b9-bio-81.qHtml: In the physiological chemical control of ventilation in a healthy human at sea level, the primary stimulus driving the central chemoreceptors located on the ventrolateral surface of the medulla oblongata is:
optionsHtml: Elevation of arterial PCO2 which diffuses across the blood-brain barrier and lowers cerebrospinal fluid pH (increasing [H⁺])
A minor drop in arterial PO2 below 95 mmHg sensed directly by the medullary respiratory center
Direct contact of arterial bicarbonate ions with medullary neuronal cell bodies
Afferent vagal input triggered by lung overinflation
mdcat-b9-bio-81.explainHtml: Arterial H⁺ cannot easily cross the blood-brain barrier, but lipid-soluble CO2 diffuses readily into cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). There, carbonic anhydrase converts it into H⁺ + HCO3⁻. The resulting drop in CSF pH directly excites central chemoreceptors on the medulla, making PaCO2 the primary homeostatic driver of resting ventilation.

mdcat-b9-bio-82.qHtml: In avian respiration, gas exchange occurs with exceptional efficiency through parabronchi via which anatomical mechanism?
optionsHtml: Unidirectional airflow driven by non-vascularized air sacs, operating with a cross-current gas exchange system
Bidirectional tidal alveolar ventilation identical to mammals
Spiracular tracheal tubes pumping air directly into individual myocytes
mdcat-b9-bio-82.explainHtml: Birds possess a system of anterior and posterior air sacs that act as bellows to pump air unidirectionally through rigid, tubular parabronchi over two complete respiratory cycles. Blood flows perpendicular to parabronchial airflow in a cross-current configuration, extracting substantially more oxygen than mammalian tidal lungs.

mdcat-b9-bio-83.qHtml: What is the volume of air inspired or expired during each normal, quiet resting respiratory cycle in an average healthy adult human?
mdcat-b9-bio-83.explainHtml: Tidal volume (TV) is the volume of air breathed in or out with each normal resting breath, averaging ~500 mL in a healthy 70 kg adult (with ~150 mL remaining in anatomical dead space).

mdcat-b9-bio-84.qHtml: Why does carbon monoxide (CO) inhalation cause rapid, severe tissue hypoxia without necessarily triggering immediate respiratory distress or dyspnea in the victim?
optionsHtml: CO binds hemoglobin with ~200-250 times greater affinity than O2 and locks it in the high-affinity R-state, while arterial PO2 and peripheral chemoreceptors remain normal
CO directly destroys central chemoreceptors in the medullary reticular formation
CO oxidizes all Fe2⁺ into Fe3⁺, forming green sulfhemoglobin precipitates
CO instantly paralyzes the phrenic nerve and diaphragm neuromuscular junctions
mdcat-b9-bio-84.explainHtml: Carbon monoxide binds to Fe2⁺ of heme with ~200-250 times the affinity of O2, forming carboxyhemoglobin. It severely limits O2 content and alters hemoglobin cooperativity, shifting the curve left and preventing O2 release to tissues. Because dissolved PaO2 remains normal, peripheral chemoreceptors do not stimulate dyspnea.

mdcat-b9-bio-85.qHtml: The Haldane effect describes the phenomenon wherein:
optionsHtml: Deoxygenation of blood increases the affinity of hemoglobin for carbon dioxide and H⁺, enhancing CO2 loading at tissues
Elevated oxygen levels cause vasodilation of peripheral arterioles
Lower blood pH decreases the affinity of myoglobin for dissolved nitric oxide
High alveolar nitrogen concentrations induce surfactant synthesis in preterm neonates
mdcat-b9-bio-85.explainHtml: The Haldane effect states that deoxygenated hemoglobin has a higher affinity for CO2 (forming carbamino compounds) and binds H⁺ more readily than oxyhemoglobin. Thus, O2 unloading in tissues facilitates CO2 uptake into venous blood.

mdcat-b9-bio-86.qHtml: During the firing of a neuronal action potential, the rapid rising phase of depolarization from threshold (-55 mV) to +30 mV is mediated by:
optionsHtml: Massive, rapid influx of Na⁺ through opened voltage-gated sodium channels
Rapid efflux of K⁺ through opened voltage-gated potassium channels
Active pumping of 3 Na⁺ outward by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump
Influx of chloride ions through GABA-A receptor channels
mdcat-b9-bio-86.explainHtml: When local depolarization reaches the threshold potential (~ -55 mV), activation gates (m-gates) of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open rapidly. Driven by both concentration and electrical gradients, Na⁺ surges into the axoplasm, driving the membrane potential toward the sodium equilibrium potential (+60 mV).

mdcat-b9-bio-87.qHtml: In a chemical synapse, the influx of which ion into the presynaptic terminal through voltage-gated channels is the immediate physiological trigger for synaptic vesicle exocytosis?
optionsHtml: Calcium (Ca2⁺)
Magnesium (Mg2⁺)
mdcat-b9-bio-87.explainHtml: Depolarization of the presynaptic axon terminal opens voltage-gated Ca2⁺ channels. Calcium influx down its steep gradient activates synaptotagmin, triggering SNARE-complex-mediated fusion of neurotransmitter vesicles with the presynaptic membrane and release of neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft.

mdcat-b9-bio-88.qHtml: Saltatory conduction, which markedly increases the velocity of action potential propagation along myelinated axons, occurs because:
optionsHtml: Voltage-gated Na⁺ and K⁺ channels are concentrated at high density exclusively at the Nodes of Ranvier, allowing the impulse to jump between nodes
Myelin sheath contains electron-conducting copper ions that transmit currents at the speed of l
Action potentials travel continuously through the cytoplasmic core without membrane interactions
Schwann cells generate ATP that propels neurotransmitters down the axon tube
mdcat-b9-bio-88.explainHtml: The lipid-rich myelin sheath acts as an electrical insulator with high resistance and low capacitance, preventing current leakage along the internodes. Depolarizing ionic currents flow passively and rapidly electrotonically down the axon, regenerating action potentials only at the unmyelinated Nodes of Ranvier where voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are densely packed.

mdcat-b9-bio-89.qHtml: Which endocrine hormone, synthesized in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary, stimulates forceful uterine myometrial contractions via a positive feedback loop during parturition?
mdcat-b9-bio-89.explainHtml: Oxytocin is synthesized by magnocellular neurosecretory neurons in the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei of the hypothalamus and stored in the posterior pituitary. During labor, cervical stretch signals hypothalamic oxytocin release (Ferguson reflex), stimulating stronger contractions in a classic positive feedback loop.

mdcat-b9-bio-90.qHtml: Cushing's syndrome is a clinical endocrine disorder characterized by central obesity, moon facies, buffalo hump, and hypertension, caused by chronic hypersecretion of:
mdcat-b9-bio-90.explainHtml: Cushing's syndrome results from prolonged exposure to excess circulating glucocorticoids (cortisol), whether from an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease), adrenal cortical adenoma, or exogenous therapeutic corticosteroid administration.

mdcat-b9-bio-91.qHtml: Which plant hormone is primarily synthesized in root apical meristems and transported upward through xylem to promote cell division, shoot initiation in tissue culture, and delay leaf senescence?
mdcat-b9-bio-91.explainHtml: Cytokinins are adenine-derived phytohormones synthesized primarily in active root tips and translocated via xylem to shoots. They stimulate cytokinesis (cell division), promote lateral bud outgrowth by releasing apical dominance, and retard protein degradation (delaying senescence).

mdcat-b9-bio-92.qHtml: In the phototropic curvature of an Avena (oat) coleoptile toward unilateral blue l, what is the underlying physiological mechanism explained by the Cholodny-Went model?
optionsHtml: Auxin (IAA) is laterally redistributed to the shaded side, stimulating proton extrusion (acid growth) and asymmetric cell elongation on the dark side
Auxin is selectively degraded on the shaded side, causing cell shrinkage
Ethylene gas accumulates on the illuminated side, driving localized apical mitosis
Gibberellins polymerize cellulose microfibrils exclusively toward the l vector
mdcat-b9-bio-92.explainHtml: Unidirectional blue l is sensed by phototropin receptors, triggering lateral PIN-mediated auxin translocation to the shaded side of the shoot tip. Increased auxin on the shaded side stimulates plasma membrane H⁺-ATPases, activating expansins that loosen cell walls (acid growth hypothesis), causing the shaded side to elongate faster and bending the shoot toward l.

mdcat-b9-bio-93.qHtml: Which structural region of the human brain functions as the primary autonomic, neuroendocrine, and visceral homeostatic integration center, regulating thirst, appetite, circadian rhythms, and core body temperature?
mdcat-b9-bio-93.explainHtml: The hypothalamus lies ventral to the thalamus and forms the floor of the third ventricle. It houses specialized nuclei controlling core body temperature, water balance (osmoreceptors), food intake (arcuate and satiety centers), and circadian clock pacing (suprachiasmatic nucleus), linking the nervous and endocrine systems.

mdcat-b9-bio-94.qHtml: In skeletal muscle sarcomeres, which protein is a giant elastic filament that anchors the thick myosin filaments to the Z-disc, providing passive elasticity and preventing overstretching?
optionsHtml: α-actinin
mdcat-b9-bio-94.explainHtml: Titin is the largest known single polypeptide (~3-4 MDa). It spans half a sarcomere from the Z-disc to the M-line, acting as a molecular bungee cord that centers thick myosin filaments within the sarcomere and provides passive restorative tension during stretch.

mdcat-b9-bio-95.qHtml: During the sliding filament cross-bridge cycle of skeletal muscle contraction, what direct biochemical event causes the myosin head to detach from the actin filament?
optionsHtml: Binding of a new molecule of ATP to the myosin nucleotide-binding site
Hydrolysis of ATP into ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi)
Release of inorganic phosphate (Pi) triggering the power stroke
Sequestration of calcium back into the terminal cisternae by SERCA
mdcat-b9-bio-95.explainHtml: Binding of a new ATP molecule to the myosin head induces a low-affinity conformational state, causing instantaneous dissociation of the myosin head from the actin filament. In death, depletion of ATP prevents this detachment, locking cross-bridges in the stiff state known as rigor mortis.

mdcat-b9-bio-96.qHtml: The functional calcium sensor protein associated with the actin thin filament in skeletal and cardiac muscle that undergoes a conformational change upon binding Ca2⁺ to displace tropomyosin is:
mdcat-b9-bio-96.explainHtml: The troponin complex has three subunits: Troponin C (binds up to four Ca2⁺ ions), Troponin I (inhibits actin-myosin interaction), and Troponin T (binds tropomyosin). Ca2⁺ binding to TnC induces a conformational shift that pulls tropomyosin into the actin groove, exposing myosin-binding sites on actin.

mdcat-b9-bio-97.qHtml: Tetanus toxin (tetanospasmin), produced by Clostridium tetani, causes spastic muscle paralysis and lockjaw by which specific molecular neurotoxic action?
optionsHtml: Cleaving synaptobrevin (VAMP) in inhibitory interneurons (Renshaw cells), preventing exocytosis of GABA and glycine
Blocking nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at skeletal motor endplates
Inhibiting the sodium-potassium ATPase pump in skeletal muscle sarcolemma
Preventing calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum ryanodine receptors
mdcat-b9-bio-97.explainHtml: Tetanospasmin undergoes retrograde axonal transport to spinal motor inhibitory interneurons (Renshaw cells). Its l chain acts as a zinc endopeptidase that cleaves synaptobrevin (SNARE protein), blocking the release of inhibitory neurotransmitters glycine and GABA. This leaves alpha motor neurons persistently uninhibited, causing spastic tetanic spasms.

mdcat-b9-bio-98.qHtml: In bone histology, the concentric cylindrical structural units that constitute compact (cortical) bone, consisting of central canals surrounded by concentric lamellae, are designated as:
mdcat-b9-bio-98.explainHtml: The structural and functional unit of compact bone is the osteon (Haversian system). Each osteon comprises concentric rings of mineralized collagenous matrix (lamellae) surrounding a central Haversian canal containing blood vessels and nerves, with osteocytes residing in lacunae interconnected by canaliculi.

mdcat-b9-bio-99.qHtml: Which bone cell type is multinucleated, originates from the monocyte-macrophage hematopoietic lineage, and resides in Howship's lacunae to resorb bone matrix by secreting acid and cathepsin K?
mdcat-b9-bio-99.explainHtml: Osteoclasts are giant multinucleated cells formed by fusion of monocyte/macrophage precursors. They adhere to the bone surface via integrins, create a sealed resorption compartment (Howship's lacuna), and pump H⁺ via V-ATPases and secrete cathepsin K to dissolve mineral and digest collagen.

mdcat-b9-bio-100.qHtml: What type of synovial joint permits multiaxial movement across all three planes, providing the greatest range of motion among all joint classifications in the human skeleton?
optionsHtml: Ball-and-socket joint (e.g., glenohumeral and hip joints)
Hinge joint (e.g., elbow and interphalangeal joints)
Saddle joint (e.g., carpometacarpal joint of the thumb)
mdcat-b9-bio-100.explainHtml: Ball-and-socket joints (spheroidal joints) consist of a globular head fitting into a cup-like cavity (e.g., shoulder and hip). They permit flexion-extension, abduction-adduction, circumduction, and rotation (multiaxial movement).

mdcat-b9-bio-101.qHtml: In human skeletal muscle, the invaginations of the sarcolemma that project deep into the muscle fiber interior to conduct action potentials rapidly to every myofibril are known as:
mdcat-b9-bio-101.explainHtml: T-tubules are deep tubular extensions of the plasma membrane (sarcolemma) running perpendicularly across myofibrils at the A-I band junctions in mammalian muscle. Together with two flanking terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, they form triads that deliver depolarization instantly to dihydropyridine receptors (DHPRs).

mdcat-b9-bio-102.qHtml: Which plant anatomical tissue is composed of dead, heavily lignified cells with thick secondary walls that provide rigid tensile support to non-growing, mature plant organs?
mdcat-b9-bio-102.explainHtml: Sclerenchyma cells possess thick, lignified secondary cell walls and are typically non-living at functional maturity. They occur as elongated fibers or irregular sclereids (stone cells), providing structural rigidity and resistance to compression and bending.

mdcat-b9-bio-103.qHtml: In the human ovarian cycle, the mid-cycle surge of which pituitary gonadotropin is the direct trigger for the rupture of the mature Graafian follicle and ovulation?
mdcat-b9-bio-103.explainHtml: High, sustained levels of estradiol produced by the dominant Graafian follicle switch estrogen feedback from negative to positive on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary. This induces a massive preovulatory surge of LH, which activates proteolytic collagenases and prostaglandins to rupture the follicular wall within 24-36 hours.

mdcat-b9-bio-104.qHtml: Following ovulation, the collapsed follicular wall transforms into the corpus luteum, which secretes high amounts of which hormone to maintain the secretory endometrium for blastocyst implantation?
mdcat-b9-bio-104.explainHtml: Under basal LH stimulation, luteinized granulosa and theca cells of the corpus luteum secrete large quantities of progesterone (and moderate estradiol). Progesterone converts proliferative endometrium into a vascular, tortuous secretory phase suitable for embryo implantation and suppresses new follicular recruitment.

mdcat-b9-bio-105.qHtml: In human testes, which cells form the structural basis of the blood-testis barrier, phagocytose redundant spermatid cytoplasm, and secrete androgen-binding protein (ABP)?
mdcat-b9-bio-105.explainHtml: Sertoli cells line the seminiferous tubules. Their t junctions (zonula occludens) establish the blood-testis barrier, shielding haploid developing spermatids from autoimmune destruction. Sertoli cells nourish spermatocytes, secrete androgen-binding protein (ABP) to concentrate intratesticular testosterone, and secrete inhibin.

mdcat-b9-bio-106.qHtml: During mammalian fertilization, the acrosome reaction is initiated when sperm bind specifically to which glycoprotein of the oocyte zona pellucida?
optionsHtml: Integrin α-V β-3
mdcat-b9-bio-106.explainHtml: Sperm capacitation primes the sperm head. Upon encountering the oocyte, the sperm surface receptor binds to ZP3 on the zona pellucida. This triggers massive Ca2⁺ influx through CatSper channels, inducing outer acrosomal membrane fusion and exocytosis of hydrolytic enzymes (hyaluronidase and acrosin).

mdcat-b9-bio-107.qHtml: The slow block to polyspermy (cortical reaction) in mammalian fertilization is executed when sperm-egg membrane fusion triggers:
optionsHtml: An intracellular wave of free Ca2⁺, stimulating cortical granule exocytosis that enzymatically cleaves ZP proteins and hardens the zona pellucida
Rapid depolarization of the egg oolemma driven by massive sodium influx lasting only 60 seconds
Immediate extrusion of all cortical mitochondria into the perivitelline space
Spontaneous synthesis of a thick chitinous shell around the secondary oocyte
mdcat-b9-bio-107.explainHtml: Sperm-egg fusion releases phospholipase C-zeta, triggering oscillatory intracellular Ca2⁺ waves. This causes thousands of cortical granules located just under the oolemma to fuse with the membrane, releasing ovastacin and other proteases that cleave ZP2 and ZP3 (zona reaction), permanently preventing secondary sperm entry.

mdcat-b9-bio-108.qHtml: In angiosperm double fertilization, one sperm nucleus fuses with the egg nucleus to form the diploid zygote (2n), while the second sperm nucleus fuses with:
optionsHtml: The two haploid polar nuclei of the central cell to produce the triploid endosperm (3n)
The two degenerating synergids to produce the seed coat (testa)
The three antipodal cells to produce the suspensor tissue
The nucellus to form the fruit pericarp
mdcat-b9-bio-108.explainHtml: Double fertilization is unique to angiosperms: of the two male gametes delivered by the pollen tube, one fertilizes the egg cell (producing the 2n zygote), and the other fuses with the diploid central cell (containing two polar nuclei), forming the primary triploid (3n) endosperm nucleus that develops into nutritive tissue.

mdcat-b9-bio-109.qHtml: Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by which corkscrew-shaped spirochete bacterium, characterized in its primary stage by a painless indurated chancre?
mdcat-b9-bio-109.explainHtml: Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum is a microaerophilic, motile spirochete that causes syphilis. Primary syphilis presents as a solitary, painless, indurated ulcer (chancre) at the site of inoculation, accompanied by regional lymphadenopathy.

mdcat-b9-bio-110.qHtml: In the developing human blastocyst, which cell layer gives rise directly to the embryo proper, embryonic germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm), and extraembryonic mesoderm?
mdcat-b9-bio-110.explainHtml: At the blastocyst stage (day 5-6 post-fertilization), cells segregate into: (1) an outer single layer of trophoblast cells (which form the embryonic portion of the placenta), and (2) an inner cell mass (embryoblast), pluripotential cells that give rise to all tissues of the embryo proper.

mdcat-b9-bio-111.qHtml: In eukaryotic DNA replication, which enzyme synthesizes a short RNA primer complementary to the template DNA strand to provide a free 3'-OH group for DNA polymerase extension?
optionsHtml: DNA Primase (part of the Pol α-primase complex)
mdcat-b9-bio-111.explainHtml: All known DNA polymerases require a pre-existing 3'-hydroxyl (-OH) terminus to add incoming deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs). DNA primase (an RNA polymerase) synthesizes de novo a short (8-12 nt) RNA primer complementary to the template, enabling DNA polymerases to initiate elongation.

mdcat-b9-bio-112.qHtml: Meselson and Stahl demonstrated that DNA replication occurs by a semiconservative mechanism using which isotope labeling technique?
optionsHtml: Growing E. coli in heavy ¹⁵N-ammonium chloride medium followed by density-gradient centrifugation in cesium chloride (CsCl)
Labeling bacteriophage T2 proteins with radioactive ³⁵S and DNA with ³²P
X-ray diffraction analysis of sodium thymonucleate crystalline fibers
Incorporating tritiated thymidine into human HeLa cell chromosomes
mdcat-b9-bio-112.explainHtml: Meselson and Stahl (1958) grew E. coli in ¹⁵NH4Cl (heavy nitrogen) and then shifted them to ¹⁴N medium. CsCl equilibrium density-gradient centrifugation after one generation showed a single hybrid ¹⁵N-¹⁴N band, and after two generations showed equal amounts of hybrid and pure ¹⁴N DNA, proving semiconservative replication.

mdcat-b9-bio-113.qHtml: In eukaryotic pre-mRNA processing, the removal of non-coding introns and ligation of coding exons is executed by the spliceosome, which is assembled from:
optionsHtml: Small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs: U1, U2, U4, U5, U6) and associated proteins
RNA Polymerase II CTD repeats and Rho termination factor
DNA topoisomerase II and DNA ligase III
mdcat-b9-bio-113.explainHtml: Nuclear pre-mRNA splicing occurs via a macromolecular ribonucleoprotein complex termed the spliceosome, composed of five small nuclear RNAs (U1, U2, U4, U5, U6) complexed with proteins (snRNPs). They recognize invariant 5' splice donor (GU), 3' splice acceptor (AG), and branch-point adenine sequences.

mdcat-b9-bio-114.qHtml: Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive bleeding disorder caused by a deficiency of clotting Factor VIII. If a normal woman whose father had hemophilia marries a healthy man, what is the probability that their first son will be affected?
mdcat-b9-bio-114.explainHtml: Because her father had hemophilia (XʰY), the woman must have inherited his Xʰ chromosome, making her an obligate carrier (XᴴXʰ). The husband is normal (XᴴY). Given that the child is a son (XY), he has a 50% probability of receiving the maternal Xʰ allele and being affected (XʰY).

mdcat-b9-bio-115.qHtml: In transcription, which consensus hexameric sequence located approximately 10 base pairs upstream of the transcription initiation site in prokaryotic promoters is recognized by the RNA polymerase sigma factor?
mdcat-b9-bio-115.explainHtml: In prokaryotes, the core RNA polymerase associates with a sigma factor (σ70) to recognize consensus promoter elements: the -35 sequence (TTGACA) and the -10 sequence (TATAAT, known as the Pribnow box), where unwinding of the DNA double helix initiates.

mdcat-b9-bio-116.qHtml: Which type of gene mutation results from an insertion or deletion of a number of nucleotides that is not a multiple of three, altering the translational reading frame for all downstream codons?
mdcat-b9-bio-116.explainHtml: Because the genetic code is read in non-overlapping triplets (codons), the insertion or deletion of 1 or 2 nucleotides (or any number not divisible by 3) changes the reading frame downstream of the mutation. This frameshift usually leads to garbled peptide sequences and premature stop codons.

mdcat-b9-bio-117.qHtml: According to the lac operon model formulated by Jacob and Monod, the lac repressor protein encoded by the lacI gene binds to which regulatory DNA element to prevent transcription in the absence of lactose?
optionsHtml: The β-galactosidase structural gene (lacZ)
mdcat-b9-bio-117.explainHtml: The lac repressor is a homotetramer that binds tightly to the lac operator (lacO) sequence, which physically overlaps the promoter. This sterically blocks RNA polymerase from initiating transcription of the polycistronic structural genes (lacZ, lacY, lacA) when allolactose inducer is absent.

mdcat-b9-bio-118.qHtml: Which of the following describes the stop (nonsense) codons that signal the termination of translation in the standard universal genetic code?
mdcat-b9-bio-118.explainHtml: Of the 64 codons, 61 code for amino acids, while 3 (UAA, UAG, and UGA) do not specify any amino acid and are not recognized by normal tRNAs. Instead, they are bound by protein release factors (eRF1 in eukaryotes; RF1/RF2 in prokaryotes), terminating translation.

mdcat-b9-bio-119.qHtml: In recombinant DNA technology, Type II restriction endonucleases (such as EcoRI) are widely utilized molecular tools because they cleave double-stranded DNA at:
optionsHtml: Specific palindromic recognition sequences, often generating cohesive ("sticky") staggered single-stranded overhangs
Random single-stranded pyrimidine tracts without sequence specificity
Methylated cytosine residues located exclusively at telomeric ends
The 5' cap of eukaryotic mature messenger RNAs
mdcat-b9-bio-119.explainHtml: Type II restriction endonucleases recognize specific palindromic sequences (e.g., EcoRI recognizes 5'-GAATTC-3') and cleave both strands at defined phosphodiester bonds within the sequence, producing self-complementary cohesive ("sticky") ends that can anneal with foreign fragments digested by the same enzyme.

mdcat-b9-bio-120.qHtml: In the Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR), what is the biochemical role of Taq DNA polymerase, and why is it preferred over human DNA polymerase?
optionsHtml: It is isolated from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus and resists thermal denaturation during the 94-95°C denaturation step
It possesses 3' to 5' exonuclease proofreading activity that is 100 times faster than eukaryotic polymerases
It can synthesize DNA directly from an RNA template without primer annealing
It operates at room temperature without requiring divalent magnesium ions
mdcat-b9-bio-120.explainHtml: Taq polymerase is extracted from Thermus aquaticus, a thermophile living in geothermal hot springs. Its optimal temperature is ~72°C, and it withstands repeated exposure to 94-95°C without denaturation, eliminating the need to add fresh enzyme after each thermal cycle.

mdcat-b9-bio-121.qHtml: In blue-white colony screening of recombinant bacterial transformants using plasmids like pUC19, insertion of foreign target DNA into the multiple cloning site (MCS) results in:
optionsHtml: Insertional inactivation of the lacZ' gene, preventing functional β-galactosidase production and producing white colonies on X-gal plates
Activation of the lacZ' gene, resulting in deep blue colony pigmentation on IPTG/X-gal agar
Inactivation of the ampicillin resistance gene, killing recombinant bacteria
Constitutive GFP fluorescence under ultraviolet excitation
mdcat-b9-bio-121.explainHtml: The Multiple Cloning Site (MCS) is located within the coding sequence of the lacZ' α-peptide. Insertion of a foreign DNA fragment interrupts the reading frame (insertional inactivation). Recombinant bacteria cannot produce functional β-galactosidase and cannot hydrolyze X-gal (5-bromo-4-chloro-3-indolyl-β-D-galactoside), forming white colonies.

mdcat-b9-bio-122.qHtml: In forensic DNA profiling, Short Tandem Repeats (STRs) are analyzed primarily by which combination of molecular techniques?
optionsHtml: Multiplex PCR amplification using fluorescent primers followed by capillary electrophoresis
Southern blotting hybridized with whole mitochondrial genome probes
Direct Sanger sequencing of the entire Y chromosome
Paper chromatography of radioactive nucleotide monophosphates
mdcat-b9-bio-122.explainHtml: Modern forensic DNA profiling assesses polymorphism in length of STR loci (2-6 bp repeating core units, e.g., TH01, vWA). Flanking primers amplify the loci via multiplex fluorescent PCR, and products are resolved by high-resolution capillary electrophoresis to determine the number of repeats.

mdcat-b9-bio-123.qHtml: What is the role of DNA ligase in molecular cloning?
optionsHtml: Catalyzing the formation of covalent phosphodiester bonds between adjacent 3'-OH and 5'-phosphate DNA termini
Cleaving interior phosphodiester bonds at specific 6-base palindromic sites
Adding single adenylate nucleotides to the 3' ends of PCR products
Removing terminal phosphate groups to prevent plasmid recircularization
mdcat-b9-bio-123.explainHtml: DNA ligase (typically from bacteriophage T4) utilizes ATP (or NAD⁺ in bacteria) to seal nicks in the double-stranded DNA backbone by forming a covalent 3'-5' phosphodiester linkage between juxtaposed 3'-hydroxyl and 5'-monophosphate ends.

mdcat-b9-bio-124.qHtml: Which molecular probe technique is specifically designed for the detection and semi-quantitative analysis of specific target RNA transcripts separated by gel electrophoresis?
mdcat-b9-bio-124.explainHtml: Blotting techniques: Southern blot = DNA detection; Northern blot = RNA detection (evaluating gene expression/transcripts); Western blot = protein detection using antibodies; Eastern blot = post-translational protein modifications (lipids/glycans).

mdcat-b9-bio-125.qHtml: In the CRISPR-Cas9 genome-editing system derived from bacterial adaptive immune defense, what component directs the Cas9 endonuclease to introduce a double-stranded break at a specific genomic locus?
optionsHtml: A synthetic single-guide RNA (sgRNA) whose 20-nucleotide spacer is complementary to the target protospacer sequence adjacent to a PAM motif
A sequence-specific transcription factor containing zinc finger motifs
A restriction methyltransferase recognizing hemimethylated CpG islands
A reverse transcriptase enzyme carrying an oligo-dT primer
mdcat-b9-bio-125.explainHtml: Cas9 is an RNA-guided DNA endonuclease. A single guide RNA (sgRNA) contains a 20-nt guide sequence that base-pairs with the target genomic DNA strand immediately adjacent to a Protospacer Adjacent Motif (PAM: 5'-NGG-3'). Cas9's RuvC and HNH nuclease domains then introduce a precise double-stranded break.

mdcat-b9-bio-126.qHtml: Human insulin produced via recombinant DNA technology in E. coli (Humulin) avoided early protein misfolding and inclusion body issues by which strategy?
optionsHtml: Expressing the A and B polypeptide chains separately as chimeric β-galactosidase fusion proteins, purifying them, and combining them chemically with disulfide bonds
Cloning the full human preproinsulin gene directly into E. coli without removing introns
Synthesizing human insulin chemically using non-biological solid-phase peptide synthesizers
Injecting the proinsulin plasmid directly into mammalian milk fat globule membranes
mdcat-b9-bio-126.explainHtml: Genentech produced recombinant human insulin by synthesizing two separate cDNA constructs encoding the A-chain (21 amino acids) and B-chain (30 amino acids), each fused to the C-terminus of β-galactosidase in E. coli. After cyanogen bromide cleavage and purification, chains were mixed and oxidized to form native disulfide bonds.

mdcat-b9-bio-127.qHtml: Which technique is employed to introduce recombinant DNA into plant cells by coating microscopic tungsten or gold microprojectiles with DNA and accelerating them into target tissues at high velocity?
optionsHtml: Microinjection with glass micropipettes under an inverted microscope
mdcat-b9-bio-127.explainHtml: Biolistics (particle bombardment or gene gun) is a physical gene delivery method especially useful for plant cells with thick, rigid cellulose walls and for chloroplast transformation. Heavy metal particles (gold or tungsten) coated with plasmid DNA are propelled at high velocity by helium discharge.

mdcat-b9-bio-128.qHtml: According to the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium principle (p2 + 2pq + q2 = 1), allele and genotype frequencies in a population remain constant across generations only in the absence of which evolutionary force?
optionsHtml: Natural selection, genetic drift, gene flow (migration), mutation, and non-random mating
Independent assortment during meiotic anaphase I
Random segregation of maternal and paternal chromosomes
Crossing over between homologous chromatids in pachytene
mdcat-b9-bio-128.explainHtml: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium requires five strict conditions: (1) infinitely large population size (no genetic drift), (2) completely random mating (panmixia), (3) no mutations, (4) no gene flow (immigration or emigration), and (5) no natural selection. Normal meiotic segregation does not alter allele frequencies.

mdcat-b9-bio-129.qHtml: In a population adhering to Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the incidence of an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder is 1 in 10,000 (q2 = 0.0001). What is the frequency of asymptomatic heterozygous carriers (2pq) in this population?
mdcat-b9-bio-129.explainHtml: q2 = 0.0001 → q = {0}.0001 = 0.01. Since p + q = 1, p = 1 - 0.01 = 0.99. The carrier frequency is 2pq = 2 × (0.99) × (0.01) = 0.0198 (1.98%), which is roughly 1 out of every 50 individuals.

mdcat-b9-bio-130.qHtml: Homologous anatomical structures, such as the pentadactyl forelimb skeleton of humans, bats, whales, and horses, provide compelling evidence for:
optionsHtml: Divergent evolution from a common ancestral tetrapod ancestor
Convergent evolution under identical selective ecological pressures
Lamarckian inheritance of acquired somatic adaptations
Analogous functional adaptations without shared phylogenetic ancestry
mdcat-b9-bio-130.explainHtml: Homologous structures share a common developmental and anatomical origin (e.g., the tetrapod pentadactyl limb architecture: humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges) despite being modified for diverse functions (grasping, flying, swimming, running), illustrating divergent evolution.

mdcat-b9-bio-131.qHtml: The hydrodynamic streamlined body morphology shared by dolphins (mammals) and sharks (cartilaginous fish) is a classic example of:
optionsHtml: Convergent evolution producing analogous structures in unrelated lineages
Divergent evolution of homologous skeletal frameworks
Adaptive radiation within a single monophyletic mammalian order
mdcat-b9-bio-131.explainHtml: Dolphins and sharks belong to separate vertebrate classes with distinct evolutionary origins (mammalian vs chondrichthyan). Their similar fusiform hydrodynamic body shapes and dorsal stabilization fins arose independently through convergent evolution in response to the physical constraints of aquatic locomotion.

mdcat-b9-bio-132.qHtml: Which evolutionary mechanism leads to random fluctuations in allele frequencies between generations purely due to stochastic sampling error, exerting its most pronounced effects in small isolated populations?
optionsHtml: Genetic drift (e.g., founder effect and population bottleneck)
Directional natural selection favoring extreme phenotypes
High rates of bidirectional gene flow between continents
mdcat-b9-bio-132.explainHtml: Genetic drift refers to random changes in allele frequencies from one generation to the next due to chance events in small populations. Major mechanisms include the bottleneck effect (catastrophic reduction in population size) and the founder effect (colonization of a new area by a few individuals).

mdcat-b9-bio-133.qHtml: In the endosymbiotic theory formulated by Lynn Margulis, which line of empirical evidence supports the evolutionary origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts from engulfed aerobic bacteria and photosynthetic cyanobacteria?
optionsHtml: They contain their own circular DNA, possess 70S ribosomes, replicate by binary fission, and have an inner membrane rich in cardiolipin
They possess linear chromosomes complexed with eukaryotic histone octamers and 80S ribosomes
Their outer membranes contain peptidoglycan and teichoic acids identical to Gram-positive bacteria
They depend entirely on nuclear transcription factors and cannot perform protein synthesis
mdcat-b9-bio-133.explainHtml: Lines of evidence for endosymbiosis: (1) semi-autonomous circular double-stranded DNA without histones; (2) prokaryotic-like 70S ribosomes sensitive to bacterial antibiotics like chloramphenicol; (3) division by binary fission; (4) inner membrane containing cardiolipin and lacking cholesterol.

mdcat-b9-bio-134.qHtml: Which mode of natural selection acts against phenotypic extremes and favors intermediate variants, reducing phenotypic variation in a population living in an unchanging environment?
optionsHtml: Directional selection (e.g., industrial melanism in peppered moths)
mdcat-b9-bio-134.explainHtml: Stabilizing selection favors average or intermediate phenotypes while selecting against both extremes of the trait distribution. A classic textbook example is human birth we: infants much lighter or much heavier than ~3.0-3.5 kg face significantly higher neonatal mortality.

mdcat-b9-bio-135.qHtml: Allopatric speciation differs primarily from sympatric speciation because it requires:
optionsHtml: Extrinsic geographic isolation (e.g., physical barriers like mountain ranges or rivers) preventing gene flow between divided sub-populations
Polyploidization during meiosis inside a shared contiguous habitat
Rapid behavioral sexual isolation without any physical geographical separation
The colonization of an oceanic island by a single pregnant female without genetic divergence
mdcat-b9-bio-135.explainHtml: Allopatric speciation ("other homeland") requires geographic separation of populations by a physical barrier (vicariance or dispersal). Over time, genetic drift and divergent natural selection accumulate reproductive isolating mechanisms, so populations cannot interbreed even if reunited.

mdcat-b10-bio-1.qHtml: In the tertiary and quaternary structure of globular proteins, which of the following covalent bonds provides the strongest stabilizing interaction against thermal denaturation?
optionsHtml: Disulfide bridges formed between cysteine sulfhydryl (-SH) residues
Hydrogen bonds between peptide backbone carbonyl and amide groups
Hydrophobic interactions between non-polar aliphatic side chains
Van der Waals dispersion forces between aromatic rings
mdcat-b10-bio-1.explainHtml: Disulfide bonds (-S-S-) are covalent linkages formed by the oxidation of two cysteine thiol (-SH) groups. Because covalent bonds have bond dissociation energies of ~200-400 kJ/mol (compared to 10-30 kJ/mol for hydrogen or ionic bonds), they confer the highest stability against thermal denaturation.

mdcat-b10-bio-2.qHtml: Which monosaccharide forms the monomeric repeating unit in cellulose, and what type of glycosidic linkage connects these units in linear, unbranched fibrillar sheets?
mdcat-b10-bio-2.explainHtml: Cellulose is a linear, unbranched homopolysaccharide of β-D-glucopyranose units connected by β-1,4-glycosidic bonds. This configuration allows stra extended chains stabilized by inter- and intra-chain hydrogen bonds, creating crystalline microfibrils.

mdcat-b10-bio-3.qHtml: Sphingomyelins, which form the primary lipid constituent of the myelin sheath insulating nerve axons, are composed of sphingosine, a fatty acid, and which polar head group?
mdcat-b10-bio-3.explainHtml: Sphingomyelins consist of an amino alcohol sphingosine backbone attached to a fatty acid via an amide linkage (forming ceramide) and a phosphocholine or phosphoethanolamine head group esterified to the terminal hydroxyl group.

mdcat-b10-bio-4.qHtml: During the chemical hydrolysis of a triglyceride molecule under physiological conditions, how many ester bonds are cleaved and what are the final stoichiometric products?
