optionsHtml: 3 ester bonds cleaved, yielding 1 molecule of glycerol and 3 free fatty acid molecules
2 ester bonds cleaved, yielding 1 molecule of diacylglycerol and 1 free fatty acid
1 ester bond cleaved, yielding 1 phosphatidic acid and 2 fatty acids
4 ester bonds cleaved, yielding 2 glycerol molecules and 4 fatty acids
mdcat-b10-bio-4.explainHtml: Triglycerides are triesters of glycerol and three fatty acids. Complete enzymatic hydrolysis by lipases cleaves all three ester bonds, consuming three water molecules and generating one glycerol and three free fatty acids.

mdcat-b10-bio-5.qHtml: Which nitrogenous base pair in double-stranded B-DNA is stabilized by exactly three intermolecular hydrogen bonds, contributing more significantly to the thermal denaturation melting temperature (Tm)?
mdcat-b10-bio-5.explainHtml: Guanine pairs with cytosine via three specific hydrogen bonds (carbonyl to amino, ring NH to ring N, amino to carbonyl), whereas adenine pairs with thymine via only two hydrogen bonds. High G-C content therefore elevates the DNA melting temperature (Tm).

mdcat-b10-bio-6.qHtml: Which of the following amino acids contains a secondary α-amino group locked into a rigid five-membered pyrrolidine ring, frequently introducing steric bends or disruptions in α-helical secondary structures?
mdcat-b10-bio-6.explainHtml: Proline has a cyclic imino acid side chain that re-enters the peptide backbone, restricting the phi (φ) dihedral angle and lacking an amide hydrogen for backbone hydrogen bonding. Thus, proline acts as a conformational "helix breaker".

mdcat-b10-bio-7.qHtml: Transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules possess a universal trinucleotide sequence at their 3'-hydroxyl terminus to which the specific activated amino acid is covalently attached by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase. What is this sequence?
mdcat-b10-bio-7.explainHtml: Every mature tRNA terminates with the conserved trinucleotide CCA at its 3' end. The activated amino acid is esterified through its carboxyl group to the 2'- or 3'-hydroxyl group of the terminal adenosine.

mdcat-b10-bio-8.qHtml: The high heat capacity and high heat of vaporization of liquid water, which enable it to act as an effective thermal buffer and evaporative coolant in living organisms, are directly attributable to:
optionsHtml: Extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding networks between dipolar water molecules
Covalent bond cleavage between hydrogen and oxygen at room temperature
High molecular we of oxygen atoms
Dipole repulsion between non-polar hydrophobic surfaces
mdcat-b10-bio-8.explainHtml: Each water molecule can donate two hydrogen bonds and accept two through its lone pairs, forming dynamic tetrahedral hydrogen-bonded networks. A large amount of thermal energy is absorbed to break these bonds, producing a high specific heat capacity (4.184 J/g°C) and high heat of vaporization (~2.26 kJ/g).

mdcat-b10-bio-9.qHtml: Which eukaryotic organelle contains acidic hydrolases maintained at an optimal internal pH of ~4.5 to 5.0 by membrane-bound vacuolar H⁺-ATPase proton pumps?
mdcat-b10-bio-9.explainHtml: Lysosomes contain around 50 acid hydrolases (nucleases, proteases, lipases, glycosidases) that require an acidic lumen (~pH 4.8) maintained by an ATP-driven V-type proton pump. Peroxisomes contain catalases and oxidases at neutral pH.

mdcat-b10-bio-10.qHtml: In the Singer-Nicolson fluid mosaic model of cellular membranes, what effect does cholesterol have on eukaryotic plasma membrane fluidity at physiologically elevated temperatures (e.g., 37°C)?
optionsHtml: Decreases fluidity by immobilizing hydrocarbon chains of adjacent phospholipids
Increases fluidity by promoting membrane crystallization
Cleaves unsaturated fatty acid double bonds
mdcat-b10-bio-10.explainHtml: Cholesterol acts as a bidirectional membrane fluidity buffer. At high temperatures (37°C), its rigid steroid planar ring system restricts the thermal motion of fatty acyl chains, decreasing fluidity. At low temperatures, it prevents t packing, hindering phase transitions to solid gel states.

mdcat-b10-bio-11.qHtml: Nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) permit selective nucleocytoplasmic transport of proteins bearing a nuclear localization signal (NLS). Which transport receptor binds the NLS and mediates transit through the pore?
mdcat-b10-bio-11.explainHtml: Proteins destined for the nucleus possess basic nuclear localization signals (NLS) recognized by importin-α, which acts as an adaptor to bind importin-β. Importin-β interacts with phenylalanine-glycine (FG) repeats in nucleoporins to facilitate translocation across the nuclear pore complex.

mdcat-b10-bio-12.qHtml: Microfilaments, which are essential for ameboid motility, cytokinesis furrowing, and microvilli core architecture, are composed of helical polymers of:
mdcat-b10-bio-12.explainHtml: Microfilaments (~7 nm diameter) are formed by the ATP-dependent polymerization of globular monomeric G-actin into two intertwined helical strands of filamentous F-actin. Tubulin forms microtubules (~25 nm).

mdcat-b10-bio-13.qHtml: Which post-translational modification and protein sorting process takes place specifically in the cis-to-trans cisternae of the Golgi apparatus?
optionsHtml: O-linked glycosylation, modification of N-linked oligosaccharides, and sorting to lysosomes, plasma membrane, or secretory vesicles
Synthesis of core lipid-linked precursor oligosaccharides on dolichol phosphate
Peptide bond synthesis during mRNA translation
Oxidation of long-chain fatty acids into acetyl-CoA
mdcat-b10-bio-13.explainHtml: The Golgi apparatus modifies glycoproteins delivered from the rough ER (trimming mannose residues, adding galactose, sialic acid, and O-linked sugars) and sorts them at the trans-Golgi network for targeted delivery to lysosomes, secretory granules, or the cell surface.

mdcat-b10-bio-14.qHtml: Bacterial cell walls contain peptidoglycan (murein) composed of alternating units of N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM) linked by β-1,4-glycosidic bonds. Which enzyme present in human tears and saliva hydrolyzes this specific bond?
mdcat-b10-bio-14.explainHtml: Lysozyme is an innate antimicrobial enzyme that hydrolyzes the β-1,4-glycosidic linkages between NAM and NAG in bacterial peptidoglycan walls, causing osmotic lysis of Gram-positive bacteria.

mdcat-b10-bio-15.qHtml: Plasmodesmata in plant tissues and gap junctions in animal tissues share which functional characteristic?
optionsHtml: Direct symplastic/cytoplasmic intercellular communication permitting transport of small ions and signaling molecules (<1 kDa)
Formation of impermeable t seals preventing paracellular solute movement
Anchoring intermediate filaments to desmosomal cadherins
Exocytosis of large polypeptide hormones via clathrin-coated pits
mdcat-b10-bio-15.explainHtml: Both plasmodesmata (in plant cells) and gap junctions (composed of connexon hexamers in animal cells) provide continuous aqueous cytoplasmic channels that allow ions, second messengers (cAMP, IP3), and metabolites to pass directly between adjacent cells.

mdcat-b10-bio-16.qHtml: The primary site for non-oxidative synthesis of steroid hormones (such as testosterone and estrogen) and detoxification of lipophilic xenobiotics in hepatic cells is the:
mdcat-b10-bio-16.explainHtml: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum lacks ribosomes and contains enzymes for lipid and steroid hormone biosynthesis (e.g., in Leydig cells and adrenal cortex) as well as the cytochrome P450 monooxygenase system for drug detoxification in hepatocytes.

mdcat-b10-bio-17.qHtml: In the Michaelis-Menten kinetic model of enzyme action, the Michaelis constant (Km) physically represents:
optionsHtml: The substrate concentration at which the reaction velocity is exactly half of the maximal velocity (1/2 Vmax)
The maximal velocity attained at infinite substrate concentration
The turnover number (kcat) of the catalytic active site
The dissociation constant of the enzyme-inhibitor complex (Ki)
mdcat-b10-bio-17.explainHtml: By definition in the Michaelis-Menten equation v = (Vmax [S]) / (Km + [S]), when [S] = Km, v = (Vmax Km) / (2 Km) = Vmax / 2. A lower Km indicates higher affinity for substrate.

mdcat-b10-bio-18.qHtml: How does a reversible competitive inhibitor affect the kinetic parameters Vmax and Km of an enzymatic reaction?
optionsHtml: Apparent Km increases, while Vmax remains unchanged
Vmax decreases, while Km remains unchanged
Both Vmax and Km decrease by identical ratios
Both Vmax and Km increase proportionally
mdcat-b10-bio-18.explainHtml: A competitive inhibitor competes directly with substrate for the active catalytic site. By adding excess substrate, the inhibitor can be outcompeted, so Vmax is unaffected. However, a higher substrate concentration is required to reach half Vmax, so apparent Km increases.

mdcat-b10-bio-19.qHtml: Which catalytic strategy explains how enzymes accelerate chemical reaction rates by factors of 10⁶ to 10¹² without altering the overall thermodynamic equilibrium constant (Keq)?
optionsHtml: Lowering the Gibbs free energy of activation (ΔG‡) by stabilizing the high-energy transition state
Increasing the standard free energy change (ΔG°) between reactants and products
Shifting the chemical equilibrium toward products by consuming reactants
Raising the ambient kinetic temperature of substrate molecules
mdcat-b10-bio-19.explainHtml: Enzymes bind preferentially to the transition state rather than ground-state substrates, thereby lowering the activation energy barrier (ΔG‡). Because ΔG° between initial reactants and final products remains unchanged, the equilibrium constant Keq is not altered.

mdcat-b10-bio-20.qHtml: An organic non-protein cofactor that is tightly and permanently covalently bound to an enzyme molecule is formally designated as a:
mdcat-b10-bio-20.explainHtml: A prosthetic group is a non-protein organic or organometallic cofactor (e.g., heme in hemoglobin/cytochromes, FAD in succinate dehydrogenase) that is covalently or tightly bound to the protein. Coenzymes are loosely associated organic molecules (e.g., NAD⁺).

mdcat-b10-bio-21.qHtml: Feedback inhibition (end-product inhibition) of an unbranched metabolic biosynthetic pathway typically operates by which biochemical mechanism?
optionsHtml: The final downstream product binds to an allosteric regulatory site on the first committed-step enzyme, causing an inhibitory conformational change
The end-product covalently degrades the mRNA transcript of all pathway enzymes
The end-product competes irreversibly for the catalytic active site of the final enzyme
The end-product activates lysosomal proteolysis of pathway cofactors
mdcat-b10-bio-21.explainHtml: Feedback inhibition occurs when the ultimate pathway product accumulates and binds to a specific allosteric site (distinct from the active site) on the first pace-making enzyme (e.g., threonine deaminase inhibited by isoleucine), downregulating flux without wasting intermediates.

mdcat-b10-bio-22.qHtml: What happens to the structure and catalytic function of most human intracellular enzymes when the temperature is elevated beyond 60°C?
optionsHtml: Thermal denaturation occurs due to disruption of non-covalent hydrogen and ionic bonds, causing irreversible loss of active-site conformation
Activation energy increases, making the reaction faster
The enzyme converts into a zymogen precursor
Peptide bonds are cleaved into free individual amino acids
mdcat-b10-bio-22.explainHtml: At high temperatures (>50-60°C for mesophilic enzymes), increased vibrational kinetic energy disrupts delicate tertiary and quaternary non-covalent interactions (hydrogen bonds, ionic attractions, hydrophobic forces), causing unfolding (denaturation) and loss of active-site geometry.

mdcat-b10-bio-23.qHtml: In the induced-fit model of enzyme action proposed by Daniel Koshland, how does substrate binding occur?
optionsHtml: Binding of the substrate induces a precise reciprocal conformational change in the enzyme active site, aligning catalytic residues optimally around the transition state
The active site is a rigid, unyielding geometric lock that perfectly matches the substrate in its ground state
Substrate molecules are cleaved before touching the enzyme surface
The enzyme unfolds entirely into an unstructured random coil upon substrate collision
mdcat-b10-bio-23.explainHtml: Koshland's induced-fit model states that the enzyme active site is flexible. Initial weak binding of the substrate triggers a conformational rearrangement of the catalytic cleft, molding the active site around the transition state to maximize catalytic efficiency.

mdcat-b10-bio-24.qHtml: In an uncompetitive enzyme inhibition pattern, how do the Lineweaver-Burk double reciprocal plots (1/v vs 1/[S]) compare between the uninhibited and inhibited states?
optionsHtml: They yield parallel lines with identical slopes (Km/Vmax) because both Vmax and apparent Km decrease by the same factor
They intersect directly on the y-axis (identical Vmax)
They intersect directly on the negative x-axis (identical Km)
They exhibit intersecting lines in the first positive quadrant
mdcat-b10-bio-24.explainHtml: An uncompetitive inhibitor binds exclusively to the enzyme-substrate complex (ES). This reduces both Vmax and apparent Km by the same factor α', so the slope (Km/Vmax) is unchanged. On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, this produces parallel lines.

mdcat-b10-bio-25.qHtml: At which sub-stage of Prophase I in meiosis does crossing over and genetic recombination between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes take place?
mdcat-b10-bio-25.explainHtml: Synapsis occurs in zygotene. Once the synaptonemal complex is fully formed, reciprocal genetic exchange (crossing over) mediated by recombination nodules occurs during pachytene. Chiasmata become visible in diplotene.

mdcat-b10-bio-26.qHtml: The spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) during eukaryotic mitosis monitors kinetochore attachment to prevent premature anaphase onset. What biochemical event triggers chromosome segregation once all kinetochores are under bipolar tension?
optionsHtml: Activation of the Anaphase-Promoting Complex/Cyclosome (APC/C), leading to ubiquitination of securin and activation of separase to cleave cohesin rings
Phosphorylation of nuclear lamin A to reform the nuclear envelope
Inhibition of cyclin B degradation by CDK1
mdcat-b10-bio-26.explainHtml: Bipolar tension silences the SAC, enabling APC/C-Cdc20 to ubiquitinate securin. Degradation of securin releases the active protease separase, which cleaves the Scc1 subunit of cohesin complexes, allowing sister chromatids to separate toward opposite poles.

mdcat-b10-bio-27.qHtml: A diploid somatic human cell in the G2 phase of the cell cycle contains how many chromatids and how many chromosomes?
mdcat-b10-bio-27.explainHtml: During S phase, DNA replication duplicates each of the 46 chromosomes into two identical sister chromatids joined at a common centromere. Thus, in G2 phase there remain 46 chromosomes, consisting of 92 sister chromatids (4C DNA content).

mdcat-b10-bio-28.qHtml: Which tumor suppressor protein, frequently termed the "guardian of the genome," arrests the cell cycle at the G1/S restriction point in response to double-stranded DNA damage by inducing transcription of the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21?
mdcat-b10-bio-28.explainHtml: ATM/ATR kinases activate p53 in response to DNA damage. Phosphorylated p53 tetramers bind promoter elements to transcribe p21 (CIP1/WAF1), which inhibits Cdk2-cyclin E complexes, arresting cells in G1 to permit DNA repair or initiate apoptosis if damage is irreparable.

mdcat-b10-bio-29.qHtml: Colchicine and nocodazole act as antimitotic agents that arrest dividing cells in metaphase by which cellular mechanism?
optionsHtml: Inhibiting tubulin polymerization, preventing mitotic spindle assembly
Stabilizing actin filaments in the contractile ring
Blocking DNA polymerase δ replication fork progression
mdcat-b10-bio-29.explainHtml: Colchicine binds free α/β-tubulin heterodimers, preventing their polymerization into spindle microtubules. This triggers the spindle assembly checkpoint, arresting cells in metaphase (used in karyotyping).

mdcat-b10-bio-30.qHtml: Cytokinesis in higher plant cells differs fundamentally from animal cells because plant cells cannot form a cleavage furrow. Instead, they divide by constructing:
optionsHtml: A cell plate (phragmoplast) assembled from Golgi-derived vesicles fusing along the equatorial plane
An actomyosin contractile ring pinching the outer cellulose cell wall inward
A septin filament bundle that invaginates the outer cuticle
Spontaneous binary fission of the nuclear membrane
mdcat-b10-bio-30.explainHtml: Because rigid plant cell walls prevent inward cleavage furrowing, plant cytokinesis proceeds centrifugally via the phragmoplast. Golgi-derived vesicles carrying cell wall precursors (pectins, hemicelluloses) fuse along the equator to form the middle lamella and primary cell plate.

mdcat-b10-bio-31.qHtml: What is the developmental significance of non-disjunction occurring during Anaphase I of meiosis versus Anaphase II?
optionsHtml: Non-disjunction in Anaphase I produces 100% abnormal gametes (two n+1 and two n-1), whereas non-disjunction in Anaphase II produces 50% normal (n, n) and 50% abnormal gametes (n+1, n-1)
Non-disjunction in Anaphase I produces 50% normal gametes, while Anaphase II produces 100% aneuploid gametes
Both events invariably produce 100% polyploid gametes
Anaphase I non-disjunction affects only sex chromosomes, never autosomes
mdcat-b10-bio-31.explainHtml: In Anaphase I non-disjunction, both homologous chromosomes migrate to one pole, yielding gametes that are all abnormal (50% n+1, 50% n-1). In Anaphase II non-disjunction, one pair of sister chromatids fails to separate, yielding two normal gametes (n), one n+1, and one n-1 (50% normal, 50% aneuploid).

mdcat-b10-bio-32.qHtml: Programmed cell death (apoptosis) is biochemically executed by a specialized family of cysteine-dependent aspartate-directed proteases termed:
mdcat-b10-bio-32.explainHtml: Caspases (cysteine aspartic proteases) exist as inactive procaspases. Initiator caspases (caspase-8, -9) activate executioner caspases (caspase-3, -6, -7), which cleave vital cytoskeletal proteins and activate CAD endonuclease to cleave genomic DNA into nucleosomal fragments.

mdcat-b10-bio-33.qHtml: Which animal phylum is characterized by primary radial or biradial symmetry, diploblastic tissue organization, and stinging capsules known as nematocysts housed in cnidocytes?
mdcat-b10-bio-33.explainHtml: Cnidarians (hydra, jellyfish, corals, sea anemones) are diploblastic (ectoderm and endoderm separated by mesoglea) with radial symmetry and specialized stinging cells (cnidocytes) containing nematocysts for prey capture and defense.

mdcat-b10-bio-34.qHtml: Flame cells (protonephridia) with flickering tufts of cilia that drive osmoregulation and nitrogenous waste excretion are characteristic of which animal phylum?
mdcat-b10-bio-34.explainHtml: Flatworms (such as Planaria and tapeworms) possess a protonephridial excretory system consisting of blind-ending flame cells whose beating cilia create negative pressure, drawing interstitial fluid into tubules for excretion.

mdcat-b10-bio-35.qHtml: Which developmental feature distinguishes Protostomes (e.g., Mollusks, Annelids, Arthropods) from Deuterostomes (e.g., Echinoderms, Chordates)?
optionsHtml: In protostomes, the blastopore develops into the mouth, whereas in deuterostomes, the blastopore develops into the anus
Protostomes have radial indeterminate cleavage, while deuterostomes have spiral determinate cleavage
Protostomes lack a true coelom, whereas deuterostomes are acoelomate
Deuterostomes develop a ventral nerve cord, while protostomes have a dorsal hollow nerve cord
mdcat-b10-bio-35.explainHtml: In protostomes ("first mouth"), the embryonic blastopore develops into the mouth, with spiral, determinate cleavage. In deuterostomes ("second mouth"), the blastopore becomes the anus (mouth forms secondarily), with radial, indeterminate cleavage.

mdcat-b10-bio-36.qHtml: The water vascular system (ambulacral system), terminating in hydraulic tube feet used for locomotion, food handling, and respiration, is a unique anatomical feature found exclusively in:
mdcat-b10-bio-36.explainHtml: Echinoderms (starfish, sea urchins, brittle stars) possess a unique coelomic water vascular system that uses hydraulic pressure from the madreporite and ampullae to operate muscular tube feet (podia) for locomotion and prey capture.

mdcat-b10-bio-37.qHtml: Which of the following is a defining diagnostic hallmark of Phylum Arthropoda that necessitates periodic physiological molting (ecdysis) for somatic growth?
optionsHtml: A hardened, chitinous cuticle exoskeleton secreted by the underlying epidermis
A fluid-filled hydrostatic pseudocoelom surrounded by longitudinal muscle
A calcareous mantle shell that enlarges by continuous marginal deposition
An endoskeleton composed of mesodermal ossicles
mdcat-b10-bio-37.explainHtml: Arthropods possess a rigid exoskeleton composed of chitin cross-linked with proteins (and calcium salts in crustaceans). Because this rigid coat cannot expand, arthropods must shed it through hormonally regulated molting (ecdysis) to accommodate growth.

mdcat-b10-bio-38.qHtml: All chordates, at some stage in their ontogenetic development, share four definitive morphological synapomorphies. Which group of structures accurately lists these four features?
optionsHtml: Notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal gill slits, and post-anal tail
Ventral solid nerve cord, notochord, open circulatory system, and radula
Vertebral column, jaws, mammary glands, and closed circulatory system
Hemocoel, dorsal heart, mantle cavity, and opercular gills
mdcat-b10-bio-38.explainHtml: The four universal chordate diagnostic traits present at some life stage are: (1) a supportive flexible notochord, (2) a dorsal tubular hollow nerve cord, (3) pharyngeal slits or pouches, and (4) a muscular post-anal tail.

mdcat-b10-bio-39.qHtml: Which subclass of mammals lays shelled cleidoic eggs (oviparous), incubates them, and nurses the hatched young with milk secreted onto specialized abdominal skin patches lacking true nipples?
optionsHtml: Prototheria (Monotremes, e.g., Duck-billed platypus and Echidna)
Eutheria (Placental mammals, e.g., Human and Whale)
mdcat-b10-bio-39.explainHtml: Prototherians (monotremes) are egg-laying oviparous mammals found in Australasia. They possess mammary glands but lack teats or nipples; milk is secreted directly onto the fur of the mother's abdomen where the hatchlings lap it up.

mdcat-b10-bio-40.qHtml: What is the primary evolutionary advantage of the amniotic egg with its four extraembryonic membranes (amnion, chorion, allantois, yolk sac) in reptiles, birds, and mammals?
optionsHtml: Complete liberation of embryonic development from an aquatic environment to dry terrestrial habitats
Ability to produce diploid parthenogenetic clones without fertilization
Direct maternal blood exchange without relying on stored yolk proteins
Rapid metamorphosis through free-swimming ciliated larval stages
mdcat-b10-bio-40.explainHtml: The amniotic egg provides a self-contained aquatic microenvironment (amnion cushioning the embryo, allantois storing nitrogenous wastes, yolk sac nourishing, and chorion exchanging O2/CO2) encased within a desiccation-resistant shell, allowing fully terrestrial reproduction.

mdcat-b10-bio-41.qHtml: In human gastric juice, hydrochloric acid (HCl) secreted by parietal (oxyntic) cells serves which crucial physiological functions?
optionsHtml: Converts inactive pepsinogen into active pepsin and kills ingested microorganisms by maintaining a gastric lumen pH of 1.5 to 2.0
Directly emulsifies dietary triglycerides into micelles
Neutralizes duodenal chyme to protect pancreatic enzymes
Cleaves maltose into two molecules of D-glucose
mdcat-b10-bio-41.explainHtml: Gastric parietal cells secrete HCl (via an apical H⁺/K⁺ ATPase proton pump), reducing gastric pH to 1.5-2.0. This acidity denatures dietary proteins, hydrolyzes the inhibitory peptide from pepsinogen to generate active pepsin, and acts as an innate antimicrobial barrier.

mdcat-b10-bio-42.qHtml: Enteropeptidase (enterokinase), an enzyme localized on the apical brush-border membrane of duodenal enterocytes, initiates the cascade of pancreatic proteolysis by converting:
mdcat-b10-bio-42.explainHtml: Enteropeptidase cleaves a hexapeptide from the N-terminus of trypsinogen, converting it to active trypsin. Trypsin then autocatalytically activates more trypsinogen as well as chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, and procarboxypeptidases.

mdcat-b10-bio-43.qHtml: Which of the following gastrointestinal hormones is released by duodenal S-cells in response to acidic chyme entering from the stomach, stimulating the secretion of bicarbonate-rich fluid from pancreatic ductal cells?
mdcat-b10-bio-43.explainHtml: Secretin is released by duodenal S-cells when luminal pH drops below 4.5. It travels via the bloodstream to pancreatic duct cells, stimulating them to secrete a watery, bicarbonate-rich (HCO3⁻) fluid that neutralizes gastric acid in the duodenum.

mdcat-b10-bio-44.qHtml: In the mammalian nephron, what is the countercurrent multiplier mechanism that establishes the osmotic hypertonicity of the renal medullary interstitium?
optionsHtml: The active transport of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ out of the water-impermeable thick ascending limb, accompanied by water reabsorption from the descending limb of the Loop of Henle
The active secretion of potassium ions in the proximal convoluted tubule
Ultrafiltration across the fenestrated glomerulus driven by hydrostatic pressure
Countercurrent exchange in the peritubular capillary plexus of cortical nephrons
mdcat-b10-bio-44.explainHtml: The descending limb is permeable to water but impermeable to solutes, whereas the thick ascending limb actively pumps NaCl out via the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter and is impermeable to water. This creates a vertical corticomedullary osmotic gradient (from 300 to 1200 mOsm/L).

mdcat-b10-bio-45.qHtml: During the cardiac cycle, the second heart sound (S2, "dub") is generated primarily by the mechanical vibration and acoustic turbulence associated with:
optionsHtml: The sudden closure of the aortic and pulmonary semilunar valves at the onset of ventricular diastole
The closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid (mitral) atrioventricular valves
The rapid inflow of blood into the ventricles during atrial systole
Turbulent blood jetting across stenotic coronary arteries
mdcat-b10-bio-45.explainHtml: The first heart sound (S1, "lub") marks the closure of the atrioventricular (mitral and tricuspid) valves at the onset of ventricular systole. The second heart sound (S2, "dub") is caused by the closure of the aortic and pulmonary semilunar valves at the onset of ventricular diastole (isovolumetric relaxation).

mdcat-b10-bio-46.qHtml: Which vitamin is an indispensable fat-soluble cofactor for the hepatic γ-glutamyl carboxylase enzyme that post-translationally modifies clotting factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX, and X?
mdcat-b10-bio-46.explainHtml: Vitamin K is required as a cofactor for the post-translational γ-carboxylation of glutamic acid residues on factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as proteins C and S. These γ-carboxyglutamate residues bind Ca²⁺ to anchor the clotting factors to platelet phospholipid surfaces.

mdcat-b10-bio-47.qHtml: In plant nutrition, the Casparian strip in the root endodermis forces water and dissolved mineral ions arriving through the apoplast to cross the plasma membrane into which pathway?
mdcat-b10-bio-47.explainHtml: The Casparian strip is a band of suberin and lignin deposited in the radial and transverse walls of root endodermal cells. It acts as an impermeable hydrophobic barrier that blocks apoplastic diffusion, forcing water and solutes through selectively permeable membranes into the symplast.

mdcat-b10-bio-48.qHtml: Which plant hormone stimulates the elongation of coleoptiles and stems by activating plasma membrane proton (H⁺) pumps, acidifying the cell wall and activating expansins according to the acid-growth hypothesis?
mdcat-b10-bio-48.explainHtml: According to the acid-growth hypothesis, auxin (IAA) stimulates H⁺-ATPases in the plasma membrane, lowering the apoplastic pH to ~4.5. This activates expansin enzymes that loosen non-covalent bonds between cellulose microfibrils, allowing turgor pressure to drive cell elongation.

mdcat-b10-bio-49.qHtml: In the l-dependent reactions of oxygenic photosynthesis, the photolysis of water molecules (Hill reaction) takes place at the water-splitting oxygen-evolving manganese complex associated with:
optionsHtml: The lumenal side of Photosystem II (P680)
The stromal side of Photosystem I (P700)
The CF0 subunit of ATP synthase
mdcat-b10-bio-49.explainHtml: Photolysis occurs at the lumenal surface of Photosystem II (PSII, reaction center P680), driven by the oxygen-evolving Mn4CaO5 cluster. Two water molecules are oxidized to yield four protons (released into the thylakoid lumen), four electrons (reducing P680⁺), and one molecule of molecular O2.

mdcat-b10-bio-50.qHtml: During non-cyclic photophosphorylation, what is the terminal electron acceptor that captures electrons flowing from Photosystem I via ferredoxin?
optionsHtml: NADP⁺ (reduced to NADPH by ferredoxin-NADP⁺ reductase)
mdcat-b10-bio-50.explainHtml: Electrons energized at PSI (P700) pass through primary acceptors A0, A1, and iron-sulfur centers to ferredoxin (Fd). The enzyme ferredoxin-NADP⁺ reductase (FNR) on the stromal face catalyzes the transfer of two electrons and one proton to NADP⁺, forming NADPH.

mdcat-b10-bio-51.qHtml: In the Calvin cycle (l-independent reactions) of C3 plants, how many molecules of ATP and NADPH are consumed to fix 6 molecules of CO2 to produce one net molecule of hexose (glucose)?
mdcat-b10-bio-51.explainHtml: Fixing one CO2 requires 2 NADPH and 2 ATP for reduction of 3-PGA to G3P, plus 1 ATP for the regeneration of RuBP (total 3 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO2). For net synthesis of one 6-carbon glucose (6 CO2 fixed), 6 × 3 = 18 ATP and 6 × 2 = 12 NADPH are consumed.

mdcat-b10-bio-52.qHtml: Under conditions of high oxygen and low carbon dioxide concentration, RuBisCO acts as an oxygenase, catalyzing the reaction between RuBP and O2 to produce:
optionsHtml: One molecule of 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA) and one molecule of 2-phosphoglycolate (photorespiration)
One molecule of oxaloacetate and one molecule of malate
mdcat-b10-bio-52.explainHtml: RuBisCO has both carboxylase and oxygenase activity. When O2 competes at the active site, RuBisCO oxygenates RuBP (5 carbons) into one 3-carbon molecule (3-PGA) and one 2-carbon molecule (2-phosphoglycolate), initiating the energy-wasteful photorespiratory C2 cycle.

mdcat-b10-bio-53.qHtml: In aerobic cellular respiration, which step represents the committed "transition reaction" (link reaction) connecting cytoplasmic glycolysis to the mitochondrial Krebs cycle?
optionsHtml: Oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA by the pyruvate dehydrogenase multienzyme complex in the mitochondrial matrix
Phosphorylation of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate by phosphofructokinase-1
Condensation of acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate to form citrate
Oxidation of malate to oxaloacetate by malate dehydrogenase
mdcat-b10-bio-53.explainHtml: Pyruvate enters the mitochondrial matrix via a H⁺/pyruvate symporter. The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) catalyzes oxidative decarboxylation: Pyruvate + CoA + NAD⁺ → Acetyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH + H⁺. This irreversible reaction links glycolysis to the Krebs cycle.

mdcat-b10-bio-54.qHtml: For each turn of the citric acid (Krebs) cycle utilizing one molecule of acetyl-CoA, how many molecules of NADH, FADH2, and GTP (or ATP) are produced by substrate-level phosphorylation and redox steps?
mdcat-b10-bio-54.explainHtml: One acetyl-CoA (2 carbons) undergoing a complete turn of the Krebs cycle yields 2 CO2, 3 NADH (at isocitrate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and malate dehydrogenase), 1 FADH2 (at succinate dehydrogenase), and 1 GTP/ATP via succinyl-CoA synthetase.

mdcat-b10-bio-55.qHtml: In the mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC), Complex IV (Cytochrome c oxidase) transfers electrons to which terminal electron acceptor, driving the formation of metabolic water?
mdcat-b10-bio-55.explainHtml: Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) contains heme a, heme a3, and copper centers (CuA, CuB). It receives electrons one by one from reduced cytochrome c and transfers them to molecular oxygen: O2 + 4 e⁻ + 4 H⁺ → 2 H2O.

mdcat-b10-bio-56.qHtml: According to Peter Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis, how does the electrochemical proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane drive ATP synthesis by ATP synthase (F0F1 complex)?
optionsHtml: Protons flow down their electrochemical gradient from the intermembrane space back into the matrix through the F0 proton channel, driving rotary conformational changes in the F1 catalytic head
Protons are actively pumped into the matrix by ATP hydrolysis
Electrons bind directly to the β-subunits of F1 to phosphorylate ADP
Phosphate ions are pumped into the intermembrane space through porins
mdcat-b10-bio-56.explainHtml: Proton pumping by Complexes I, III, and IV generates a proton motive force across the inner membrane (positive and acidic in the intermembrane space). Protons flow back into the matrix via the F0 c-ring of ATP synthase, causing mechanical rotation of the γ-stalk, which changes β-subunit conformations in F1 to synthesize ATP from ADP and Pi.

mdcat-b10-bio-57.qHtml: In human skeletal muscle during intense anaerobic exertion when oxygen supply is insufficient, what is the physiological purpose of converting pyruvate to lactate via lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)?
optionsHtml: Regeneration of NAD⁺ from NADH to maintain a continuous supply of NAD⁺ required for the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step of glycolysis
Direct production of two additional ATP molecules per lactate formed
Preventing cellular acidification by trapping hydrogen ions in glycogen
mdcat-b10-bio-57.explainHtml: Glycolysis requires oxidized NAD⁺ at the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) step. Under anaerobic conditions, the electron transport chain cannot reoxidize NADH. Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate while oxidizing NADH to NAD⁺, allowing glycolysis to continue producing 2 ATP per glucose.

mdcat-b10-bio-58.qHtml: According to the Münch pressure-flow (mass flow) hypothesis, what drives the long-distance translocation of photoassimilates (sucrose) in phloem sieve tubes from source to sink?
optionsHtml: A turgor (hydrostatic) pressure gradient established between the loading site (source, high turgor) and unloading site (sink, low turgor)
Capillary action inside lignified dead vessel elements
Transpirational pull generated by negative hydrostatic water potential in leaf stomata
Active flagellar streaming along phloem parenchyma cells
mdcat-b10-bio-58.explainHtml: Active loading of sucrose at the source reduces water potential in sieve tubes, causing water to enter by osmosis from the xylem and creating high hydrostatic pressure. At the sink, sucrose is unloaded and water exits, creating low pressure. This hydrostatic pressure differential drives mass bulk flow.

mdcat-b10-bio-59.qHtml: The cohesion-tension theory (Dixon and Joly) explains the upward ascent of sap in tall xylem vessels without energy expenditure by relying on:
optionsHtml: Transpirational pull creating negative water potential tension, transmitted down unbroken water columns through strong intermolecular hydrogen-bonded cohesion
Positive hydrostatic pressure generated exclusively by root endodermal pumps
Active peristaltic contractions of companion cell walls
Atmospheric pressure pushing water upward into a Torricellian vacuum
mdcat-b10-bio-59.explainHtml: Evaporation of water from leaf mesophyll cell walls creates negative surface tension (transpirational pull). Because water molecules exhibit strong mutual cohesion (via hydrogen bonds) and adhesion to hydrophilic xylem walls, a continuous, unbroken tension column is pulled upward from roots to leaves.

mdcat-b10-bio-60.qHtml: During environmental water stress, which phytohormone synthesized in mesophyll and root cells acts rapidly to trigger stomatal closure by inducing K⁺ and Cl⁻ efflux from guard cells?
mdcat-b10-bio-60.explainHtml: Under drought stress, roots and leaves synthesize abscisic acid (ABA). ABA binds receptors on guard cell membranes, stimulating cytosolic Ca²⁺ influx and opening outward-rectifying K⁺ and Cl⁻ anion channels. The resulting loss of ions lowers turgor, causing guard cells to become flaccid and close the stomatal pore.

mdcat-b10-bio-61.qHtml: In the human circulatory system, which anatomical blood vessel possesses the highest total cross-sectional area and the lowest velocity of blood flow, facilitating microvascular exchange of gases and nutrients?
mdcat-b10-bio-61.explainHtml: Although individual capillaries are microscopic (~8 μm diameter), their parallel branching yields a vast combined cross-sectional area (~4500 cm² vs ~4.5 cm² for the aorta). Because velocity v = Flow Rate (Q) / Area (A), blood velocity drops to its minimum (~0.03 cm/s), allowing time for diffusion of gases and solutes.

mdcat-b10-bio-62.qHtml: What is the primary electrical function of the atrioventricular (AV) node in delaying cardiac impulse propagation by approximately 0.09 to 0.12 seconds before conducting through the Bundle of His?
optionsHtml: It allows complete atrial contraction and ventricular filling (atrial kick) before ventricular systole begins
It prevents backwards regurgitation of venous blood into the superior vena cava
It ensures both atria and ventricles contract simultaneously
It generates the primary resting heart rate of 100 beats per minute
mdcat-b10-bio-62.explainHtml: Impulses initiated by the SA node reach the AV node, where slow conduction velocity (~0.05 m/s, due to smaller fibers and fewer gap junctions) delays excitation by ~0.1 s. This delay allows atrial systole to completely fill the ventricles before ventricular contraction begins.

mdcat-b10-bio-63.qHtml: According to Starling's forces governing fluid filtration across capillary walls, what primary inward force opposes filtration and pulls interstitial fluid back into the venous end of the capillary?
optionsHtml: Plasma colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure exerted by plasma albumin (π_c)
mdcat-b10-bio-63.explainHtml: Plasma colloid osmotic pressure (~25-28 mmHg), predominantly generated by serum albumin that cannot cross the capillary endothelium, pulls water from the interstitium into the vascular lumen. At the venous end, capillary hydrostatic pressure drops (~15 mmHg), so oncotic pressure dominates, driving reabsorption.

mdcat-b10-bio-64.qHtml: In the lymphatic system, dietary long-chain triglycerides and fat-soluble vitamins packaged into chylomicrons by intestinal enterocytes enter which specialized lymphatic vessels?
mdcat-b10-bio-64.explainHtml: Chylomicrons (diameter 75-1200 nm) are too large to penetrate the continuous basement membrane of blood capillaries. Instead, they enter wide, permeable lymphatic capillaries called lacteals in intestinal villi, forming milky chyle that drains via the thoracic duct into the left subclavian vein.

mdcat-b10-bio-65.qHtml: In ABO and Rh blood grouping, an individual with blood type O-negative is classified as a "universal red blood cell donor" because their erythrocytes:
optionsHtml: Lack A, B, and Rh (D) antigens on their plasma membrane surface, preventing recognition by recipient isoantibodies
Contain neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies in their circulating plasma
Possess both A and B antigens alongside high levels of Rh factor
Have nucleated erythrocytes that resist phagocytic clearance
mdcat-b10-bio-65.explainHtml: Type O-negative RBCs lack A, B, and Rh(D) surface antigens. When transfused into any ABO/Rh recipient, their erythrocytes will not be cross-linked or lysed by recipient anti-A, anti-B, or anti-D agglutinins.

mdcat-b10-bio-66.qHtml: Erythroblastosis fetalis (hemolytic disease of the newborn) typically occurs under which parental and fetal Rh immunological combination?
optionsHtml: An Rh-negative mother sensitized by a previous Rh-positive fetus carrying a subsequent Rh-positive fetus
An Rh-positive mother carrying an Rh-negative fetus
An Rh-positive mother and an Rh-positive father carrying an Rh-positive fetus
An Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-negative fetus
mdcat-b10-bio-66.explainHtml: When an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive fetus, fetal-maternal hemorrhage during delivery sensitizes the mother to produce anti-Rh (anti-D) IgG antibodies. In a subsequent Rh-positive pregnancy, maternal anti-D IgG crosses the placenta and lyses fetal red blood cells.

mdcat-b10-bio-67.qHtml: In the mammalian liver, the urea cycle (ornithine cycle) disposes of toxic free ammonia derived from amino acid deamination by condensing it with carbon dioxide into urea. What is the initial rate-limiting enzyme localized in the mitochondrial matrix?
mdcat-b10-bio-67.explainHtml: CPS-I catalyzes the condensation of NH4⁺ and HCO3⁻ using 2 ATP to form carbamoyl phosphate inside liver mitochondria. It is allosterically activated by N-acetylglutamate (NAG) and represents the obligatory rate-limiting pace-maker of the urea cycle.

mdcat-b10-bio-68.qHtml: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH / vasopressin), synthesized in the hypothalamus and secreted by the posterior pituitary, promotes water reabsorption in the renal collecting ducts primarily by:
optionsHtml: Inducing the exocytic insertion of Aquaporin-2 (AQP2) water channels into the apical membrane of principal cells
Directly opening sodium-potassium ATPases in the loop of Henle
Constricting the afferent glomerular arterioles to reduce filtration
Inhibiting aldosterone synthesis in the adrenal cortex
mdcat-b10-bio-68.explainHtml: ADH binds to basolateral V2 G-protein coupled receptors on principal cells, activating adenylyl cyclase to increase cAMP. Protein kinase A then phosphorylates vesicular Aquaporin-2 channels, mobilizing them to fuse with the apical membrane and increasing water permeability.

mdcat-b10-bio-69.qHtml: Which physiological homeostatic response is triggered in human cutaneous circulation when the core body temperature drops below 36.5°C?
optionsHtml: Sympathetic vasoconstriction of precapillary dermal arterioles and arteriovenous anastomoses, shunting blood to deep core vessels
Direct vasodilation of superficial dermal capillary loops to maximize convective heat loss
Inhibition of piloerection muscles to flatten body hair
Activation of eccrine sweat glands to lower peripheral skin temperature
mdcat-b10-bio-69.explainHtml: Cold stress stimulates posterior hypothalamic thermoregulatory centers, increasing sympathetic α1-adrenergic outflow to dermal arterioles and AV shunts. Vasoconstriction reduces skin blood flow from ~2.5 L/min down to ~50 mL/min, minimizing radiant and convective heat dissipation.

mdcat-b10-bio-70.qHtml: Marine bony fishes (teleosts) maintain internal osmolarity hypotonic to seawater (~300 mOsm/L vs ~1000 mOsm/L). How do they prevent severe dehydration?
optionsHtml: Drinking large quantities of seawater and actively eliminating excess monovalent ions (Na⁺, Cl⁻) through chloride cells in their gills
Retaining high concentrations of urea and TMAO in their blood like marine elasmobranchs
Producing voluminous dilute urine to flush out dietary salts
Absorbing pure water by active osmosis across their impermeable scales
mdcat-b10-bio-70.explainHtml: Marine teleosts drink seawater to replace osmotic water lost across gills and body surfaces. Specialized gill chloride cells (mitochondria-rich cells) actively secrete excess Na⁺ and Cl⁻ into seawater, while their kidneys excrete divalent ions (Mg²⁺, SO4²⁻) in minimal, highly concentrated urine.

mdcat-b10-bio-71.qHtml: In the juxtaglomerular apparatus of the kidney, what stimulus triggers the granular (juxtaglomerular) cells of the afferent arteriole to release the proteolytic enzyme renin?
optionsHtml: Decreased renal perfusion pressure and diminished NaCl delivery sensed by the macula densa
Elevated mean systemic arterial blood pressure exceeding 150 mmHg
High extracellular sodium concentration in the distal convoluted tubule
Excessive expansion of intravascular circulating plasma volume
mdcat-b10-bio-71.explainHtml: Renin release is stimulated by: (1) decreased stretch in afferent arteriolar baroreceptors, (2) decreased NaCl delivery sensed by macula densa cells in the early distal tubule, and (3) increased sympathetic β1-adrenergic stimulation.

mdcat-b10-bio-72.qHtml: What is the primary nitrogenous excretory end-product in terrestrial birds, reptiles, and insects, and why is this an evolutionary adaptation for arid terrestrial life?
optionsHtml: Uric acid; it is almost insoluble in water, non-toxic, and excreted as a semi-solid paste with minimal water loss
Ammonia; it requires the least metabolic ATP to synthesize
Urea; it can be stored indefinitely in tissues without altering osmotic balance
Creatinine; it is rapidly filtered across the glomerulus without requiring reabsorption
mdcat-b10-bio-72.explainHtml: Uricotelic animals (birds, reptiles, terrestrial snails, insects) convert toxic ammonia into uric acid. Because uric acid has low water solubility (~0.06 g/L), it precipitates out of solution and is eliminated as a paste with negligible water loss (saving ~400 mL water per gram of nitrogen compared to ammonia).

mdcat-b10-bio-73.qHtml: In human thermoregulation, non-shivering thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue (BAT) generates heat without producing ATP through the uncoupling action of which mitochondrial inner membrane protein?
mdcat-b10-bio-73.explainHtml: Brown adipocytes express thermogenin (UCP-1) in their inner mitochondrial membrane. UCP-1 provides an alternate pathway for protons to re-enter the matrix, dissipating the proton electrochemical gradient directly as heat instead of driving ATP synthase.

mdcat-b10-bio-74.qHtml: The proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) of the human nephron is responsible for obligate reabsorption of what percentage of filtered glucose and amino acids under normal physiological conditions?
optionsHtml: 100% of filtered glucose and amino acids (via Na⁺-dependent secondary active cotransporters like SGLT2)
Exactly 50%, with the remainder reabsorbed in the collecting duct
Only 25%, since glucose is predominantly metabolized by podocytes
0%, because glucose is too large to cross the glomerular filtration barrier
mdcat-b10-bio-74.explainHtml: In healthy individuals, 100% of filtered glucose is actively reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule via sodium-glucose cotransporters (SGLT2 in early PCT, SGLT1 in late PCT) paired with basolateral GLUT2 uniporters, unless blood glucose exceeds the renal threshold (~180-200 mg/dL).

mdcat-b10-bio-75.qHtml: Aldosterone, secreted by the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex in response to angiotensin II or hyperkalemia, acts on renal principal cells to:
optionsHtml: Increase apical Na⁺ reabsorption via ENaC channels and stimulate basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps, coupled to K⁺ excretion
Promote massive calcium excretion in the loop of Henle
Inhibit aquaporin synthesis to dilute the urine
Stimulate glucose excretion in distal tubules
mdcat-b10-bio-75.explainHtml: Aldosterone binds intracellular mineralocorticoid receptors in principal cells, upregulating epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) on the apical membrane and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPases on the basolateral membrane. This drives sodium retention (and secondary water reabsorption) while enhancing potassium excretion.

mdcat-b10-bio-76.qHtml: What is the primary physical mechanism of gas exchange across the alveolar-capillary respiratory membrane in the human lungs?
optionsHtml: Simple passive diffusion driven by partial pressure gradients according to Fick's law of diffusion
Active transport mediated by ATP-driven gas permeases
Facilitated diffusion through clathrin-mediated endocytic vesicles
Bulk convective solvent drag through t junctions
mdcat-b10-bio-76.explainHtml: Respiratory gas exchange (O2 and CO2) occurs strictly by simple passive diffusion down partial pressure differentials across the ultra-thin alveolar-capillary barrier (~0.2 to 0.5 μm), as governed by Fick's law of diffusion (Rate = D × A × ΔP / T).

mdcat-b10-bio-77.qHtml: Pulmonary surfactant, secreted by alveolar type II epithelial cells (pneumocytes), prevents alveolar atelectasis (end-expiratory collapse) primarily by:
optionsHtml: Lowering the surface tension of the aqueous alveolar lining fluid proportionally as alveolar radius decreases (Laplace's law)
Generating an osmotic pressure gradient that draws air into the alveoli
Digesting foreign bacterial proteins in the alveolar lumen
Acting as a sticky adhesive that binds hemoglobin molecules
mdcat-b10-bio-77.explainHtml: According to Laplace's law for spheres, P = 2T / r. Without surfactant, smaller alveoli would experience higher collapsing pressure than larger ones. Surfactant (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine, DPPC) concentrates more densely in smaller alveoli, lowering surface tension T and stabilizing alveolar volumes.

mdcat-b10-bio-78.qHtml: How is the majority (~70%) of carbon dioxide transported from peripheral tissues back to the pulmonary capillaries in human venous blood?
optionsHtml: As bicarbonate ions (HCO3⁻) dissolved in blood plasma following conversion by intra-erythrocytic carbonic anhydrase
Directly dissolved as molecular CO2 gas bubbles in plasma
As carbaminohemoglobin bound to heme iron atoms
Chemically esterified to plasma cholesterol molecules
mdcat-b10-bio-78.explainHtml: Approximately 70% of CO2 is carried as bicarbonate (HCO3⁻) ions. In RBCs, carbonic anhydrase hydrates CO2: CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H⁺ + HCO3⁻. Bicarbonate is transported into plasma via the AE1 anion exchanger (chloride shift). 23% is bound as carbaminohemoglobin, and 7% is physically dissolved.

mdcat-b10-bio-79.qHtml: The "chloride shift" (Hamburger phenomenon) occurs in erythrocytes traversing systemic capillary beds in order to:
optionsHtml: Maintain electrical neutrality across the erythrocyte membrane when HCO3⁻ diffuses out into the plasma in exchange for Cl⁻
Promote the binding of oxygen to deoxyhemoglobin
Neutralize lactic acid produced by anaerobic skeletal muscle
Prevent erythrocyte swelling in hypotonic venous plasma
mdcat-b10-bio-79.explainHtml: As bicarbonate (HCO3⁻) ions accumulate inside erythrocytes in peripheral capillaries, they diffuse out into plasma down their concentration gradient via the AE1 band 3 antiporter. To maintain electrical neutrality, chloride ions (Cl⁻) move from the plasma into the erythrocyte.

mdcat-b10-bio-80.qHtml: A rightward shift of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve (the Bohr effect) signifies reduced affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen, facilitating O2 unloading to metabolically active tissues. Which combination of physiological factors produces this rightward shift?
optionsHtml: Increased partial pressure of CO2 (PCO2), increased [H⁺] (decreased pH), elevated temperature, and increased 2,3-BPG concentration
Decreased PCO2, increased pH, decreased temperature, and reduced 2,3-BPG
Decreased PCO2 and hypothermia during resting sleep
mdcat-b10-bio-80.explainHtml: A rightward shift (Bohr effect) lowers Hb affinity for O2, promoting oxygen delivery to tissues. Factors causing this include: elevated PCO2, increased [H⁺] (lower pH), elevated temperature, and increased 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG), all of which stabilize the T (taut/deoxygenated) conformation.

mdcat-b10-bio-81.qHtml: Under normal resting conditions at sea level, the central chemoreceptors located on the ventrolateral surface of the medulla oblongata regulate the primary respiratory drive by responding to changes in:
optionsHtml: The hydrogen ion concentration [H⁺] of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) generated by CO2 diffusing across the blood-brain barrier
Arterial oxygen partial pressure (PaO2) below 95 mmHg
Blood hemoglobin saturation percentage in systemic veins
Atmospheric humidity detected in the nasal mucosa
mdcat-b10-bio-81.explainHtml: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla are sensitive to [H⁺] in brain interstitial fluid and CSF. Because the blood-brain barrier is impermeable to H⁺ but freely permeable to lipophilic CO2, arterial CO2 diffuses across, forming carbonic acid and protons that stimulate chemoreceptors to increase ventilation.

mdcat-b10-bio-82.qHtml: In the human respiratory tree, which structural zone represents the transition from the purely conducting anatomical dead space to the actual gas-exchanging respiratory zone?
optionsHtml: Respiratory bronchioles (where alveoli first appear budding along the wall)
mdcat-b10-bio-82.explainHtml: The conducting zone terminates at the terminal bronchioles (generations 0 to 16, anatomical dead space ~150 mL). The respiratory zone begins at generation 17 with the respiratory bronchioles, which feature outpocketing alveoli and transition into alveolar ducts and alveolar sacs.

mdcat-b10-bio-83.qHtml: Carbon monoxide (CO) inhalation is lethal even at low concentrations because its affinity for hemoglobin is approximately 200-250 times greater than that of oxygen, forming:
optionsHtml: Carboxyhemoglobin, which blocks O2 binding and shifts the remaining oxyhemoglobin curve to the left, preventing tissue O2 release
Methemoglobin, which oxidizes ferrous iron to ferric iron
Carbaminohemoglobin, which permanently precipitates in renal tubules
mdcat-b10-bio-83.explainHtml: CO binds with ~240-fold greater affinity than O2 to heme iron, forming carboxyhemoglobin (COHb). This locks bound subunits in the relaxed R-state, shifting the remaining O2 dissociation curve sharply to the left and severely impairing tissue oxygen release (cellular hypoxia).

mdcat-b10-bio-84.qHtml: During quiet resting inhalation in humans, which active muscular contraction is responsible for approximately 75% of the inspiratory air volume entering the lungs?
optionsHtml: Contraction and downward flattening of the dome-shaped diaphragm
Contraction of the internal intercostal muscles
Contraction of the rectus abdominis muscles
mdcat-b10-bio-84.explainHtml: Normal resting inspiration is an active process driven predominantly (~75%) by contraction of the diaphragm, which flattens downward by 1-2 cm, expanding the vertical dimension of the thoracic cavity. Contraction of the external intercostal muscles accounts for the remaining ~25%.

mdcat-b10-bio-85.qHtml: What is the molecular basis of the resting membrane potential (approximately -70 mV) in a mammalian myelinated axon?
optionsHtml: High resting membrane permeability to K⁺ via non-gated leak channels, combined with the electrogenic action of the 3 Na⁺ out / 2 K⁺ in ATPase pump
Continuous influx of sodium ions through open voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
Active extrusion of intracellular proteins into the extracellular fluid
Complete impermeability of the plasma membrane to all inorganic ions
mdcat-b10-bio-85.explainHtml: The neuronal resting potential (-70 mV) is established predominantly by K⁺ leak channels, allowing K⁺ to diffuse down its chemical gradient out of the cell until its electrical gradient balances it (Goldman equation). The electrogenic Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (3 Na⁺ pumped out for 2 K⁺ pumped in) maintains these ion gradients.

mdcat-b10-bio-86.qHtml: During the depolarizing upstroke of a neuronal action potential, what event is responsible for the rapid, regenerative reversal of membrane polarity toward +35 mV?
optionsHtml: The opening of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, permitting a massive influx of Na⁺ down its electrochemical gradient
The opening of voltage-gated K⁺ channels, driving rapid K⁺ influx
Active pumping of Ca²⁺ out of the axon into the synaptic cleft
The opening of ligand-gated chloride channels causing hyperpolarization
mdcat-b10-bio-86.explainHtml: Depolarization beyond threshold (~ -55 mV) causes rapid opening of m-activation gates on voltage-gated Na⁺ channels. This positive feedback loop (Hodgkin cycle) leads to massive inward Na⁺ current until membrane potential approaches the sodium equilibrium potential (~+35 to +40 mV).

mdcat-b10-bio-87.qHtml: Saltatory conduction in myelinated axons increases the velocity of action potential propagation by factors of 10-100 because action potentials:
optionsHtml: Regenerate exclusively at unmyelinated nodes of Ranvier where voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are densely clustered
Travel continuously through the insulating lipid bilayer of the myelin sheath
Skip across synaptic junctions without requiring neurotransmitter vesicle release
Rely exclusively on passive electron flow along the external myelin wrap
mdcat-b10-bio-87.explainHtml: Myelin acts as an electrical insulator that increases membrane resistance and decreases capacitance. Electrotonic current spreads rapidly beneath the myelin sheath, depolarizing the membrane only at the unmyelinated nodes of Ranvier, where voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are clustered at high density (~10,000/μm²).

mdcat-b10-bio-88.qHtml: At a chemical synapse, the arrival of an action potential at the presynaptic terminal triggers neurotransmitter exocytosis by directly opening:
optionsHtml: Voltage-gated calcium (Ca²⁺) channels, allowing Ca²⁺ influx that interacts with synaptotagmin on SNARE vesicle complexes
Voltage-gated chloride channels causing terminal repolarization
Ligand-gated sodium channels on the presynaptic terminal
Proton pumps that acidify the synaptic cleft
mdcat-b10-bio-88.explainHtml: Terminal depolarization opens N- and P/Q-type voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels. Calcium rushes inward down its 10,000-fold concentration gradient, binding to the vesicle sensor synaptotagmin. This triggers SNARE complexes (synaptobrevin, syntaxin, SNAP-25) to fuse vesicles with the presynaptic membrane, releasing neurotransmitter.

mdcat-b10-bio-89.qHtml: Which lobe of the human cerebral cortex houses the primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus) and Broca's motor speech area?
mdcat-b10-bio-89.explainHtml: The frontal lobe contains the precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex, Brodmann area 4), the premotor cortex, the prefrontal association cortex (executive function), and Broca's motor speech area (Brodmann areas 44 and 45 in the dominant hemisphere).

mdcat-b10-bio-90.qHtml: The hypothalamus exerts master neuroendocrine control over the anterior pituitary gland (adenohypophysis) via which vascular transport route?
optionsHtml: The hypophyseal portal system of capillaries
Unbroken continuous nerve tract axons extending into the infundibular stalk
The systemic circle of Willis arterial circulation
mdcat-b10-bio-90.explainHtml: Hypothalamic neurosecretory neurons release releasing and inhibiting hormones (e.g., TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH) into the primary capillary plexus in the median eminence. These hormones travel via the hypophyseal portal venules directly to the secondary capillary plexus in the anterior pituitary.

mdcat-b10-bio-91.qHtml: Which endocrine hormone produced by the parafollicular (C-cells) of the thyroid gland acts to decrease blood calcium levels by inhibiting osteoclastic bone resorption?
mdcat-b10-bio-91.explainHtml: Calcitonin is a 32-amino acid peptide hormone secreted by thyroid parafollicular C-cells in response to hypercalcemia. It lowers blood Ca²⁺ levels by inhibiting osteoclast activity and stimulating renal calcium clearance, opposing the actions of parathyroid hormone (PTH).

mdcat-b10-bio-92.qHtml: In the mechanism of action of peptide and catecholamine hormones (e.g., epinephrine, glucagon), which intracellular second messenger is generated when the Gs protein α-subunit stimulates adenylyl cyclase?
mdcat-b10-bio-92.explainHtml: Binding of hydrophilic peptide hormones or epinephrine to Gs-coupled receptors induces GTP binding to Gαs, activating membrane-bound adenylyl cyclase. Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP into cAMP, which allosterically activates Protein Kinase A (PKA) to phosphorylate metabolic enzymes.

mdcat-b10-bio-93.qHtml: A patient presents with persistent hyperglycemia, central truncal obesity, "moon face", abdominal purple striae, and muscle wasting. Serum testing demonstrates chronically elevated cortisol levels that fail to suppress with low-dose dexamethasone. What is the clinical diagnosis?
mdcat-b10-bio-93.explainHtml: Cushing's syndrome results from chronic glucocorticoid (cortisol) excess. Clinical signs include truncal adiposity, moon facies, buffalo hump, purple striae (due to collagen degradation), and hyperglycemia. Addison's disease is primary adrenal insufficiency (hypocortisolism).

mdcat-b10-bio-94.qHtml: According to the sliding filament theory of skeletal muscle contraction, what morphological change occurs to the sarcomere during active muscular shortening?
optionsHtml: The I-band and H-zone narrow or disappear, while the width of the A-band remains strictly constant
The A-band narrows, while the I-band remains constant
Both the A-band and I-band lengthen significantly
The Z-lines move further apart from each other
mdcat-b10-bio-94.explainHtml: During contraction, thin (actin) filaments slide over thick (myosin) filaments toward the M-line. Consequently, the distance between adjacent Z-lines decreases, the I-bands (actin only) and H-zones (myosin only) narrow or disappear, while the A-band (length of thick filaments) remains constant.

mdcat-b10-bio-95.qHtml: In skeletal muscle, action potentials propagating down transverse tubules (T-tubules) trigger calcium release from the terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum by mechanical coupling between:
optionsHtml: Dihydropyridine receptors (DHPR) in the T-tubule and Ryanodine receptors (RyR1) in the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane
Myosin l chain kinase and titin filaments
mdcat-b10-bio-95.explainHtml: Action potentials traversing T-tubules induce conformational changes in voltage-sensing L-type calcium channels (dihydropyridine receptors, DHPR). In skeletal muscle, DHPR is mechanically coupled directly to the ryanodine receptor (RyR1) Ca²⁺-release channel on the terminal cisternae, causing rapid Ca²⁺ efflux.

mdcat-b10-bio-96.qHtml: During the cross-bridge power stroke of skeletal muscle contraction, what precise biochemical event triggers the pivoting of the myosin head and mechanical displacement of the actin filament?
optionsHtml: The release of inorganic phosphate (Pi) from the myosin head
The binding of a new ATP molecule to the empty nucleotide site
The hydrolysis of ATP into ADP and inorganic phosphate
The binding of calcium ions directly to the myosin neck region
mdcat-b10-bio-96.explainHtml: After the energized myosin head (bearing ADP and Pi) binds actin, the release of inorganic phosphate (Pi) triggers the conformational power stroke, pulling the actin filament ~10 nm toward the M-line. ADP is subsequently released. Binding of a fresh ATP is required to dissociate the cross-bridge.

mdcat-b10-bio-97.qHtml: Why does rigor mortis develop in skeletal muscles several hours following somatic death?
optionsHtml: Intracellular ATP is completely depleted, preventing the detachment of myosin cross-bridge heads from actin active sites
Lactic acid overproduction permanently lyses troponin complexes
Calcium is actively sequestered back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Myosin filaments are enzymatically degraded by lysosomal proteases
mdcat-b10-bio-97.explainHtml: Cross-bridge detachment requires the binding of a fresh ATP molecule to the myosin ATPase site. Following death, cellular ATP synthesis ceases while membrane permeability allows Ca²⁺ to diffuse into the sarcoplasm, forming cross-bridges. Lacking ATP to detach, muscles remain in a rigid state (rigor mortis).

mdcat-b10-bio-98.qHtml: In the microscopic architecture of compact mammalian bone, concentric cylindrical layers of calcified bone matrix termed lamellae surround a central neurovascular channel known as the:
mdcat-b10-bio-98.explainHtml: The structural unit of compact bone is the osteon (Haversian system). It consists of concentric lamellae of mineralized matrix surrounding a longitudinal central Haversian canal containing blood vessels and nerve fibers. Perforating Volkmann canals run perpendicular to connect osteons.

mdcat-b10-bio-99.qHtml: Which of the following bones belongs strictly to the axial skeleton of the human body rather than the appendicular skeleton?
mdcat-b10-bio-99.explainHtml: The human axial skeleton (80 bones) consists of the skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum, and hyoid bone. The pectoral girdle (clavicle and scapula) and pelvic girdle (ilium, ischium, pubis) belong to the appendicular skeleton (126 bones).

mdcat-b10-bio-100.qHtml: The shoulder (glenohumeral) joint and the hip joint are functional and structural examples of which class of synovial joint?
optionsHtml: Ball-and-socket joint (permitting multiaxial rotation in all planes)
Hinge joint (permitting uniaxal flexion and extension)
mdcat-b10-bio-100.explainHtml: Ball-and-socket (spheroidal) joints consist of a globular head fitting into a cup-like socket. They are multiaxial/triaxial joints allowing flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, circumduction, and medial/lateral rotation (e.g., glenohumeral and acetabulofemoral joints).

mdcat-b10-bio-101.qHtml: Tetanus toxin (tetanospasmin), produced by Clostridium tetani, induces sustained, spastic muscular contractions and lockjaw by which specific neurological mechanism?
optionsHtml: Retrograde axonal transport to spinal motor interneurons, where it cleaves synaptobrevin to block the release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (GABA and glycine)
Directly stimulating excessive acetylcholine synthesis at neuromuscular junctions
Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft
Blocking voltage-gated potassium channels along motor axons
mdcat-b10-bio-101.explainHtml: Tetanospasmin undergoes retrograde transport into spinal cord inhibitory Renshaw interneurons. Its zinc endopeptidase l chain cleaves synaptobrevin (VAMP), blocking the exocytosis of inhibitory neurotransmitters GABA and glycine. Without inhibition, α-motor neurons fire uncontrollably, causing spastic paralysis.

mdcat-b10-bio-102.qHtml: In the structure of a skeletal muscle thin filament, which protein subunit directly binds Ca²⁺ ions to initiate the conformational movement of tropomyosin away from myosin-binding sites on actin?
mdcat-b10-bio-102.explainHtml: The troponin complex contains three subunits: Troponin T (binds tropomyosin), Troponin I (inhibits actin-myosin interaction), and Troponin C (binds Ca²⁺). When Ca²⁺ binds to TnC, a conformational change pulls tropomyosin into the actin groove, exposing myosin-binding sites.

mdcat-b10-bio-103.qHtml: In the human female menstrual cycle, the mid-cycle surge of which pituitary gonadotropic hormone directly induces final follicular maturation and ovulation?
mdcat-b10-bio-103.explainHtml: Sustained high estradiol levels (>200 pg/mL for ~50 hours) from the mature Graafian follicle switch estrogen feedback from negative to positive at the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary. This triggers a massive LH surge, causing resumption of meiosis I, follicular rupture, and ovulation ~24-36 hours later.

mdcat-b10-bio-104.qHtml: Spermatogenesis in the human testes occurs within the seminiferous tubules. Which somatic cells support, nourish developing germ cells, and form the blood-testis barrier via t junctions?
mdcat-b10-bio-104.explainHtml: Sertoli cells span from the basement membrane to the lumen of seminiferous tubules. Their continuous t junctions form the blood-testis barrier, isolating post-meiotic haploid germ cells from the systemic immune system. Leydig cells reside in the interstitial space and produce testosterone.

mdcat-b10-bio-105.qHtml: At the time of ovulation, the secondary oocyte released into the fallopian tube (oviduct) is arrested at which stage of cell division, resuming only upon fertilization by a spermatozoon?
mdcat-b10-bio-105.explainHtml: Human oogenesis completes meiosis I just prior to ovulation, extruding the first polar body. The secondary oocyte promptly begins meiosis II but arrests at metaphase II under the influence of cytostatic factor (CSF). Entry of a fertilizing sperm induces a Ca²⁺ wave that triggers completion of meiosis II.

mdcat-b10-bio-106.qHtml: During fertilization, the cortical reaction in the oocyte prevents polyspermy (fertilization by multiple sperm) primarily by which mechanism?
optionsHtml: Exocytosis of cortical granules releasing ovastacin and proteases that cleave ZP2 and harden the zona pellucida (slow block to polyspermy)
Immediate shedding of the entire plasma membrane
Rapid influx of magnesium ions that denatures sperm flagella
Hyperpolarization of the vitelline envelope to -100 mV
mdcat-b10-bio-106.explainHtml: Sperm-egg fusion triggers IP3-mediated oscillatory release of intracellular Ca²⁺, stimulating exocytosis of cortical granules beneath the oolemma. Cortical enzymes cleave ZP2 and alter ZP3, hardening the zona pellucida and preventing additional spermatozoa from binding (slow block to polyspermy).

mdcat-b10-bio-107.qHtml: In human early embryogenesis, the blastocyst consists of an outer cell layer that develops into the embryonic portion of the placenta. What is this outer epithelial layer called?
mdcat-b10-bio-107.explainHtml: At day 5-6 post-fertilization, the blastocyst comprises an inner cell mass (which forms the embryo proper) and an outer monolayer of trophoblast cells. The trophoblast differentiates into the syncytiotrophoblast and cytotrophoblast, which invade the endometrium to form the placenta and secrete hCG.

mdcat-b10-bio-108.qHtml: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast during early pregnancy. What is its primary physiological function during the first trimester?
optionsHtml: Maintaining the corpus luteum so it continues secreting progesterone and estrogen to prevent menstruation
Directly stimulating fetal lung surfactant production
Triggering maternal milk ejection from alveolar mammary glands
mdcat-b10-bio-108.explainHtml: hCG binds LH receptors on the corpus luteum, preventing its involution during the first 8-10 weeks of pregnancy. This ensures sustained secretion of progesterone and estrogens, maintaining the decidualized endometrium until the placenta assumes endocrine autonomy (luteal-placental shift).

mdcat-b10-bio-109.qHtml: In angiosperms (flowering plants), double fertilization involves two separate nuclear fusion events. What are these two events and their respective products?
optionsHtml: One sperm nucleus fuses with the egg cell to form a diploid zygote (2n), while the second sperm fuses with the diploid central cell secondary nucleus to form a triploid endosperm (3n)
Two sperm nuclei fuse with two separate eggs to form fraternal twin embryos
One sperm nucleus fuses with a synergid to form the seed coat, and one fuses with the antipodal cell
One sperm nucleus fertilizes the stigma, while the other fertilizes the style
mdcat-b10-bio-109.explainHtml: Double fertilization is unique to angiosperms. The pollen tube delivers two haploid sperm: one fertilizes the haploid egg to form the diploid zygote (2n), while the second fertilizes the binucleate central cell (polar nuclei) to generate the triploid nutritive endosperm tissue (3n).

mdcat-b10-bio-110.qHtml: Which sexually transmitted infection (STI) is caused by the spirochete bacterium Treponema pallidum, initially presenting with a painless genital ulcer (chancre) during its primary stage?
mdcat-b10-bio-110.explainHtml: Syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum. Primary syphilis presents with a solitary, painless, indurated ulcer (chancre) at the inoculation site. Secondary syphilis presents with a diffuse maculopapular rash (including palms/soles) and condyloma lata, while tertiary syphilis can involve neurosyphilis and gummas.

mdcat-b10-bio-111.qHtml: In a classical Mendelian dihybrid cross between two individuals heterozygous for two independently assorting unlinked genes (AaBb × AaBb), what is the expected phenotypic ratio in the F2 progeny assuming complete dominance?
mdcat-b10-bio-111.explainHtml: By Mendel's law of independent assortment, combining the two independent monohybrid 3:1 phenotypic ratios (3/4 dominant, 1/4 recessive) yields: (3/4 A + 1/4 a)(3/4 B + 1/4 b) = 9/16 A_B_ : 3/16 A_bb : 3/16 aaB_ : 1/16 aabb (a 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio).

mdcat-b10-bio-112.qHtml: The ABO blood group system in humans exhibits which genetic phenomenon when an individual inherits the IA allele from one parent and the IB allele from the other parent?
optionsHtml: Codominance (both A and B antigens are simultaneously and fully expressed on the red blood cell surface)
Incomplete dominance (yielding an intermediate hybrid antigen)
mdcat-b10-bio-112.explainHtml: In codominance, both alleles are fully and independently expressed in the heterozygote without blending. An IAIB individual produces both A transferase (adding N-acetylgalactosamine) and B transferase (adding D-galactose), expressing both intact antigens on the RBC surface.

mdcat-b10-bio-113.qHtml: Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive coagulopathy. If a carrier female (X^H X^h) has children with a normal male (X^H Y), what is the probability that their first son will be affected by hemophilia A?
mdcat-b10-bio-113.explainHtml: The mother contributes either X^H (normal) or X^h (hemophilia) with equal 50% probability to male offspring, who always receive the Y chromosome from their father. Thus, among sons, 50% will inherit X^h Y (affected) and 50% will inherit X^H Y (unaffected).

mdcat-b10-bio-114.qHtml: Which human genetic syndrome is caused by chromosomal non-disjunction producing a 47,XXY karyotype in phenotypic males, characterized by tall stature, testicular atrophy, gynecomastia, and azoospermia?
mdcat-b10-bio-114.explainHtml: Klinefelter syndrome is characterized by a 47,XXY chromosomal constitution. Presence of the Y chromosome guides male phenotypic differentiation, but the extra X chromosome causes dysgenesis of seminiferous tubules, hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, small firm testes, azoospermia, and elevated gonadotropins.

mdcat-b10-bio-115.qHtml: In human molecular genetics, the molecular basis of sickle-cell anemia is a point mutation in the β-globin gene (HBB) resulting in which specific single amino acid substitution at position 6 of the polypeptide chain?
optionsHtml: Glutamic acid is replaced by Valine (Glu6Val)
Valine is replaced by Glutamic acid (Val6Glu)
mdcat-b10-bio-115.explainHtml: Sickle cell disease is caused by a single nucleotide transversion (GAG to GTG in codon 6 of the β-globin gene on chromosome 11). This substitutes a negatively charged hydrophilic glutamic acid with a non-polar hydrophobic valine residue, causing HbS polymerization under hypoxia.

mdcat-b10-bio-116.qHtml: According to the operon model of prokaryotic gene regulation proposed by Jacob and Monod, the lac repressor protein encoded by the lacI gene shuts off transcription of the lactose operon by binding to which DNA element?
mdcat-b10-bio-116.explainHtml: In the absence of allolactose (inducer), the lac repressor homotetramer binds tightly to the palindromic lac operator sequence (lacO). This sterically prevents RNA polymerase from binding to the promoter and transcribing the polycistronic structural genes (lacZ, lacY, lacA).

mdcat-b10-bio-117.qHtml: In eukaryotic pre-mRNA processing, the ribonucleoprotein molecular machine responsible for recognizing consensus 5' splice sites, branch-point adenosines, and 3' splice sites to excise introns is the:
optionsHtml: Spliceosome (composed of snRNAs U1, U2, U4, U5, U6 and associated proteins)
mdcat-b10-bio-117.explainHtml: The spliceosome is a large dynamic ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex consisting of five small nuclear RNAs (U1, U2, U4, U5, U6) complexed with proteins (forming snRNPs). It catalyzes two transesterification reactions that excise non-coding introns as a lariat and ligate coding exons.

mdcat-b10-bio-118.qHtml: Polygenic inheritance, where multiple additive genes influence a single continuous quantitative phenotypic trait, typically produces which type of phenotypic distribution in a large population?
optionsHtml: A bell-shaped Gaussian normal distribution curve
A discrete 1:1 ratio with no intermediate phenotypes
mdcat-b10-bio-118.explainHtml: Continuous variation in quantitative traits (such as human he, skin color, and blood pressure) results from polygenic inheritance involving multiple additive gene loci. In a large population, environmental influences and multiple alleles combine to yield a continuous bell-shaped Gaussian distribution.

mdcat-b10-bio-119.qHtml: Type II restriction endonucleases (such as EcoRI) widely utilized in recombinant DNA technology are characterized by their ability to recognize and cleave which specific DNA sequences?
optionsHtml: Palindromic sequences (symmetrical 4-8 base-pair sequences reading identically in the 5' to 3' direction on both complementary strands)
mdcat-b10-bio-119.explainHtml: Type II restriction endonucleases recognize specific inverted palindromic sequences (e.g., EcoRI recognizes 5'-GAATTC-3') and cleave both phosphodiester backbones at precise positions, often leaving sticky cohesive staggered ends that facilitate molecular ligation.

mdcat-b10-bio-120.qHtml: In the polymerase chain reaction (PCR), what is the role of the high-temperature incubation step (typically 94-96°C) at the beginning of each cyclic round?
optionsHtml: Thermal denaturation of double-stranded template DNA into separate single strands by breaking hydrogen bonds between base pairs
Enzymatic extension by thermostable Taq DNA polymerase
mdcat-b10-bio-120.explainHtml: Each PCR cycle begins with a denaturation step (94-96°C for 20-30 seconds). High thermal energy disrupts the hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs without breaking covalent phosphodiester bonds, yielding two single-stranded DNA templates.

mdcat-b10-bio-121.qHtml: Why is Taq polymerase, isolated from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus, uniquely suited for automated PCR amplification?
optionsHtml: It remains enzymatic and structurally stable at the 95°C denaturation temperature without needing replenishment after each cycle
It possesses a 3' to 5' proofreading exonuclease activity 100 times higher than mammalian polymerases
It synthesizes RNA primers de novo without requiring free 3'-OH groups
It cleaves restriction sites directly during extension
mdcat-b10-bio-121.explainHtml: Traditional DNA polymerases (e.g., E. coli DNA Pol I) denature irreversibly at 95°C and had to be added manually after every cycle. Taq polymerase is thermophilic and retains catalytic activity through multiple high-temperature cycles (optimal extension at 72°C).

mdcat-b10-bio-122.qHtml: In agarose gel electrophoresis of nucleic acids, DNA fragments migrate toward the positive electrode (anode) at rates inversely proportional to the log of their molecular we because:
optionsHtml: DNA molecules possess a constant negative charge-to-mass ratio due to their phosphate-sugar backbone, migrating through molecular sieve pores
DNA is positively charged due to basic purine rings
Larger DNA molecules experience less frictional drag through agarose polymer fibers
Ethidium bromide pushes smaller fragments toward the cathode
