tcat-stat-5.explainHtml: A fundamental algebraic property of the arithmetic mean is that ∑(X - X̄) = 0.

tcat-stat-6.qHtml: According to Karl Pearson's empirical relationship for moderately skewed distributions, what is the connection between Mean, Median, and Mode?
tcat-stat-6.explainHtml: The empirical relationship is Mean - Mode = 3(Mean - Median), which rearranges to Mode = 3(Median) - 2(Mean).

tcat-stat-7.qHtml: What is the formula for calculating the Coefficient of Variation (C.V.), used to compare relative variability between distributions?
tcat-stat-7.explainHtml: Coefficient of Variation expresses the standard deviation as a percentage of the arithmetic mean: C.V. = (s / X̄) × 100.

tcat-stat-8.qHtml: If each observation in a dataset is multiplied by a constant factor of 3, what happens to the standard deviation?
optionsHtml: The standard deviation is multiplied by 3
The standard deviation is multiplied by 9
The standard deviation remains completely unchanged
tcat-stat-8.explainHtml: Multiplying every value by a constant c multiplies the standard deviation by ∣c∣. Here, standard deviation becomes 3 × original.

tcat-stat-9.qHtml: In a positively (r) skewed frequency distribution, what is the relative order of the three central tendency measures?
tcat-stat-9.explainHtml: In a r-skewed distribution, extreme high values pull the mean toward the r tail, resulting in Mean > Median > Mode.

tcat-stat-10.qHtml: Which measure of central tendency is mathematically most appropriate for calculating the average rate of speed over equal distance intervals?
tcat-stat-10.explainHtml: Harmonic Mean is the reciprocal of the arithmetic mean of reciprocals, providing the exact average for rates and speed over fixed distances.

tcat-stat-11.qHtml: For any set of positive non-identical real numbers, what strict inequality holds between their Arithmetic Mean (A.M.), Geometric Mean (G.M.), and Harmonic Mean (H.M.)?
tcat-stat-11.explainHtml: The AM-GM-HM inequality proves that for positive unequal numbers, A.M. > G.M. > H.M. (equality holds only if all values are identical).

tcat-stat-12.qHtml: What is the Quartile Deviation (Semi-Interquartile Range) for a distribution with first quartile Q₁ = 24 and third quartile Q₃ = 40?

tcat-stat-13.qHtml: If a frequency distribution has a coefficient of kurtosis β₂ = 3 (or excess kurtosis γ₂ = 0), how is the peakedness of the distribution classified?
tcat-stat-13.explainHtml: A normal distribution has moment ratio β₂ = μ₄ / σ⁴ = 3 (excess kurtosis = 0) and is called mesokurtic. β₂ > 3 is leptokurtic; β₂ < 3 is platykurtic.

tcat-stat-14.qHtml: The variance of 10 observations is 16. If a constant value of 5 is added to every single observation, what is the new variance?
tcat-stat-14.explainHtml: Variance is independent of change of origin; adding or subtracting a constant to each value leaves the variance unchanged (Var = 16).

tcat-stat-15.qHtml: What is the probability of rolling a sum of 7 when tossing two fair, six-sided dice simultaneously?
tcat-stat-15.explainHtml: Pairs summing to 7 are (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1) = 6 favorable outcomes out of 36 total outcomes = 6/36 = 1/6.

tcat-stat-16.qHtml: For two mutually exclusive events A and B, what is the probability of their intersection P(A ∩ B)?
tcat-stat-16.explainHtml: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur simultaneously, so their intersection is empty: P(A ∩ B) = 0.

tcat-stat-17.qHtml: What are the two parameters of a Binomial Probability Distribution?
optionsHtml: n (number of independent trials) and p (probability of success)
tcat-stat-17.explainHtml: A Binomial distribution is denoted B(n, p) where n is the number of identical Bernoulli trials and p is the probability of success on each trial.

tcat-stat-18.qHtml: What is the numerical value of the total area under the probability density curve of any continuous random variable?
tcat-stat-18.explainHtml: By the second axiom of probability, the integral of any valid probability density function across its entire domain equals exactly 1.0.

tcat-stat-19.qHtml: In a Standard Normal Distribution Z ~ N(0, 1), what are the values of the Mean and Variance respectively?
tcat-stat-19.explainHtml: A standard normal variable Z has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation (and variance) of 1.

tcat-stat-20.qHtml: For two independent events A and B with P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.5, what is the probability P(A ∪ B)?

tcat-stat-21.qHtml: In a Poisson distribution with mean parameter λ, what is the mathematical relationship between the Mean and the Variance?
optionsHtml: Variance = Mean2 = λ²
tcat-stat-21.explainHtml: A unique characteristic of the Poisson distribution is that its mean and variance are identical and equal to parameter λ.

tcat-stat-22.qHtml: In a Binomial distribution B(n, p), what are the formulas for the expected value (mean) and variance respectively?
optionsHtml: Mean = np, Variance = npq (where q = 1 - p)
tcat-stat-22.explainHtml: For B(n, p), E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 - p) = npq.

tcat-stat-23.qHtml: According to the Empirical Rule (68-95-99.7 rule) for a normal distribution, what percentage of values lie within μ ± 2σ?
tcat-stat-23.explainHtml: In a normal distribution, ~68.3% falls within 1 SD, ~95.45% within 2 SDs, and ~99.73% within 3 SDs.

tcat-stat-24.qHtml: What is the conditional probability formula P(A | B), assuming P(B) > 0?
tcat-stat-24.explainHtml: By definition of conditional probability, P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B) for P(B) > 0.

tcat-stat-25.qHtml: Under what limiting conditions does a Binomial distribution B(n, p) converge to a Poisson distribution?
optionsHtml: When n → ∞, p → 0, such that the product np = λ remains constant and finite
When both n and p approach infinity simultaneously
tcat-stat-25.explainHtml: The Poisson distribution is the law of rare events, derived as the limit of B(n, p) as n → ∞ and p → 0 with np = λ constant.

tcat-stat-26.qHtml: What is the probability of obtaining exactly 3 heads when tossing a fair coin 5 times?
tcat-stat-26.explainHtml: P(X = 3) = (35​) × (0.5)^{3} × (0.5)^{2} = 10 × (1/32) = 10/32 = 5/16.

tcat-stat-27.qHtml: If a random variable X has mean E(X) = 10 and variance Var(X) = 4, what is the expected value of E(X2)?
tcat-stat-27.explainHtml: Var(X) = E(X2) - [E(X)]² → 4 = E(X2) - 100 → E(X2) = 100 + 4 = 104.

tcat-stat-28.qHtml: What does Bayes' Theorem calculate in statistical inference?
optionsHtml: Posterior probability of an event given prior probability and conditional likelihood evidence
The marginal variance of two correlated continuous variables
The exact sample size required for zero standard error
The degree of peakedness in a multimodal probability density
tcat-stat-28.explainHtml: Bayes' theorem computes posterior probability: P(Ai | B) = [P(B | Ai)P(Ai)] / ∑[P(B | Aj)P(Aj)], updating prior beliefs with observed evidence.

tcat-stat-29.qHtml: What is any measurable numerical characteristic calculated from a sample called?
tcat-stat-29.explainHtml: A numerical measure calculated from sample data is a statistic (e.g., sample mean x̄); a measure describing an entire population is a parameter (e.g., μ).

tcat-stat-30.qHtml: What is the Standard Error of the mean (S.E.) for a simple random sample of size n drawn from a population with standard deviation σ?
tcat-stat-30.explainHtml: The standard error of the sample mean is the standard deviation of its sampling distribution: SE(x̄) = σ / {n}.

tcat-stat-31.qHtml: How many total possible samples of size n = 2 can be drawn from a population of size N = 5 WITH replacement?
optionsHtml: 25 samples (Nn)
tcat-stat-31.explainHtml: With replacement, each selection is independent: Nn=52 = 25 possible samples.

tcat-stat-32.qHtml: An estimator θ̂ is called an "unbiased estimator" of parameter θ if its expected value satisfies:
tcat-stat-32.explainHtml: An estimator is unbiased if its expected value equals the true population parameter: E(θ̂) = θ.

tcat-stat-33.qHtml: According to the Central Limit Theorem (CLT), as the sample size n becomes sufficiently large (typically n ≥ 30), what happens to the sampling distribution of the sample mean x̄?
optionsHtml: It approaches a normal distribution regardless of the shape of the parent population
It becomes uniform across all intervals
It adopts the exact shape of the underlying population
Its variance increases proportionally to n
tcat-stat-33.explainHtml: CLT states that for large n, the distribution of sample mean approaches N(μ, σ²/n), regardless of the original population distribution.

tcat-stat-34.qHtml: When sampling WITHOUT replacement from a finite population of size N, what finite population correction factor (FPC) is multiplied into the standard error formula?
tcat-stat-34.explainHtml: Without replacement from a finite population, the standard error is adjusted by the finite population multiplier √[(N - n)/(N - 1)].

tcat-stat-35.qHtml: What is the critical Z-value (Z_α/2) used to construct a two-sided 95% confidence interval for a population mean?
tcat-stat-35.explainHtml: For a 95% confidence interval, α = 0.05, α/2 = 0.025, and the critical standard normal value is Z = 1.96.

tcat-stat-36.qHtml: Why is the sample variance formula divided by (n - 1) instead of n when estimating the population variance σ² from sample data?
optionsHtml: To correct for downward bias, making s2 = ∑(x - x̄)² / (n - 1) an unbiased estimator (Bessel's correction)
To account for measurement instrument inaccuracies
To ensure the variance is always an integer
Because one observation is always discarded as an outlier
tcat-stat-36.explainHtml: Dividing by n underestimates σ²; Bessel's correction dividing by degrees of freedom (n - 1) produces an unbiased estimator: E(s2) = σ².

tcat-stat-37.qHtml: If the sample size n is quadrupled from 25 to 100, what happens to the standard error of the mean?
optionsHtml: The standard error is halved (reduced by 50%)
The standard error is reduced to 1/4th of its value
tcat-stat-37.explainHtml: Since SE = σ / {n}, quadrupling n (4n) divides the standard error by {4} = 2, halving it.

tcat-stat-38.qHtml: A sample of 64 observations from a population with known standard deviation σ = 16 has a sample mean x̄ = 50. What is the 95% confidence interval for the population mean μ?
tcat-stat-38.explainHtml: SE = 16 / {64} = 16 / 8 = 2. Margin of error = 1.96 × 2 = 3.92. CI = 50 ± 3.92 = [46.08, 53.92].

tcat-stat-39.qHtml: What property must an estimator possess if, as sample size n approaches infinity, the probability that the estimator differs from the parameter by any arbitrary amount approaches zero?
tcat-stat-39.explainHtml: Consistency means the estimator converges in probability to the true population parameter as n → ∞.

tcat-stat-40.qHtml: In Stratified Random Sampling, when is Neyman Optimal Allocation used to determine stratum sample sizes?
optionsHtml: When stratum variances differ, allocating larger sample sizes to larger and more variable strata
When all strata have identical standard deviations
When costs per unit are equal and variances are negligible
When the population cannot be partitioned into homogeneous subgroups
tcat-stat-40.explainHtml: Neyman allocation determines stratum sample size n_h proportional to N_h × σ_h, minimizing sample variance for a fixed overall sample size.

tcat-stat-41.qHtml: Between two unbiased estimators θ̂₁ and θ̂₂ of parameter θ, why is θ̂₁ called "more efficient" than θ̂₂?
optionsHtml: θ̂₁ can be computed in fewer arithmetic steps
θ̂₁ is derived from a smaller sample size
tcat-stat-41.explainHtml: Statistical efficiency compares the sampling variances of unbiased estimators: the estimator with the smaller variance is more efficient.

tcat-stat-42.qHtml: What is the required sample size n to estimate a population mean within a margin of error E = 2 with 95% confidence (Z = 1.96), given population variance σ² = 64?

tcat-stat-43.qHtml: In statistical testing, what does the Null Hypothesis (H₀) typically state?
optionsHtml: There is no significant difference, effect, or relationship (status quo)
The proposed treatment causes a massive significant increase
The sample parameter is exactly equal to the alternative hypothesis
The probability of error is zero
tcat-stat-43.explainHtml: The null hypothesis (H0) posits no real effect, difference, or association, serving as the benchmark tested against evidence.

tcat-stat-44.qHtml: What error is committed when a true null hypothesis (H₀) is mistakenly rejected?
optionsHtml: Type I error (False Positive, probability α)
Type II error (False Negative, probability β)
tcat-stat-44.explainHtml: Rejecting H0 when H0 is actually true is a Type I error; its maximum probability is the level of significance α.

tcat-stat-45.qHtml: What is the statistical power of a hypothesis test defined as?
optionsHtml: 1 - β (Probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis)
tcat-stat-45.explainHtml: The power of a test is 1 - β, the probability of correctly rejecting H0 when H1 is true.

tcat-stat-46.qHtml: When testing a hypothesis about a single population mean with a small sample (n < 30) and unknown population variance σ², which test statistic is appropriate?
optionsHtml: Student's t-test with (n - 1) degrees of freedom
tcat-stat-46.explainHtml: When n < 30 and σ is unknown (estimated by sample SD s), the test statistic follows Student's t-distribution with df = n - 1.

tcat-stat-47.qHtml: What is the decision rule in hypothesis testing when using the p-value approach with significance level α?
tcat-stat-47.explainHtml: If the p-value is less than or equal to the significance level α, the observed result is statistically significant and H0 is rejected.

tcat-stat-48.qHtml: What error is committed when an investigator fails to reject a false null hypothesis (H₀)?
optionsHtml: Type II error (False Negative, probability β)
tcat-stat-48.explainHtml: A Type II error occurs when H0 is false, but the test fails to reject it. Its probability is denoted by β.

tcat-stat-49.qHtml: In a contingency table with r rows and c columns, what are the degrees of freedom for the Chi-Square (χ²) test of independence of attributes?
tcat-stat-49.explainHtml: For an r × c contingency table, degrees of freedom are (r - 1)(c - 1).

tcat-stat-50.qHtml: When is a two-tailed hypothesis test used instead of a one-tailed test?
optionsHtml: When the alternative hypothesis H₁ specifies an inequality (μ ≠ μ₀) in either direction
When the alternative hypothesis specifies strictly μ > μ₀
When the sample size is greater than 1000
When the population variance is strictly zero
tcat-stat-50.explainHtml: A two-tailed test is employed when H1 is non-directional (μ ≠ μ0), testing for significant deviations in either direction.

tcat-stat-51.qHtml: What is the formula for the Chi-Square test statistic used in testing goodness-of-fit or independence?
optionsHtml: χ² = ∑[(O - E) / E2]
χ² = ∑[(O2−E2) / E]
tcat-stat-51.explainHtml: The Chi-Square statistic sums squared differences between observed (O) and expected (E) frequencies divided by expected: χ² = ∑[(O - E)^{2} / E].

tcat-stat-52.qHtml: In a two-tailed Z-test with α = 0.05, the calculated test statistic is Z_calc = -2.35. What is the statistical conclusion?
optionsHtml: Reject H₀ because |-2.35| > 1.96 (the result falls in the critical rejection region)
Fail to reject H₀ because -2.35 is negative
The test is inconclusive without knowing degrees of freedom
tcat-stat-52.explainHtml: Critical values for two-tailed α = 0.05 are ±1.96. Since -2.35 < -1.96, the test statistic falls in the critical region, so H0 is rejected.

tcat-stat-53.qHtml: When testing for the equality of variances between two independent normally distributed populations (σ₁² = σ₂²), which test statistic is used?
optionsHtml: F-test (F = s₁² / s₂² where s₁² > s₂²)
Student's t-test with n₁ + n₂ - 2 degrees of freedom
tcat-stat-53.explainHtml: The F-test (variance ratio test) compares two sample variances: F = s₁² / s₂² with (n₁ - 1, n₂ - 1) degrees of freedom.

tcat-stat-54.qHtml: Under what experimental design is a Paired-Sample t-test mandatory rather than an independent two-sample t-test?
optionsHtml: When two sets of observations are matched, paired, or collected from the same subjects in a before-and-after repeated measures study
When the two samples have drastically different sample sizes
When both population variances are known and identical
When the data is measured on a nominal categorical scale
tcat-stat-54.explainHtml: A paired t-test analyzes differences d = x₁ - x₂ between matched pairs (e.g. before-and-after tests on the same subjects), removing subject variability.

tcat-stat-55.qHtml: In Chi-Square testing, what is the expected frequency formula for a cell in row i and column j of an r × c contingency table under H₀?
optionsHtml: E_ij = (Row i Total × Column j Total) / Grand Total (N)
E_ij = (Row i Total + Column j Total) / 2
E_ij = (Row i Total - Column j Total) / N
tcat-stat-55.explainHtml: Under independence, E_ij = P(Row i) × P(Col j) × N = (R_i / N) × (C_j / N) × N = (R_i × C_j) / N.

tcat-stat-56.qHtml: If the significance level α is decreased from 0.05 to 0.01 while keeping sample size n constant, what happens to the probability of Type II error (β) and the Power (1 - β)?
optionsHtml: Type II error β increases, and Power (1 - β) decreases
Type II error β decreases, and Power increases
Both Type I error and Type II error decrease simultaneously
tcat-stat-56.explainHtml: For fixed n, reducing α makes the rejection region smaller and more stringent, increasing the risk of Type II error (β) and decreasing power (1 - β).

tcat-stat-57.qHtml: What is the numerical range of Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient (r)?
tcat-stat-57.explainHtml: Pearson's correlation coefficient r is bounded strictly between -1.0 (perfect negative linear correlation) and +1.0 (perfect positive linear correlation).

tcat-stat-58.qHtml: What does a correlation coefficient r = 0 indicate regarding the relationship between two variables X and Y?
optionsHtml: No linear association between X and Y
That X and Y are identical variables
That both variables have zero variance
tcat-stat-58.explainHtml: An r value of zero signifies the absence of any linear relationship (though non-linear relationships could still exist).

tcat-stat-59.qHtml: In the simple linear regression equation Ŷ = a + bX, what does parameter 'b' represent?
optionsHtml: The slope (regression coefficient) indicating the expected change in Y for a one-unit change in X
The Y-intercept when X equals zero
The total sum of squared residuals
tcat-stat-59.explainHtml: In Ŷ = a + bX, b is the slope (regression coefficient of Y on X), measuring the rate of change of Ŷ per unit increase in X.

tcat-stat-60.qHtml: What graphical representation plots pairs of bivariate observations (X, Y) as individual points on a Cartesian plane?
tcat-stat-60.explainHtml: A scatter plot/diagram visually displays bivariate data points to inspect the direction and strength of association.

tcat-stat-61.qHtml: What is the sign of the correlation coefficient r if both regression coefficients b_yx and b_xy are negative?
optionsHtml: Negative (r is always negative when both slopes are negative)
tcat-stat-61.explainHtml: The correlation coefficient r has the exact same mathematical sign as both regression coefficients: if b_yx and b_xy are negative, r is negative.

tcat-stat-62.qHtml: What does the Coefficient of Determination (r2) quantify in regression analysis?
optionsHtml: The proportion of total variation in the dependent variable Y explained by the independent variable X
The slope of the orthogonal regression line
The ratio of the sample sizes
The probability that the true slope is zero
tcat-stat-62.explainHtml: r2 (coefficient of determination) measures the fraction of total variance in Y that is accounted for by the linear model with X.

tcat-stat-63.qHtml: What is the mathematical relationship between the correlation coefficient r and the two regression coefficients b_yx and b_xy?
optionsHtml: r = ±{b_yx × b_xy}
tcat-stat-63.explainHtml: The correlation coefficient is the geometric mean of the two regression slopes: r = ±{b_yx × b_xy}.

tcat-stat-64.qHtml: What criterion does the Method of Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) use to fit the best regression line?
optionsHtml: Minimizing the sum of squared vertical residuals: ∑(Y - Ŷ)²
Maximizing the sum of horizontal deviations
Setting the sum of absolute errors to infinity
Equating the mean of X to the variance of Y
tcat-stat-64.explainHtml: OLS determines intercept 'a' and slope 'b' such that the sum of squared errors ∑(Y_i - Ŷ_i)^{2} is minimized.

tcat-stat-65.qHtml: At what specific coordinate point do the two regression lines (Y on X and X on Y) always intersect?
optionsHtml: (s_x, s_y) — the point of standard deviations
tcat-stat-65.explainHtml: Both regression lines pass through the centroid of bivariate data: the point of means (X̄, Ȳ).

tcat-stat-66.qHtml: If the two regression coefficients are b_yx = 0.8 and b_xy = 0.45, what is the value of the correlation coefficient r?
tcat-stat-66.explainHtml: r = {b_yx × b_xy} = {0.8 × 0.45} = {0}.36 = +0.60.

tcat-stat-67.qHtml: If the correlation coefficient between X and Y is r = 0.8, what percentage of the variance in Y remains unexplained by variable X?
tcat-stat-67.explainHtml: Explained variation r2 = (0.8)^{2} = 0.64 (64%). Unexplained variation is 1 - r2 = 1 - 0.64 = 0.36 = 36%.

tcat-stat-68.qHtml: If the two regression lines are completely perpendicular to each other (angle θ = 90∘), what is the correlation coefficient r?
tcat-stat-68.explainHtml: tan θ = (1 - r2) / ∣r∣ × [s_x s_y / (s_x2 + s_y2)]. When lines are perpendicular (θ = 90∘), tan θ → ∞, which occurs when r = 0.

tcat-stat-69.qHtml: What is the formula for Spearman's Rank Correlation Coefficient (r_s) when there are no tied ranks across n paired observations?
optionsHtml: r_s = 1 - [6∑d2 / (n(n2 - 1))]
r_s = 1 + [6∑d2 / (n(n2 - 1))]
r_s = 1 - [∑d2/n3]
r_s = [6∑d2 / (n2 - 1)]
tcat-stat-69.explainHtml: Spearman's rank correlation formula without ties is r_s = 1 - [6∑d2 / (n(n2 - 1))], where d is the rank difference for each pair.

tcat-stat-70.qHtml: How is Pearson's correlation coefficient r affected by a change of origin and change of scale on the variables: U = (X - a)/c and V = (Y - b)/d, where c > 0 and d > 0?
optionsHtml: r is completely invariant to both changes of origin and positive changes of scale
tcat-stat-70.explainHtml: The correlation coefficient r is a pure dimensionless number, invariant to changes of origin and positive scale changes: r_uv = r_xy.

tcat-stat-71.qHtml: What weighting system does the Laspeyres Price Index use when calculating price changes across time?
optionsHtml: Average quantities of base and current years

tcat-stat-72.qHtml: What weighting system does the Paasche Price Index employ?

tcat-stat-73.qHtml: Fisher's "Ideal" Index Number is mathematically defined as:
optionsHtml: The Geometric Mean of the Laspeyres and Paasche index numbers (√[L × P])
The Arithmetic Mean of Laspeyres and Paasche index numbers
The Harmonic Mean of Laspeyres and Paasche index numbers
Laspeyres index multiplied by Paasche index
tcat-stat-73.explainHtml: Irving Fisher's Ideal Index is the geometric mean of Laspeyres (L) and Paasche (P): Fisher = {L × P}.

tcat-stat-74.qHtml: What are the four classical components that constitute an economic Time Series?
optionsHtml: Secular Trend (T), Seasonal Variations (S), Cyclical Fluctuations (C), and Irregular/Random Variations (I)
Base year, Current year, Index, and Deflator
tcat-stat-74.explainHtml: Classical time series decomposition identifies four components: Trend (T), Seasonal (S), Cyclical (C), and Irregular (I).

tcat-stat-75.qHtml: Which component of a time series represents regular, repeating periodic movements within a single annual cycle (e.g., umbrella sales in monsoon)?
tcat-stat-75.explainHtml: Seasonal variations are recurring intra-year patterns caused by weather seasons, holidays, and institutional calendars.

tcat-stat-76.qHtml: Why is Fisher's Index called an "Ideal" index number in economic statistics?
optionsHtml: It satisfies both the Time Reversal Test and the Factor Reversal Test
It uses zero weights and requires no quantity data
It is computationally simpler than simple aggregative indices
It eliminates the need for selecting a base year
tcat-stat-76.explainHtml: Fisher's formula satisfies both rigorous consistency tests: Time Reversal Test (P₀₁ × P₁₀ = 1) and Factor Reversal Test (P₀₁ × Q₀₁ = V₀₁).

tcat-stat-77.qHtml: In the multiplicative model of time series decomposition, how is the observed series Y_t expressed?
tcat-stat-77.explainHtml: The multiplicative model assumes components interact proportionally: Y = T × S × C × I, where S, C, and I are expressed as indices/ratios around 1.0.

tcat-stat-78.qHtml: Which method of trend estimation fits a mathematical trend line by minimizing the sum of squared deviations from observed data points?
tcat-stat-78.explainHtml: The Method of Least Squares fits an analytical trend equation (e.g. Y = a + bX) minimizing ∑(Y - Ŷ)².

tcat-stat-79.qHtml: What is a recognized disadvantage of using a 3-year or 5-year Moving Average to smooth out short-term fluctuations in a time series?
optionsHtml: Trend values cannot be calculated for the beginning and end periods (loss of data at both ends)
It introduces complex quadratic curvature into linear series
It requires equal weighting of all past centuries
tcat-stat-79.explainHtml: An m-period moving average cannot provide trend estimates for the first and last (m - 1)/2 periods, losing endpoint information.

tcat-stat-80.qHtml: If the Laspeyres Price Index is L = 144 and the Paasche Price Index is P = 100, what is Fisher's Ideal Price Index?
tcat-stat-80.explainHtml: Fisher's Index = {L × P} = {144 × 100} = {14400} = 120.

tcat-stat-81.qHtml: What mathematical condition is required for an index number formula to satisfy the Time Reversal Test (excluding the factor 100)?
tcat-stat-81.explainHtml: The time reversal test requires that reversing the time subscripts produces the reciprocal of the forward index: P₀₁ × P₁₀ = 1.

tcat-stat-82.qHtml: In the method of least squares for linear trend Y = a + bX with an odd number of years (e.g., N = 7), what simplification occurs when the origin X = 0 is placed at the middle year?
optionsHtml: ∑X = 0, so the normal equations simplify to a = ∑Y / N and b = ∑XY / ∑X^{2}
All squared residuals sum to zero
a equals the sample variance of Y
tcat-stat-82.explainHtml: Placing origin at the middle year makes ∑X = 0, simplifying the normal equations to direct formulas: a = ∑Y/N and b = ∑XY/∑X2.

tcat-stat-83.qHtml: What test of index numbers is satisfied when the product of the price index and the quantity index equals the true value ratio: P₀₁ × Q₀₁ = ∑(p₁q₁) / ∑(p₀q₀)?
tcat-stat-83.explainHtml: The Factor Reversal Test mandates that interchanging prices and quantities yields the true value ratio V₀₁ = ∑(p₁q₁) / ∑(p₀q₀).

tcat-stat-84.qHtml: How does Laspeyres Price Index typically behave relative to the true cost-of-living index during periods of inflation?
optionsHtml: It overstates (upward bias) price increases because it assumes consumers maintain a fixed base-period basket without substituting cheaper goods
It understates inflation because it uses current-period quantities
It equals the true geometric cost of living index exactly
It exhibits zero substitution bias under all economic conditions
tcat-stat-84.explainHtml: Laspeyres has an upward substitution bias: by holding base quantities fixed, it fails to account for consumer substitution toward relatively cheaper items.

tcat-stat-85.qHtml: Which measure of central tendency is the most suitable average for computing the average rate of speed over equal distances or price per unit?
tcat-stat-85.explainHtml: Harmonic Mean is the reciprocal of the arithmetic mean of the reciprocals and is mathematically appropriate for rates and ratios involving equal distance/work.

tcat-stat-86.qHtml: For the dataset {4, 7, 7, 9, 10, 12, 14}, what is the median value?
tcat-stat-86.explainHtml: There are n = 7 ordered observations. The median is the (7 + 1)/2 = 4th observation, which is 9.

tcat-stat-87.qHtml: What is the sum of the deviations of a set of observations taken from their arithmetic mean, Σ(X - X̄)?
tcat-stat-87.explainHtml: By the algebraic property of the arithmetic mean, the algebraic sum of deviations from the mean is always exactly zero: Σ(X - X̄) = 0.

tcat-stat-88.qHtml: Which measure of dispersion is expressed as a pure, unitless percentage to compare the relative variability of two distributions with different units?
tcat-stat-88.explainHtml: Coefficient of Variation is C.V. = (s / X̄) * 100%, expressing dispersion as a dimensionless relative percentage.

tcat-stat-89.qHtml: In a frequency distribution, if the mean is 45 and the mode is 42, what is the empirical estimate of the median?
tcat-stat-89.explainHtml: By Pearson's empirical relationship: Mode = 3·Median - 2·Mean. Thus: 42 = 3·Median - 2(45) \implies 42 = 3·Median - 90 \implies 3·Median = 132 \implies Median = 44.

tcat-stat-90.qHtml: If each observation in a dataset is multiplied by a constant c = 3, what happens to the variance of the transformed dataset?
optionsHtml: The variance is multiplied by 9 (32)
tcat-stat-90.explainHtml: By the properties of variance: Var(cX) = c2 · Var(X). When multiplied by 3, the new variance is 32 = 9 times the original variance.

tcat-stat-91.qHtml: In a unimodal frequency curve skewed to the r (positively skewed), what is the correct relative ordering of the Mean, Median, and Mode?
tcat-stat-91.explainHtml: In a positively skewed distribution, the long r tail pulls the mean to the highest value, so Mode < Median < Mean.

tcat-stat-92.qHtml: What is the value of the second moment about the mean, μ2?
tcat-stat-92.explainHtml: The second central moment is μ2 = Σ(X - X̄)^2 / N, which by definition is the population variance.

tcat-stat-93.qHtml: A distribution with moment coefficient of kurtosis β2 = 3 (or excess kurtosis γ2 = 0) is classified as:
tcat-stat-93.explainHtml: A distribution with β2 = 3 (identical to the normal distribution kurtosis) is called mesokurtic. Values > 3 are leptokurtic; < 3 are platykurtic.

tcat-stat-94.qHtml: Given first quartile Q1 = 30 and third quartile Q3 = 70, what is the Semi-Interquartile Range (Quartile Deviation)?
tcat-stat-94.explainHtml: The Quartile Deviation is Q.D. = (Q3 - Q1) / 2 = (70 - 30) / 2 = 20.

tcat-stat-95.qHtml: According to Chebyshev's Inequality, what is the minimum proportion of any distribution's observations that must fall within k = 2 standard deviations of the mean?
tcat-stat-95.explainHtml: Chebyshev's theorem states P(|X - μ| < kσ) ≥ 1 - 1/k2. For k = 2: 1 - 1/4 = 3/4 = 75% for any arbitrary distribution.

tcat-stat-96.qHtml: Under Bowley's coefficient of skewness Sk_B = (Q3 + Q1 - 2·Q2) / (Q3 - Q1), if Q1 = 20, Q2 = 35, and Q3 = 60, what is the coefficient of skewness?

tcat-stat-97.qHtml: When calculating moments from grouped frequency distributions, what do Sheppard's corrections adjust for?
optionsHtml: Missing data values in the tails
Grouping error caused by assuming observations are concentrated at the class midpoints
tcat-stat-97.explainHtml: Sheppard's corrections adjust the central moments for the grouping error arising from the assumption that frequencies are concentrated at the class midpoints.

tcat-stat-98.qHtml: If the relationship between two variables is given by Y = 10 - 2X, and the variance of X is 4, what is the standard deviation of Y?
tcat-stat-98.explainHtml: Var(Y) = Var(10 - 2X) = (−2)2 · Var(X) = 4 · 4 = 16. Standard deviation is SD(Y) = 16​ = 4 (dispersion is always non-negative).

tcat-stat-99.qHtml: Two unbiased six-sided dice are rolled simultaneously. What is the probability that the sum of the numbers showing is 7?
tcat-stat-99.explainHtml: Out of 36 equally likely outcomes, the pairs summing to 7 are (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1) — exactly 6 outcomes. P = 6/36 = 1/6.

tcat-stat-100.qHtml: If events A and B are mutually exclusive, what is P(A ∩ B)?
tcat-stat-100.explainHtml: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur simultaneously, so their intersection is the null event: P(A ∩ B) = 0.

tcat-stat-101.qHtml: In a single throw of a fair coin 4 times, what is the probability of obtaining exactly 2 heads?
tcat-stat-101.explainHtml: By binomial formula: P(X=2) = (24​) · (1/2)2 · (1/2)2 = 6 · 1/16 = 6/16 = 3/8.

tcat-stat-102.qHtml: What is the sum of all probabilities in a discrete probability distribution, Σ P(X = x)?
tcat-stat-102.explainHtml: The total probability across an exhaustive and mutually exclusive sample space is always exactly 1.

tcat-stat-103.qHtml: What are the mean (μ) and variance (σ^2) of the standard normal distribution Z?
tcat-stat-103.explainHtml: The standard normal distribution is specifically normalized so that its mean μ = 0 and variance σ^2 = 1.

tcat-stat-104.qHtml: Given P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5, and P(A ∩ B) = 0.3. What is the conditional probability P(A | B)?
tcat-stat-104.explainHtml: By definition of conditional probability: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B) = 0.3 / 0.5 = 0.6. (Since P(A|B) = P(A), A and B are also independent).

tcat-stat-105.qHtml: For a Binomial distribution with n = 100 trials and probability of success p = 0.2, what are its mean and variance?

tcat-stat-106.qHtml: Under what conditions does the Binomial distribution converge asymptotically to the Poisson distribution?
optionsHtml: n is small and p is very large (close to 1)
n is very large (n → ∞) and p is very small (p → 0) such that λ = np remains constant
Variance is greater than the mean
tcat-stat-106.explainHtml: The Poisson distribution is the law of rare events, derived as n → ∞ and p → 0 with constant mean λ = np.

tcat-stat-107.qHtml: For a continuous random variable X with probability density function f(x) over [a, b], what does the integral ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx equal?
tcat-stat-107.explainHtml: The total area under the entire probability density curve equals 1.

tcat-stat-108.qHtml: In a normal distribution N(μ, σ^2), what percentage of total observations approximately lies in the interval (μ - 2σ, μ + 2σ)?
tcat-stat-108.explainHtml: By the empirical rule of the normal curve: ~68.27% lies within ±1σ, ~95.45% lies within ±2σ, and ~99.73% lies within ±3σ.

tcat-stat-109.qHtml: In a Poisson distribution with parameter λ, if P(X = 1) = P(X = 2), what is the numerical value of the parameter λ?

tcat-stat-110.qHtml: A continuous random variable X follows a Uniform distribution U(a, b) on the interval [2, 8]. What is the variance of X?
tcat-stat-110.explainHtml: The variance of a continuous uniform distribution U(a, b) is Var(X) = (b−a)2 / 12. For [2, 8]: (8−2)2 / 12 = 36 / 12 = 3.

tcat-stat-111.qHtml: If a random variable follows an Exponential distribution with rate parameter λ = 0.5, what is its expected value E(X)?
tcat-stat-111.explainHtml: For an exponential distribution with parameter λ, the expected value is E(X) = 1 / λ = 1 / 0.5 = 2.0.

tcat-stat-112.qHtml: Which theoretical probability distribution is appropriate when sampling without replacement from a finite population of size N containing M successes?
tcat-stat-112.explainHtml: The Hypergeometric distribution models successes in draws from a finite population without replacement, where trials are dependent.

tcat-stat-113.qHtml: Let X be a continuous random variable with cumulative distribution function F(x). What is P(a < X ≤ b)?
tcat-stat-113.explainHtml: By the fundamental property of CDF: P(a < X ≤ b) = F(b) - F(a).

tcat-stat-114.qHtml: What is a numerical characteristic computed from an entire population called (as opposed to a statistic computed from a sample)?
tcat-stat-114.explainHtml: A parameter is a descriptive index of an entire population (e.g., μ, σ), while a statistic is computed from sample data (e.g., X̄, s).

tcat-stat-115.qHtml: What is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a statistic known as?
tcat-stat-115.explainHtml: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of an estimator (such as the sample mean) is called its Standard Error.

tcat-stat-116.qHtml: Which probability sampling technique involves dividing a heterogeneous population into non-overlapping homogeneous sub-groups (strata) and taking a random sample from each?
tcat-stat-116.explainHtml: Stratified sampling ensures representation by partitioning a population into homogeneous strata and sampling proportionally within each stratum.

tcat-stat-117.qHtml: If a population has standard deviation σ = 20 and a simple random sample of size n = 100 is drawn with replacement, what is the standard error of the sample mean X̄?
tcat-stat-117.explainHtml: Standard Error = σ / n​ = 20 / 100​ = 20 / 10 = 2.

tcat-stat-118.qHtml: What does the Central Limit Theorem state regarding the distribution of the sample mean X̄ as the sample size n becomes large (typically n ≥ 30)?
optionsHtml: The sample mean becomes exactly equal to the population variance
The sampling distribution of X̄ approaches a Normal distribution regardless of the underlying population shape
The sample standard deviation approaches zero
The population distribution converts into a uniform distribution
tcat-stat-118.explainHtml: The Central Limit Theorem guarantees that the sampling distribution of X̄ approaches normality as n increases, even if the parent population is non-normal.

tcat-stat-119.qHtml: An estimator T is defined as an "unbiased estimator" of a population parameter θ if:
tcat-stat-119.explainHtml: An estimator T is unbiased if its mathematical expected value equals the true population parameter: E(T) = θ.

tcat-stat-120.qHtml: Why is the sample variance calculated using divisor (n - 1) instead of n, i.e., s2 = Σ(X - X̄)^2 / (n - 1)?
optionsHtml: To make s2 an unbiased estimator of the population variance σ^2
Because one observation is always corrupted by measurement error
To account for the finite population correction factor
To make the calculation easier without a calculator
tcat-stat-120.explainHtml: Dividing by (n - 1) corrects for Bessel's correction; dividing by n produces a negatively biased estimate of σ^2.

tcat-stat-121.qHtml: In sampling without replacement from a finite population of size N, what is the Finite Population Correction (FPC) factor multiplied into the variance of X̄?
tcat-stat-121.explainHtml: For finite populations sampled without replacement, the variance of X̄ is adjusted by the FPC factor: (N - n) / (N - 1).

tcat-stat-122.qHtml: What is the critical Z-value for a two-sided 95% confidence interval for a population mean?
tcat-stat-122.explainHtml: For a two-tailed standard normal interval with α = 0.05, the critical value Z_(0.025) is 1.96.

tcat-stat-123.qHtml: When estimating a population mean from a normally distributed population with unknown variance using a small sample (n < 30), which sampling distribution must be used?
optionsHtml: Student's t-distribution with (n - 1) degrees of freedom
tcat-stat-123.explainHtml: When σ is unknown and n < 30, the statistic follows Student's t-distribution with df = n - 1.

tcat-stat-124.qHtml: An estimator T is termed "consistent" if, as the sample size n approaches infinity:
optionsHtml: The bias of T increases exponentially
T converges in probability to the true parameter θ (Var(T) → 0 and Bias → 0)
T is always normally distributed with variance 1
T equals the median of the sample
tcat-stat-124.explainHtml: Consistency means that as n → ∞, the estimator converges in probability to the true parameter θ, which occurs if its variance and bias both approach zero.

tcat-stat-125.qHtml: Between two unbiased estimators T1 and T2 of a parameter θ, T1 is said to be "more efficient" than T2 if:
optionsHtml: T1 is based on a smaller sample size
tcat-stat-125.explainHtml: Efficiency compares the dispersion of unbiased estimators; the one with the smaller sampling variance is more efficient.

tcat-stat-126.qHtml: To reduce the margin of error (width of a confidence interval) of a sample mean by half (factor of 1/2) while maintaining the same confidence level, by what factor must the sample size n be increased?
tcat-stat-126.explainHtml: Margin of error E = Z · σ / n​. Halving E requires doubling n​, which means n must be multiplied by 22 = 4.

tcat-stat-127.qHtml: In Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE), how is the maximum likelihood estimator θ̂ determined from the likelihood function L(θ)?
optionsHtml: By finding the value of θ that minimizes the sum of squared residuals
By solving d[ln L(θ)] / dθ = 0 for θ
By calculating the sample median of the likelihood ratios
By setting L(θ) equal to zero
tcat-stat-127.explainHtml: The MLE maximizes the log-likelihood function by setting its first derivative with respect to θ equal to 0 (score equation) and verifying a negative second derivative.

tcat-stat-128.qHtml: What is the primary hypothesis of "no effect", "no difference", or "status quo" denoted in statistical inference?
tcat-stat-128.explainHtml: The Null Hypothesis (H0) represents the default assertion of no difference or no treatment effect.

tcat-stat-129.qHtml: What is a Type I error in statistical hypothesis testing?
optionsHtml: Rejecting H0 when H0 is actually true
Failing to reject H0 when H0 is actually false
Accepting H1 when H1 is true
tcat-stat-129.explainHtml: A Type I error occurs when a true null hypothesis is erroneously rejected (false positive), with probability α.

tcat-stat-130.qHtml: The probability of committing a Type I error is denoted by which Greek letter, which also represents the level of significance?
tcat-stat-130.explainHtml: The level of significance α is the predetermined maximum threshold probability of committing a Type I error.

tcat-stat-131.qHtml: If the p-value computed from a test statistic is 0.015 and the significance level is set at α = 0.05, what is the statistical decision?
optionsHtml: Reject the null hypothesis H0 (statistically significant)
Fail to reject the null hypothesis H0
Accept the null hypothesis as definitively proven
Discard the sample data and retest
tcat-stat-131.explainHtml: When p-value ≤ α (0.015 < 0.05), we reject the null hypothesis in favor of the alternative hypothesis.

tcat-stat-132.qHtml: Which statistical test is standardly used to test whether two qualitative attributes are independent in a contingency table?
tcat-stat-132.explainHtml: The Chi-Square test of independence assesses whether two categorical variables are independent in a contingency table.

tcat-stat-133.qHtml: What does the "Power of a Test" represent in statistical inference?
optionsHtml: The probability of committing a Type I error (α)
The probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis (1 - β)
The probability of failing to reject a true null hypothesis (1 - α)
The ratio of sample size to population size
tcat-stat-133.explainHtml: Power of a test is 1 - β, the probability of rejecting H0 when H0 is false (correct detection of a true effect).

tcat-stat-134.qHtml: In testing H0: μ = 50 against H1: μ > 50 at α = 0.05 with known population variance, which type of test is conducted?
tcat-stat-134.explainHtml: Because the alternative hypothesis specifies μ > 50, the rejection region lies exclusively in the upper (r) tail.

tcat-stat-135.qHtml: What is the formula for the degrees of freedom in a Chi-Square test of independence for an r × c contingency table (r rows, c columns)?
tcat-stat-135.explainHtml: The degrees of freedom for an r × c contingency table is df = (r - 1)(c - 1).

tcat-stat-136.qHtml: When conducting a two-sample pooled t-test for comparing two independent population means with sample sizes n1 and n2, what are the total degrees of freedom?
tcat-stat-136.explainHtml: Estimating two sample means consumes 2 degrees of freedom, leaving df = n1 + n2 - 2 for the pooled variance.

tcat-stat-137.qHtml: Which statistical test is designed to test the equality of two population variances, H0: σ12 = σ22?
tcat-stat-137.explainHtml: The F-test evaluates the ratio of two sample variances F = s12/s22 to test whether their population variances are equal.

tcat-stat-138.qHtml: In a one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) with k groups and N total observations, what is the F-statistic ratio?
optionsHtml: Within-group Mean Square / Between-group Mean Square
Between-group Mean Square / Within-group Mean Square (Error)
Total Sum of Squares / Error Sum of Squares
tcat-stat-138.explainHtml: The ANOVA test statistic is F = MS_between / MS_within (treatment variance divided by residual error variance).

tcat-stat-139.qHtml: What is the consequence of testing multiple independent hypotheses simultaneously at α = 0.05 without a family-wise error rate correction (like Bonferroni)?
optionsHtml: The overall probability of at least one false positive (Type I error) increases substantially above 0.05
The statistical power of each individual test drops to zero
The degrees of freedom become negative
Type II errors are completely eliminated
tcat-stat-139.explainHtml: Running m independent tests increases the family-wise error rate to 1 - (1 - α)^m, making false positive discoveries highly probable.

tcat-stat-140.qHtml: When is a Paired t-test used instead of an independent two-sample t-test?
optionsHtml: When the two samples have unequal variances and large sample sizes
When observations in the two groups are naturally paired or matched (such as pre-test and post-test on the same subjects)
When the data is measured on a nominal classification scale
When testing more than three experimental treatment groups
tcat-stat-140.explainHtml: The paired t-test analyzes differences (d = X1 - X2) for matched-pair or before-and-after repeated measures on the same subjects.

tcat-stat-141.qHtml: What is the Neyman-Pearson Lemma primarily used for in the theoretical foundation of hypothesis testing?
optionsHtml: Constructing the Most Powerful (MP) test for simple null against simple alternative hypotheses based on likelihood ratio
Proving the Central Limit Theorem for non-independent variables
tcat-stat-141.explainHtml: The Neyman-Pearson lemma proves that the likelihood ratio test produces the most powerful test of a given size α for simple hypotheses.

tcat-stat-142.qHtml: In a Chi-square goodness-of-fit test with k categories and m parameters estimated from the sample data, what are the degrees of freedom?
tcat-stat-142.explainHtml: Each parameter estimated from the sample consumes 1 degree of freedom, resulting in df = k - 1 - m.

tcat-stat-143.qHtml: If the coefficient of determination between two variables is r2 = 0.64, what is the coefficient of non-determination (proportion of unexplained variation)?
tcat-stat-143.explainHtml: The coefficient of non-determination is k2 = 1 - r2 = 1 - 0.64 = 0.36, representing the proportion of total variation in Y left unexplained by the regression.

tcat-stat-144.qHtml: If the correlation coefficient between X and Y is r = 0, what does this specifically imply regarding their relationship?
optionsHtml: There is no linear association between X and Y
There is no relationship of any kind (linear or non-linear) between X and Y
X and Y are identical variables
X causes Y to be zero
tcat-stat-144.explainHtml: r = 0 indicates absence of linear correlation; a strong non-linear (e.g., quadratic) relationship could still exist.

tcat-stat-145.qHtml: In the simple linear regression model Y = a + bX, what does the parameter "b" represent?
optionsHtml: The slope of the regression line (change in Y per unit increase in X)
The standard error of the estimate
tcat-stat-145.explainHtml: The regression coefficient b is the slope, indicating the expected change in the dependent variable Y for every one-unit increase in X.

tcat-stat-146.qHtml: Through which point do both regression lines (Y on X and X on Y) always intersect?
optionsHtml: (X̄, Ȳ) [the means of X and Y]
tcat-stat-146.explainHtml: Both regression lines pass through the centroid of the data: the point of means (X̄, Ȳ).

tcat-stat-147.qHtml: If the correlation coefficient r = 0.8, what is the coefficient of determination (r2)?
tcat-stat-147.explainHtml: Coefficient of determination is r2 = (0.8)^2 = 0.64 (indicating 64% of variation in Y is explained by X).

tcat-stat-148.qHtml: In simple linear regression of Y on X with sample size n, what are the degrees of freedom associated with the residual variance (sum of squared errors)?
tcat-stat-148.explainHtml: Estimating two parameters (intercept a and slope b) consumes 2 degrees of freedom from the sample, leaving df = n - 2 for the residual sum of squares.

tcat-stat-149.qHtml: Given the two regression coefficients b_yx = 0.8 and b_xy = 0.45, what is the correlation coefficient r?
tcat-stat-149.explainHtml: r = ± by​x⋅bx​y​. Since both coefficients are positive: r = +0.8⋅0.45​ = +0.36​ = +0.60.

tcat-stat-150.qHtml: What is the sum of the residuals Σ(Y - Ŷ) in an ordinary least squares (OLS) linear regression model with an intercept?
tcat-stat-150.explainHtml: A fundamental mathematical property of OLS regression with an intercept term is that the sum of the residuals is identically zero: Σ e_i = 0.

tcat-stat-151.qHtml: What is the formula for Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (r_s) when there are no tied ranks?
optionsHtml: 1 - [6 Σ d2 / (n(n2 - 1))]
6 Σ d2 / (n(n - 1))
1 + [6 Σ d2 / (n(n2 - 1))]
tcat-stat-151.explainHtml: Spearman's rank correlation formula is r_s = 1 - [6 Σ d_i^2 / (n(n2 - 1))], where d_i is the difference between ranks.

tcat-stat-152.qHtml: If the two regression lines are perpendicular (at an angle of 90∘), what is the correlation between the two variables?
tcat-stat-152.explainHtml: When r = 0, the regression lines are parallel to the coordinate axes and perpendicular to each other. When r = ±1, they coincide.

tcat-stat-153.qHtml: Why can the two regression coefficients b_yx and b_xy NEVER have opposite signs?
optionsHtml: Because b_yx · b_xy = r2, which must be non-negative, and both share the sign of the covariance Cov(X, Y)
Because least squares requires positive intercepts
Because the sample variance of X must equal the sample variance of Y
Because the angle between regression lines cannot exceed 45 degrees
tcat-stat-153.explainHtml: Both b_yx = Cov(X,Y)/Var(X) and b_xy = Cov(X,Y)/Var(Y) have variances (which are positive) in the denominator; hence both take the exact sign of Cov(X,Y).

tcat-stat-154.qHtml: In multiple regression, what phenomenon occurs when two or more predictor variables are highly correlated with each other, inflating the variance of regression coefficients?
tcat-stat-154.explainHtml: Multicollinearity occurs when independent variables share strong linear relationships, leading to unstable coefficient estimates and high standard errors.

tcat-stat-155.qHtml: What does the statistical assumption of "Homoscedasticity" require in a linear regression model?
optionsHtml: The independent variables are normally distributed
The variance of the error terms (residuals) is constant across all values of the independent variable
The error terms are mutually correlated over time
The regression line passes through the origin (0, 0)
tcat-stat-155.explainHtml: Homoscedasticity means constant error variance: Var(ε_i | X) = σ^2 for all i. Heteroscedasticity refers to non-constant error variance.

tcat-stat-156.qHtml: If the arithmetic mean of the two regression coefficients is greater than or equal to the correlation coefficient, i.e., (b_yx + b_xy) / 2 ≥ r, this property is known as:
optionsHtml: The fundamental inequality of regression coefficients
The Cauchy-Schwarz theorem applied to residuals
tcat-stat-156.explainHtml: Since (by​x​−bx​y​)^2 ≥ 0 \implies b_yx + b_xy ≥ 2 by​x⋅bx​y​ = 2r \implies (b_yx + b_xy) / 2 ≥ r.

tcat-stat-157.qHtml: What is an index number that measures the relative change in price of a single commodity over time called?
tcat-stat-157.explainHtml: A price relative is the ratio of the price of a single commodity in the current year to its price in the base year: (P1 / P0) * 100.

tcat-stat-158.qHtml: Which price index formula uses base-period quantities (q0) as weights?
tcat-stat-158.explainHtml: Laspeyres price index uses base-year quantities: P_01^L = [Σ(p1 · q0) / Σ(p0 · q0)] * 100.

tcat-stat-159.qHtml: Which price index formula uses current-period quantities (q1) as weights?
tcat-stat-159.explainHtml: Paasche price index weights by current-year quantities: P_01^P = [Σ(p1 · q1) / Σ(p0 · q1)] * 100.

tcat-stat-160.qHtml: In time series analysis, which component reflects regular, repeating fluctuations occurring within a period of one year or less (such as holiday shopping spikes)?
tcat-stat-160.explainHtml: Seasonal variation refers to rhythmic patterns that repeat within a calendar year due to seasons, climate, or cultural holidays.

tcat-stat-161.qHtml: What is the standard multiplicative model equation for decomposing a time series Y into its four components?
tcat-stat-161.explainHtml: The multiplicative time series decomposition model expresses the observed value as the product of Trend, Seasonal, Cyclical, and Irregular components: Y = T · S · C · I.

tcat-stat-162.qHtml: Why is Fisher's Ideal Index designated as "ideal"?
optionsHtml: It is the arithmetic mean of Laspeyres and Paasche indices
It is the geometric mean of Laspeyres and Paasche indices and satisfies both the Time Reversal Test and Factor Reversal Test
It requires no quantity data to calculate
It is always exactly equal to 100
tcat-stat-162.explainHtml: Fisher's index P_01^F = P0​1L⋅P0​1P​ satisfies both the Time Reversal Test and Factor Reversal Test, free from single-period weighting bias.

tcat-stat-163.qHtml: What mathematical condition defines the Time Reversal Test for an index number P_01?
tcat-stat-163.explainHtml: The Time Reversal Test requires that reversing the time subscripts yields the reciprocal: P_01 · P_10 = 1.

tcat-stat-164.qHtml: What mathematical condition defines the Factor Reversal Test for price and quantity index numbers?
tcat-stat-164.explainHtml: The Factor Reversal Test requires the product of the price index and quantity index to equal the true value ratio: P_01 · Q_01 = Σ(p1 q1) / Σ(p0 q0).

tcat-stat-165.qHtml: In trend estimation using the Method of Moving Averages, what is the primary effect of taking a k-period moving average?
optionsHtml: It smooths out short-term fluctuations and seasonal variations to reveal the underlying long-term trend
It eliminates the need for historical baseline data
It fits a parabolic second-degree polynomial exactly
tcat-stat-165.explainHtml: Moving averages smooth out periodic, seasonal, and random irregular fluctuations to isolate the secular trend.

tcat-stat-166.qHtml: Which test of adequacy is satisfied by simple aggregates of prices and the Kelly's fixed-we index, but failed by Fisher's index?
tcat-stat-166.explainHtml: The Circular Test (P_01 · P_12 · P_20 = 1) is an extension of the time reversal test satisfied by Kelly's and simple aggregate methods, but NOT by Fisher's ideal index.

tcat-stat-167.qHtml: When fitting a linear trend line Y = a + bX by the method of least squares to an odd number of years (n = 2m + 1), how does setting the origin X = 0 at the middle year simplify the normal equations?
optionsHtml: Σ X = 0, reducing the equations to a = (Σ Y) / n and b = (Σ XY) / (Σ X2)
Σ Y becomes 0, eliminating the intercept parameter a
Σ X2 becomes 1, simplifying the denominator
The residuals become exactly zero for all data points
tcat-stat-167.explainHtml: Centering X at the middle year ensures Σ X = 0, which decouples the normal equations directly into a = ΣY / n and b = ΣXY / ΣX2.

tcat-stat-168.qHtml: Which component of a time series is associated with multi-year economic cycles of prosperity, recession, depression, and recovery?
tcat-stat-168.explainHtml: Cyclical fluctuations represent oscillatory business cycle movements recurring over periods longer than one year (typically 3 to 10 years).

tcat-stat-169.qHtml: Why does Laspeyres' price index tend to have an inherent upward bias (overstating inflation)?
optionsHtml: It uses current-year quantities that reflect consumer substitution away from items whose prices rose
It uses base-year quantities and fails to account for consumer substitution toward cheaper alternatives as relative prices change
It divides by zero when prices drop
It squares price ratios before averaging
tcat-stat-169.explainHtml: Because it fixes base-period quantities, Laspeyres ignores consumer substitution toward cheaper substitute goods, systematically overestimating the cost-of-living increase.

tcat-stat-170.qHtml: In time series analysis, what does "deseasonalizing" the data accomplish in a multiplicative model?
optionsHtml: Dividing the observed series Y by the seasonal index S to yield T · C · I
Subtracting the trend component T from the observed data Y
Multiplying Y by the cyclical component C
Setting all quarterly seasonal indices equal to 0
tcat-stat-170.explainHtml: Deseasonalizing (seasonally adjusting) in a multiplicative model divides the original data by the seasonal index: Y / S = (T · S · C · I) / S = T · C · I.

tcat-stat-171.qHtml: In statistical classification, the temperature measured on the Celsius scale is an example of which scale of measurement?
tcat-stat-171.explainHtml: Celsius temperature is measured on an interval scale because it has equal distances between points, but no absolute zero (0°C does not mean the complete absence of heat).

tcat-stat-172.qHtml: What graphical representation uses adjacent rectangular bars whose areas are proportional to the frequencies of continuous class intervals?
tcat-stat-172.explainHtml: A histogram represents continuous frequency distributions using adjacent rectangular columns where column area represents class frequency.

tcat-stat-173.qHtml: In a cumulative frequency polygon, the curve obtained by plotting cumulative frequencies against class upper boundaries is known as an:
tcat-stat-173.explainHtml: An ogive (cumulative frequency curve) is constructed by plotting cumulative frequencies against the upper (or lower) class boundaries of a grouped frequency distribution.

tcat-stat-174.qHtml: Data collected by an investigator directly from original primary sources through surveys or laboratory experiments is defined as:
tcat-stat-174.explainHtml: Primary data is first-hand information collected directly by the researcher for a specific study, unlike secondary data which is retrieved from published records.

tcat-stat-175.qHtml: In constructing a pie chart, what central angle represents a component that accounts for 25% of the total aggregate value?
tcat-stat-175.explainHtml: The total central angle in a circle is 360∘. A 25% component subtends an angle of 0.25 * 360∘=90∘.

tcat-stat-176.qHtml: According to Sturges' Rule, how many class intervals k should be constructed for a sample size of N = 64 observations?

tcat-stat-177.qHtml: When class limits for continuous data are given as 10-19, 20-29, and 30-39, what are the exact class boundaries for the 20-29 interval?
tcat-stat-177.explainHtml: To convert inclusive class limits into true continuous class boundaries, subtract 0.5 from the lower limit (20 - 0.5 = 19.5) and add 0.5 to the upper limit (29 + 0.5 = 29.5).

tcat-stat-178.qHtml: In a Lorenz Curve used to analyze income distribution, what does the 45-degree diagonal line represent?
tcat-stat-178.explainHtml: The 45-degree diagonal represents the line of perfect equality, where every cumulative percentage of the population possesses the exact same cumulative percentage of wealth.

tcat-stat-179.qHtml: Which statistical graph represents time-series data plotted against chronological time intervals?
tcat-stat-179.explainHtml: A historigram (chronological line chart) plots observations on the vertical axis against regular intervals of time on the horizontal axis.

tcat-stat-180.qHtml: What is the relative frequency of a class interval with frequency f = 35 in a total sample of N = 140 observations?

tcat-stat-181.qHtml: In a grouped frequency distribution with unequal class widths w_i, how must the heights of the histogram bars be adjusted to maintain correct frequency representation?
optionsHtml: He must equal frequency density (frequency divided by class width: f_i / w_i)
He must be multiplied by class midpoint
He must equal cumulative frequency up to that class
tcat-stat-181.explainHtml: Because bar area in a histogram represents frequency (Area = width * he), when class widths vary, the he must be set to frequency density: h_i = f_i / w_i.

tcat-stat-182.qHtml: In the construction of a stem-and-leaf display for the dataset {102, 107, 115, 118, 124}, what are the leaves for stem 11?
tcat-stat-182.explainHtml: With stem representing the leading digits "11" (tens/hundreds place), the trailing units digits for 115 and 118 are 5 and 8.

tcat-stat-183.qHtml: What geometric property is true of the point of intersection between a "less than" ogive and a "more than" ogive?
optionsHtml: Its x-coordinate corresponds exactly to the Median of the distribution
Its x-coordinate corresponds to the Arithmetic Mean
Its y-coordinate equals the total frequency N
Its x-coordinate corresponds to the Mode
tcat-stat-183.explainHtml: The intersection point between the "less than" ogive and "more than" ogive corresponds to cumulative frequency N/2, whose x-axis projection is the Median.

tcat-stat-184.qHtml: When tabular data is categorized simultaneously according to two qualitative attributes in a two-way classification grid, the resulting table is formally termed a:
tcat-stat-184.explainHtml: A contingency table (cross-tabulation matrix) presents joint frequency distributions for two categorical or qualitative variables cross-classified into rows and columns.

tcat-stat-185.qHtml: Calculate the arithmetic mean of the dataset: 8, 12, 15, 20, 25:

tcat-stat-186.qHtml: What is the median of the ordered array: 4, 7, 9, 13, 18, 22, 29?
tcat-stat-186.explainHtml: For n = 7 (odd), the median is the (7 + 1)/2 = 4th observation, which is 13.

tcat-stat-187.qHtml: What is the mode of the dataset: 3, 5, 7, 5, 9, 5, 11, 7, 12?
tcat-stat-187.explainHtml: The value 5 occurs with the highest frequency (3 times), making 5 the unimodal value of the dataset.

tcat-stat-188.qHtml: The algebraic sum of deviations of a set of n observations from their arithmetic mean is always equal to:
tcat-stat-188.explainHtml: A fundamental mathematical property of the arithmetic mean is that sum(x_i - mean) = sum(x_i) - n * mean = n * mean - n * mean = 0.

tcat-stat-189.qHtml: Which measure of central tendency is uniquely suited for computing average rates of speed or unit ratios?
tcat-stat-189.explainHtml: The Harmonic Mean is the reciprocal of the arithmetic mean of reciprocals, making it mathematically ideal for averaging rates, speeds, and price-per-unit ratios.

tcat-stat-190.qHtml: Calculate the Geometric Mean of the three positive numbers: 2, 8, and 32:

tcat-stat-191.qHtml: In a moderately skewed unimodal frequency distribution with Mean = 45 and Median = 42, what is the empirical estimate of the Mode?
tcat-stat-191.explainHtml: By Pearson's empirical relationship: Mode ≈ 3 * Median - 2 * Mean = 3(42) - 2(45) = 126 - 90 = 36.

tcat-stat-192.qHtml: For two positive non-identical numbers a and b, what is the strict mathematical ordering among their AM, GM, and HM?
tcat-stat-192.explainHtml: For any set of positive unequal real numbers, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality dictates that AM > GM > HM. (They are equal only if all values are identical).

tcat-stat-193.qHtml: A sample of 20 male students has a mean test score of 70, and a sample of 30 female students has a mean score of 80. What is the combined pooled arithmetic mean?

tcat-stat-194.qHtml: If each observation in a dataset x_i is transformed linearly by y_i = 3 * x_i - 7, and the original mean was 15, what is the new mean of y?
tcat-stat-194.explainHtml: The arithmetic mean satisfies linear change of scale and origin: Mean(y) = 3 * Mean(x) - 7 = 3(15) - 7 = 45 - 7 = 38.

tcat-stat-195.qHtml: What is the Harmonic Mean of two positive numbers if their Arithmetic Mean is 16 and their Geometric Mean is 8?
tcat-stat-195.explainHtml: For two numbers, GM2 = AM * HM. Therefore, HM = GM2 / AM = 82 / 16 = 64 / 16 = 4.

tcat-stat-196.qHtml: The sum of squared deviations sum(x_i - A)^2 is minimized if and only if the constant A is chosen to be:
optionsHtml: The Arithmetic Mean of the dataset
The Geometric Mean of the dataset
tcat-stat-196.explainHtml: A defining mathematical theorem of least squares states that sum(x_i - A)^2 attains its global minimum when A = Mean(x). (Sum of absolute deviations is minimized at the Median).

tcat-stat-197.qHtml: In a positively skewed frequency distribution, what is the relative positional order of the three classical averages from left to r along the x-axis?
tcat-stat-197.explainHtml: In positive (r) skewness, extreme high values pull the mean rightward the most, while the mode stays at the peak: Mode < Median < Mean.

tcat-stat-198.qHtml: Which fractile divides an ordered dataset such that 75% of observations lie below it and 25% lie above it?
tcat-stat-198.explainHtml: The Third Quartile (Q_3 or 75th percentile) partitions the upper 25% of the data from the lower 75%.

tcat-stat-199.qHtml: What is the range of the numerical dataset: 14, 28, 9, 35, 42, 17, 23?

tcat-stat-200.qHtml: What is the variance of a dataset where every single observed value is identical to a constant c = 5?
tcat-stat-200.explainHtml: If all observations are identical, there is zero variability; every deviation (x_i - mean) = 0, so the variance is strictly 0.

tcat-stat-201.qHtml: What is the mathematical relationship between the standard deviation (s) and variance (s2) of a sample?
optionsHtml: Standard deviation is the positive square root of the variance
Variance is the square root of the standard deviation
Standard deviation is half of the variance
Variance is double the standard deviation
tcat-stat-201.explainHtml: Standard deviation is defined as the positive square root of the variance: s = s^{2}.

tcat-stat-202.qHtml: Which dimensionless measure of relative dispersion is defined as the ratio of standard deviation to arithmetic mean expressed as a percentage?
tcat-stat-202.explainHtml: The Coefficient of Variation is CV = (s / mean) * 100%, providing a unitless measure of relative risk or dispersion.

tcat-stat-203.qHtml: Calculate the population standard deviation of the values: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 (where mean = 7):
optionsHtml: 8​ ≈ 2.83
10​ ≈ 3.16
tcat-stat-203.explainHtml: Squared deviations from 7: (3−7)2=16, (5−7)2=4, (7−7)2=0, (9−7)2=4, (11−7)2=16. Sum = 40. Variance = 40 / 5 = 8. SD = 8​ ≈ 2.83.

tcat-stat-204.qHtml: If the first and third quartiles of an income distribution are Q_1 = 30 and Q_3 = 70, what is the Semi-Interquartile Range (Quartile Deviation)?

tcat-stat-205.qHtml: If each observation in a dataset is increased by adding a constant 10, how does the standard deviation change?
optionsHtml: The standard deviation remains completely unchanged
The standard deviation is multiplied by 10
tcat-stat-205.explainHtml: Standard deviation is independent of changes of origin (adding or subtracting a constant); shifting data preserves all relative distances between points.

tcat-stat-206.qHtml: Product A has a mean lifespan of 500 hours with SD = 25 hours. Product B has a mean lifespan of 800 hours with SD = 32 hours. Which product exhibits higher relative consistency?
optionsHtml: Product B (CV = 4.0% vs Product A CV = 5.0%)
Product A (CV = 5.0% vs Product B CV = 4.0%)
Cannot be determined without sample size
tcat-stat-206.explainHtml: CV_A = (25 / 500) * 100% = 5.0%. CV_B = (32 / 800) * 100% = 4.0%. Lower CV indicates higher relative consistency, so Product B is more consistent.

tcat-stat-207.qHtml: What is the Mean Deviation about the mean for the dataset: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 (mean = 6)?

tcat-stat-208.qHtml: If the linear transformation y_i = -4 * x_i + 25 is applied to a dataset with variance Var(x) = 9, what is the variance of y?
tcat-stat-208.explainHtml: Variance under linear transformation: Var(a * x + b) = a2 * Var(x). Here a = -4, so Var(y) = (−4)2 * 9 = 16 * 9 = 144.

tcat-stat-209.qHtml: In a mesokurtic standard normal distribution, what are the theoretical values of the moment coefficients beta_1 (skewness) and beta_2 (kurtosis)?
tcat-stat-209.explainHtml: For a normal distribution: beta_1 = mu_3^2 / mu_2^3 = 0 (symmetric), and beta_2 = mu_4 / mu_2^2 = 3 (mesokurtic). Excess kurtosis is beta_2 - 3 = 0.

tcat-stat-210.qHtml: According to Chebyshev's inequality, what minimum proportion of any distribution must lie within k = 3 standard deviations of its mean?
tcat-stat-210.explainHtml: Chebyshev's theorem guarantees that P(|X - mu| < k * sigma) \ge 1 - 1/k2. For k = 3: 1 - 1/9 = 8/9 ≈ 88.89% for any arbitrary distribution.

tcat-stat-211.qHtml: For two independent samples with n_1 = 10, mean_1 = 50, s_1^2 = 16 and n_2 = 10, mean_2 = 50, s_2^2 = 25, what is the pooled variance s_p^2?

tcat-stat-212.qHtml: What is the probability of rolling a prime number on a single throw of a standard fair six-sided die?
tcat-stat-212.explainHtml: The prime outcomes on a six-sided die are {2, 3, 5}. Total outcomes = 6. P(Prime) = 3/6 = 1/2.

tcat-stat-213.qHtml: For two mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive events E_1 and E_2 defined on sample space S, what is the value of P(E_1) + P(E_2)?
tcat-stat-213.explainHtml: Collectively exhaustive events encompass all outcomes in sample space S (E_1 ∪ E_2 = S). Because they are disjoint, the addition axiom yields P(E_1) + P(E_2) = P(S) = 1.0.

tcat-stat-214.qHtml: If a fair coin is tossed 3 times independently, what is the probability of obtaining exactly 2 Heads?
tcat-stat-214.explainHtml: Using binomial probability: P(X = 2) = (23​)∗(1/2)2 * (1/2)1 = 3 * (1/8) = 3/8.

tcat-stat-215.qHtml: What is the expected value E(X) of a discrete random variable X having possible values {0, 1} with P(X=0) = 0.4 and P(X=1) = 0.6?
tcat-stat-215.explainHtml: E(X) = sum(x * P(x)) = (0 * 0.4) + (1 * 0.6) = 0 + 0.6 = 0.6 (the Bernoulli parameter p).

tcat-stat-216.qHtml: Two independent events A and B have probabilities P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.5. What is P(A ∪ B)?
tcat-stat-216.explainHtml: For independent events, P(A ∩ B) = P(A) * P(B) = 0.4 * 0.5 = 0.20. Then P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B) = 0.4 + 0.5 - 0.20 = 0.70.

tcat-stat-217.qHtml: In a Poisson distribution with mean parameter lambda = 4, what is the variance of the distribution?
tcat-stat-217.explainHtml: A signature property of the Poisson distribution is that its mean and variance are identical: Mean = lambda and Variance = lambda = 4.

tcat-stat-218.qHtml: In a standard normal distribution Z ~ N(0, 1), what percentage of total probability lies within the interval [-1, +1]?
tcat-stat-218.explainHtml: Under the empirical rule for normal curves, approximately 68.27% of total probability mass falls within 1 standard deviation of the mean (mu ± 1*sigma).

tcat-stat-219.qHtml: What is the variance of a Binomial random variable with n = 100 trials and probability of success p = 0.2?

tcat-stat-220.qHtml: A medical diagnostic test has 95% sensitivity (true positive) and 90% specificity (true negative). In a population with 2% disease prevalence, what is the posterior probability P(Disease | Positive) using Bayes' Theorem?

tcat-stat-221.qHtml: If continuous random variable X has probability density function f(x) = 2x for 0 \le x \le 1 (and 0 elsewhere), what is the expected value E(X)?
tcat-stat-221.explainHtml: E(X) = integral from 0 to 1 of x * f(x) dx = integral from 0 to 1 of 2x2 dx = [ (2/3) * x3 ]_0^1 = 2/3.

tcat-stat-222.qHtml: In a Hypergeometric distribution, sampling is conducted under which physical condition?
optionsHtml: Without replacement from a finite population of known size N
With replacement from an infinite population
tcat-stat-222.explainHtml: The Hypergeometric distribution models the number of successes in n draws without replacement from a finite population of size N containing M successes.

tcat-stat-223.qHtml: What is the moment-generating function (MGF) M_X(t) of an Exponential distribution with rate parameter lambda?
tcat-stat-223.explainHtml: M_X(t) = E(e^{tX}) = integral_0^inf e^{tx} * lambda * e^{-lambda*x} dx = lambda * integral_0^inf e^{-(lambda - t}x) dx = lambda / (lambda - t) for t < lambda.

tcat-stat-224.qHtml: If X and Y are independent random variables with Var(X) = 9 and Var(Y) = 16, what is the variance of the difference: Var(2X - 3Y)?
tcat-stat-224.explainHtml: For independent variables, Var(aX - bY) = a2 * Var(X) + b2 * Var(Y) = 22(9) + (−3)2(16) = 4(9) + 9(16) = 36 + 144 = 180.

tcat-stat-225.qHtml: A numerical characteristic calculated from a complete census of an entire population is called a:
tcat-stat-225.explainHtml: A parameter is a fixed numerical characteristic describing a population (e.g., mu, sigma), whereas a statistic is computed from a sample.

tcat-stat-226.qHtml: Which sampling technique guarantees that every possible sample of size n has an equal probability of selection?
tcat-stat-226.explainHtml: Simple Random Sampling (SRS) ensures that every individual unit and every possible sample subset of size n has an identical, non-zero probability of being selected.

tcat-stat-227.qHtml: What is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a sample statistic formally called?
tcat-stat-227.explainHtml: The standard deviation of a sampling distribution (such as the distribution of sample means) is specifically designated as the Standard Error.

tcat-stat-228.qHtml: What happens to the Standard Error of the sample mean (sigma / n​) when the sample size n is quadrupled (multiplied by 4)?
tcat-stat-228.explainHtml: Because Standard Error = sigma / n​, replacing n with 4n gives sigma / 4n​ = (1/2) * (sigma / n​), cutting the standard error in half.

tcat-stat-229.qHtml: According to the Central Limit Theorem (CLT), as sample size n becomes sufficiently large (typically n \ge 30), what form does the sampling distribution of the sample mean assume?
optionsHtml: Approaches a Normal distribution regardless of the underlying population shape
Matches the exact skewness of the parent population
Collapses to a single deterministic point
tcat-stat-229.explainHtml: The CLT establishes that the sampling distribution of the mean tends toward a normal distribution as n increases, even if the parent population is non-normal.

tcat-stat-230.qHtml: In sampling without replacement from a finite population of size N, what multiplier must be applied to the variance of the sample mean?
tcat-stat-230.explainHtml: When sampling without replacement from a finite population N, the variance is scaled by the Finite Population Correction (FPC) factor: (N - n) / (N - 1).

tcat-stat-231.qHtml: When a population is heterogeneous overall but consists of homogeneous sub-groups, which sampling method yields the most representative sample?
tcat-stat-231.explainHtml: Stratified Random Sampling divides a heterogeneous population into mutually exclusive homogeneous strata and samples randomly within each stratum, reducing variance.

tcat-stat-232.qHtml: If a population has standard deviation sigma = 20 and a random sample of size n = 64 is drawn, what is the Standard Error of the mean?
tcat-stat-232.explainHtml: SE = sigma / n​ = 20 / 64​ = 20 / 8 = 2.5.

tcat-stat-233.qHtml: An estimator T of a population parameter theta is defined as "unbiased" if and only if:
tcat-stat-233.explainHtml: An estimator is unbiased if its mathematical expected value equals the true population parameter being estimated: E(T) = theta.

tcat-stat-234.qHtml: Why is the sample variance formula s2 divided by (n - 1) rather than n?
optionsHtml: To correct for downward bias and make s2 an unbiased estimator of population variance sigma^{2}
To account for measurement instrument uncertainty
Because one degree of freedom is lost to the population median
To ensure standard deviation equals the mean deviation
tcat-stat-234.explainHtml: Dividing by n underestimates sigma2 because deviations are taken from sample mean x_bar rather than true population mean mu. Bessel's correction (dividing by n - 1) makes E(s2) = sigma2.

tcat-stat-235.qHtml: If X_1, X_2, ..., X_k are independent standard normal random variables Z_i ~ N(0, 1), what distribution does the sum of their squares sum(Z_i^2) follow?
optionsHtml: Chi-Square distribution with k degrees of freedom
Student's t-distribution with k degrees of freedom
Snedecor's F-distribution with (k, 1) degrees of freedom
tcat-stat-235.explainHtml: By definition, the sum of k independent squared standard normal random variables follows a Chi-Square distribution with k degrees of freedom: sum(Z_i^2) ~ Chi2(k).

tcat-stat-236.qHtml: What sampling distribution arises from the ratio: Z / Y/nu​, where Z ~ N(0, 1) and Y ~ Chi2(nu) are independent random variables?
optionsHtml: Student's t-distribution with nu degrees of freedom
F-distribution with (1, nu) degrees of freedom
Gamma distribution with scale parameter nu
tcat-stat-236.explainHtml: Gosset's Student's t-distribution is mathematically defined as the ratio of a standard normal variable Z to the square root of an independent chi-square variable divided by its degrees of freedom.

tcat-stat-237.qHtml: According to the Rao-Blackwell theorem, how can an existing unbiased estimator of a parameter be improved?
optionsHtml: By conditioning the estimator upon a sufficient statistic
By taking the reciprocal of its variance
By multiplying it by Bessel's degrees of freedom factor
By increasing the confidence interval width to 99%
tcat-stat-237.explainHtml: The Rao-Blackwell theorem proves that conditioning any unbiased estimator on a sufficient statistic produces an estimator whose variance is less than or equal to the original estimator.

tcat-stat-238.qHtml: In statistical hypothesis testing, what error is committed when a true null hypothesis H_0 is incorrectly rejected?
tcat-stat-238.explainHtml: A Type I error occurs when the researcher rejects the null hypothesis H_0 when H_0 is in fact true (probability designated as alpha, the significance level).

tcat-stat-239.qHtml: What is the theoretical range of values for Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient r?
tcat-stat-239.explainHtml: Pearson's correlation coefficient r is bounded strictly between -1 (perfect negative linear relationship) and +1 (perfect positive linear relationship).

tcat-stat-240.qHtml: In the simple linear regression equation Y = beta_0 + beta_1 * X, what does beta_1 physically represent?
optionsHtml: The slope: change in Y for a one-unit increase in X
tcat-stat-240.explainHtml: beta_1 is the regression slope, representing the expected marginal change in response variable Y corresponding to a single unit increase in predictor variable X.

tcat-stat-241.qHtml: What does a p-value less than the chosen significance level (p < 0.05) indicate in a hypothesis test?
optionsHtml: Reject the null hypothesis H_0 in favor of the alternative hypothesis H_1
Fail to reject the null hypothesis H_0
Accept the null hypothesis as proven beyond doubt
The test is invalid due to high variance
tcat-stat-241.explainHtml: When the observed p-value is less than the pre-set significance threshold alpha, the observed sample evidence is sufficiently extreme under H_0 to reject the null hypothesis.

tcat-stat-242.qHtml: If the two linear regression coefficients between X and Y are b_yx = 0.8 and b_xy = 0.45, what is the value of Pearson's correlation coefficient r?
